result.text: The paper addresses Generalized Category Discovery (GCD), where a model must recognize both known classes from labeled data and novel classes within unlabeled data, and identifies that existing methods couple learning of known and novel categories which harms generalization and prevents explicit transfer of category-specific knowledge. The key insight is to decouple the treatment of known and novel categories while explicitly aligning prototypes of known classes across labeled and unlabeled domains, enabling targeted training objectives for each group and preserving high-level semantic information. The proposed Decoupled Prototypical Network (DPN) formulates prototype alignment as a bipartite matching problem to pair known-class prototypes between datasets, and introduces Semantic-aware Prototypical Learning (SPL) that uses semantic-weighted soft assignments to produce discriminative features and reduce noisy hard pseudo-labels for both known and novel categories. Extensive experiments demonstrate that this decoupled, prototype-aligned approach substantially outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods on multiple benchmarks.

result.text: The paper tackles the lack of disease-aware generative models that can synthesize multi-view (multi-lead) ECG signals reflecting specific heart conditions, which limits data augmentation, privacy-preserving data sharing, and downstream diagnostic training. Its key insight is to learn a panoptic electrocardio latent representation conditioned on disease labels and to precisely inject disease-specific waveform changes at localized signal regions, while enforcing correct view-specific morphology across leads. The method, ME-GAN, implements a disease-conditioned GAN that uses a novel "mixup normalization" to inject condition information into appropriate temporal locations, projects the learned representation to multiple standard ECG views, and trains with a view discriminator that reorders shuffled leads to supervise accurate view characteristics; they also introduce rFID as a metric to evaluate synthesized ECG quality and show that ME-GAN generates multi-view signals with faithful morbid manifestations.

result.text: The paper addresses how to choose model size to minimize loss given a fixed compute (FLOP) budget in the infinite-data regime by analyzing a solvable three-parameter neural scaling model (data complexity, target complexity, and parameter count). The key insight is that compute-optimal scaling is governed by distinct regimes where model capacity, optimizer noise, and feature embedding dominate, producing four main phases and three subphases in the data/target-complexity plane that each admit different scaling exponents for loss and optimal parameter count. Methodologically, the authors train the model with one-pass SGD on mean-squared loss to derive an analytic representation of loss curves valid for all iteration counts (and asymptotically exact as parameter count grows), then analyze these formulas to identify phase boundaries and prove—supported by extensive numerics—the closed-form scaling-law exponents and the optimal model-parameter-count as a function of FLOP budget.

The paper addresses whether large pretrained language models can perform complex multi-step reasoning without task-specific few-shot exemplars, challenging the assumption that chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting requires example demonstrations. result.text: The paper investigates whether sarcasm detection in large language models is best approached as a step-by-step reasoning process or as a holistic cue integration task, motivated by the view that human sarcasm understanding may be non-sequential. The key insight is that different prompting schemas—sequential (chain of contradiction, CoC) and structured/non-sequential (graph of cues, GoC; bagging of cues, BoC; tensor of cues, ToC)—elicit complementary reasoning behaviors in LLMs, with larger models favoring sequential-like strategies while smaller models benefit more from richly structured, non-sequential cue aggregation. Methodologically, the authors introduce SarcasmCue, implement the four sub-methods to extract and combine linguistic, contextual, and emotional cues, and perform a comprehensive empirical comparison on four benchmarks, showing CoC/GoC improve performance for advanced models, ToC dramatically helps smaller models, and the framework consistently advances state-of-the-art F1 scores across datasets.

The key insight is that creating a trigger that maximizes the feature gap between poisoned and benign samples and embedding it as imperceptible attractive and repulsive perturbations lets the model learn both benign and trigger features without obvious artifacts, resolving the overfitting-stealth trade-off. result.text: This paper tackles the problem of crafting transferable adversarial perturbations for complex natural scenes containing multiple semantically related objects, where prior attacks have largely focused on single-object images and single-object classifiers. The key insight is that leveraging joint image-text representations from a pre-trained vision-language model (CLIP) allows modeling inter-object semantics and yields stronger, more transferable perturbations than image-only generative attacks. The method, called GAMA, trains a generative perturbation network adversarially using CLIP’s joint image-text features as the objective (rather than only visual logits), so the generator learns to produce perturbations that disrupt semantic alignment across objects and transfer to unknown victim classifiers and data distributions. Empirically, GAMA substantially improves black-box misclassification rates—about 16% higher than prior generative approaches—demonstrating CLIP’s utility as an attacker tool for multi-object scene attacks.

result.text: The paper addresses how to learn disentangled representations from observations that come in pairs sharing some underlying generative factors, aiming to avoid requiring strong supervision like labeled factors or group annotations. The key insight is that knowing only that two paired images share at least one factor — and in theory even just the count of changed factors — provides enough weak supervision to identify disentangled latents without labeling which factors changed. result.text: The paper addresses dataset distillation: how to compress large training sets into a tiny synthetic dataset that still trains models well, which is increasingly important as models and data grow. The key insight is that infinitely wide convolutional neural networks can be analyzed via their corresponding kernel (the neural tangent/kernel regime), and that performing distillation in this kernel/meta-learning framework yields more faithful and transferable synthetic examples than prior methods. Methodologically, the authors develop a distributed kernel-based meta-learning algorithm that optimizes a small set of synthetic images by matching kernel-predicted model behavior (or gradients) on the full data, and demonstrate dramatic gains—e.g., 10 distilled CIFAR-10 images achieving >65% accuracy—across MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10/100 and SVHN, along with analyses comparing distilled and natural data.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem that Natural Language Inference (NLI) models pick up dataset-specific biases and spurious artifacts that hurt generalization to unseen datasets. Its key insight is that instead of merely trying to prevent bias learning, teaching models to mimic how humans solve NLI—via natural language explanations—can guide them to attend to genuinely informative features that generalize better. The method supervises the model’s attention weights using human explanations by encouraging higher attention on explanation-relevant words (especially in the premise) and lower attention on punctuation and stopwords, which yields both in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance gains. Experimental analysis shows that this attention supervision shifts focus to important tokens and improves robustness across different NLI datasets.

result.text: The paper tackles fast, high-quality 3D object generation from multi-view or single-image inputs without requiring 3D supervision, focusing on probabilistic modeling of unseen object parts and sharp texture synthesis. The key insight is to integrate a transformer-based 3D large reconstruction model that represents scenes as a triplane NeRF and performs denoising in the 3D reconstruction-rendering loop, so multi-view diffusion noise can be removed in a geometry-aware manner. The method trains this model on large-scale multi-view image datasets using only image reconstruction losses, and uses the trained model to denoise noisy multi-view images (or single-image-conditioned noises) via NeRF reconstruction and differentiable rendering, enabling single-stage 3D generation in ~30s on a single A100 GPU. Empirically, DMV3D achieves state-of-the-art single-image reconstruction and text-to-3D results, producing diverse, sharp-textured reconstructions that outperform prior 3D diffusion approaches.

result.text: The paper addresses shortcomings in the standard microfoundations used for modeling strategic agents in binary classification, showing that assuming perfectly rational, fully informed manipulators yields discontinuous aggregate responses, destroys the existence of desirable stable points when any agents are non-strategic, and drives classifiers to maximize social burden. Its key insight is that these brittle outcomes stem from idealized agent behavior assumptions, and that introducing modest, structured imperfections in responses both matches empirical observations and restores robustness. Methodologically, the authors articulate desiderata for plausible response models, analyze constraints on feature manipulations that guarantee stable points, and introduce a tractable noisy response model—inspired by smoothed analysis—that injects stochasticity into agent reactions, proving it preserves analytic tractability while ensuring robust existence of equilibria and reducing social burden at optimal classifiers.

result.text: The paper addresses fine-grained visual classification where subtle intra-class and inter-class variations and diverse object contexts make it hard to mine discriminative parts without part or bounding-box annotations. The key insight is that attending to informative integral regions while modeling their spatial and semantic consistency—using sub-pixel gradient information—lets a network capture subtle, context-aware differences that distinguish subcategories. The method, Context-aware Attentional Pooling (CAP), is a lightweight module that learns attention over integral image regions and encodes the consistency between region informativeness and spatial structure into feature representations, and can be plugged on top of standard CNN backbones; experiments on eight benchmarks with six backbones show substantial gains over state-of-the-art methods.

The paper tackles the paucity of formalized mathematical training data for teaching large language models to work with proof assistant languages (Lean 4), aiming to bridge the gap between natural-language math problems and formal theorem statements and proofs. Its key insight is that an iterative generate-and-filter synthetic-data pipeline—alternating automated translation between informal problems and formal Lean statements and applying filtering/search to validate and improve outputs—can scale high-quality parallel corpora even when human-labeled formal data are scarce. The method builds this pipeline to produce, verify, and augment synthetic formal-informal question pairs, incorporates searched proofs from a math contest forum, and adds new IMO problems to yield a 57K-pair dataset; experiments show this synthetic data improves LLM performance on Lean translation and understanding tasks.

result.text: The paper investigates two fundamental limitations of graph neural networks (GNNs): their representational limits when restricted to purely local information and their generalization behavior in data-dependent settings. The key insight is that any GNN that computes node representations solely from local neighborhoods—including standard message-passing models and stronger spatial variants that use local ordering or orientations—cannot distinguish or compute certain global graph properties, a fact formalized via a new graph-theoretic framework. Complementing this negative result, the authors derive the first data-dependent generalization bounds for message-passing GNNs that explicitly incorporate their local permutation invariance, yielding much tighter guarantees than prior VC-dimension analyses and comparable tightness to Rademacher bounds for recurrent networks. Together, these contributions delineate both what local GNNs cannot learn and how reliably they generalize when trained on graph data.

result.text: This paper studies regret minimization in latent Markov Decision Processes (LMDPs), where an episode samples one of M possible MDPs unknown to the agent, and shows that without structure learning an optimal policy can be intractable. The key insight is that learning is feasible in polynomial time when the underlying MDPs exhibit sufficient separation in their dynamics (or under PSR-style statistical sufficiency and reachability), which enables identification or discrimination of latent models. Methodologically, the authors prove a worst-case exponential lower bound Ω((SA)^M) for general LMDPs, then design an efficient algorithm that, given a good initialization, achieves sublinear (local) regret under the separation condition, and further extend the approach to remove the initialization requirement by leveraging PSR assumptions and reachability to obtain global regret guarantees.

result.text: The paper tackles self-supervised representation learning for audio by adapting image-based Masked Autoencoders (MAE) to spectrograms, aiming to learn strong audio features without supervised pretraining. The key insight is that high-ratio masking combined with an encoder-decoder MAE adapted to audio — notably by adding local window attention in the decoder to exploit strong local time–frequency correlations — yields rich contextual representations that transfer well to downstream audio and speech tasks. The method splits spectrograms into patches, feeds only unmasked tokens through a Transformer encoder, then reorders and decodes the encoded context padded with mask tokens to reconstruct the full spectrogram, and finally fine-tunes the encoder with lower masking on target datasets; this simple extension achieves state-of-the-art results on six classification benchmarks.

result.text: The paper examines whether commonly-used (first-order) influence functions, which estimate how individual training samples affect test predictions using gradients and the Hessian, remain reliable for non-convex deep neural networks. The key insight is that influence estimates are not generally robust in deep learning: their accuracy depends strongly on architecture, depth/width, degree of overparameterization, regularization (notably weight decay), and even which test point is analyzed, so methods that work for convex linear models can fail widely in non-convex settings. To support this, the authors run a comprehensive empirical study across datasets (Iris, MNIST, CIFAR-10, ImageNet) and model families, measuring when first-order influence approximations match true retraining effects and showing systematic breakdowns for deeper networks, improvements with weight decay in some cases, and large per-example variability—leading them to conclude that influence functions are fragile in neural networks and that better influence estimation methods are needed.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of obtaining generalization guarantees for learning algorithms that minimize Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR), a coherent risk measure used as an alternative to expectation for robustness, regularization, and fairness. The key insight is that estimating CVaR can be reduced to estimating an ordinary expectation of an auxiliary truncated/shifted loss, which lets one leverage PAC-Bayesian techniques developed for expectations to control CVaR. Concretely, the authors derive a PAC-Bayesian generalization bound showing that if the empirical CVaR is small then the true CVaR is small with high probability, by expressing CVaR as an expectation of a hinge-like transformation and applying PAC-Bayesian concentration to that transformed variable; as a by-product they also obtain concentration inequalities for CVaR even for unbounded losses.

The paper tackles building a single scalable model that can jointly understand and generate across vision and many languages, addressing limitations of prior work that scaled language far more than vision and lacked a unified multilingual multimodal interface. The key insight is that jointly scaling both vision and language components and leveraging large pretrained encoder–decoder LMs together with much larger vision backbones improves multimodal capabilities, so a balanced increase in visual capacity yields substantial gains. The method constructs PaLI by combining large pretrained language models with a newly trained 4B-parameter Vision Transformer (ViT-e), training on a massive multilingual image–text mixture (≈10 billion image–text pairs across 100+ languages) with a unified text-generation interface for tasks like captioning, VQA, and scene-text understanding. The resulting model is simple and modular yet achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple vision–language benchmarks while demonstrating the importance of joint scaling.

result.text: The paper addresses the gap between known guarantees for envy-freeness relaxations for indivisible goods—EF1 (always achievable) and the stronger but elusive EFX (existence unknown)—by proposing an intermediate fairness notion and algorithmic guarantees. The key insight is that a probabilistic relaxation, envy-freeness up to a random good (EFR), sits strictly between EF1 and EFX and can be approximated better than known bounds for EFX by leveraging connections to Nash Social Welfare (NSW). Methodologically, the authors define EFR and design a polynomial-time algorithm that constructs allocations via a Nash Social Welfare Matching approach, proving it achieves a 0.73-approximation to EFR and thereby demonstrating a constructive tradeoff between fairness strength and achievable guarantees.

result.text: The paper addresses improving solution quality and scalability of the classical Lin–Kernighan–Helsgaun (LKH) heuristic for the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) by leveraging learned guidance. Its key insight is that a neural model can predict useful edge scores and node penalties that meaningfully reshape LKH’s search (via candidate sets and transformed distances), so that learned priors direct the powerful local search rather than replace it. The method trains a Sparse Graph Network (SGN) with supervised loss for edge scoring and an unsupervised objective for node penalties, uses SGN outputs to construct candidate edge sets and modify edge distances, and then runs LKH on these guided inputs; experiments show a single model trained across sizes improves LKH’s performance and generalizes to much larger TSP instances and related routing problems.

They propose Sequence Likelihood Calibration (SLiC), a training procedure that adjusts likelihoods of model-generated sequences to align with reference sequences—improving ranking of candidates, removing the need for heuristic decoding fixes, and scaling effectively with model size. Empirically, SLiC boosts generation quality across diverse conditional tasks (summarization, question generation, QA, data-to-text), matching or exceeding state-of-the-art even with modest models and limited compute.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of adapting very large pretrained language models to downstream tasks in a parameter- and sample-efficient way, avoiding the instability and storage costs of full fine-tuning. Its key insight is to combine adapter-style task-specific weights with low-rank and hypercomplex (Kronecker-product) structure so that many layer-specific parameters can be generated from a small set of shared components. The proposed Compacter method inserts compact task-specific weight matrices into a pretrained model, where each such matrix is formed as a sum of Kronecker products between shared "slow" tensors and per-layer "fast" rank-one factors, enabling efficient computation and extreme parameter reduction. With only about 0.047% of model parameters trained, Compacter matches or outperforms full fine-tuning on GLUE, SuperGLUE, and low-resource settings.

result.text: The paper tackles the computational intractability of the Projection Robust Wasserstein (PRW) distance—a robust variant of the Wasserstein distance designed to compare high-dimensional probability measures but hindered by a non-convex, non-smooth optimization formulation. Its key insight is that, despite theoretical minimax hardness results, the original PRW/WPP formulation can be practically and efficiently optimized by exploiting the low-dimensional search structure through Riemannian optimization on the Grassmann manifold, often outperforming convex relaxations. The authors propose three simple Riemannian algorithms (with provable complexity bounds for each) that directly optimize the projection subspace and transport plan, and validate their approach with extensive synthetic and real-data experiments showing improved robustness and computational efficiency. This work thus establishes a practical computational framework linking optimal transport and Riemannian optimization and provides the first concrete complexity guarantees for computing PRW.

Its key insight is that carefully chosen matrix factorizations (private linear operators) tailored to the adaptive stream can minimize added noise while preserving privacy, and that optimal factorizations can be found via a parameter-free fixed-point computation. The authors prove theoretical results on when and how matrix factorizations apply to adaptive streams, provide the fixed-point algorithm for computing optimal factorizations, and demonstrate the approach on natural matrices from machine learning to train user-level differentially private models, achieving significant empirical improvements.

Its key insight is that without prior structural knowledge of the data distribution, backdoor patterns can be indistinguishable from legitimate predictive features—making general-purpose detection impossible—and thus defenses implicitly rely on latent assumptions. Empirically, this method proves effective, and the analysis clarifies which assumptions underpin prior defenses and when they succeed or fail.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of learning flexible, tractable meta-distributions over functions for tasks like regression and Bayesian inference, improving on limitations of existing neural process methods. The key insight is to combine denoising diffusion generative modeling with architectural inductive biases for stochastic processes—specifically exchangeability—so the model directly learns to sample finite marginals of function-valued distributions. The proposed method, Neural Diffusion Processes (NDPs), uses a diffusion-based generation scheme together with a custom attention block that enforces permutation invariance and other process properties, training the model to reverse a noising process on function values conditioned on inputs. Empirically, NDPs closely approximate true Bayesian posteriors (e.g., emulating Gaussian processes), outperform neural processes, and support tasks like implicit hyperparameter marginalization, non-Gaussian posterior prediction, and global optimization.

result.text: The paper addresses understanding and unifying policy gradient methods by formalizing them as the repeated application of two operators: a policy improvement operator I that outputs an improved (possibly unrepresentable) policy and a projection operator P that maps that improved policy back into the class of realizable parameterized policies. The key insight is that many policy-gradient algorithms can be interpreted as alternating I and P, which clarifies how approximation and optimization interact and links policy-based updates to value-based operators (e.g., showing REINFORCE and the Bellman optimality operator are conceptually related). Methodologically, the authors derive operator-based variants of standard algorithms (REINFORCE, PPO) within this I–P framework, analyze properties such as performance bounds, and introduce a new global lower bound on expected return that follows from the operator decomposition, thereby providing both theoretical insights and practical algorithmic reformulations.

result.text: The paper addresses why value baselines help on-policy stochastic policy gradient methods and closes theoretical gaps explaining their empirical benefits, particularly for natural policy gradient (NPG). The key insight is that baselines do not primarily work by reducing variance of gradient estimates—in fact variance can remain unbounded—but instead by tempering the aggressiveness of policy updates, which prevents optimal actions' probabilities from vanishing and ensures sufficient exploration. Methodologically, the authors prove that with a state-value baseline the expected NPG progress satisfies a stochastic non-uniform Łojasiewicz inequality and that the baseline guarantees almost-sure prevention of action-probability collapse, yielding global O(1/t) convergence to the optimal policy; empirical experiments corroborate that controlling update aggressiveness, not variance, explains the baseline’s utility.

result.text: The paper addresses multimodal fake news detection, aiming to overcome shallow fusion of modalities and insufficient modeling of cross-modal inconsistencies. Its key insight is to mimic diverse human "reading habits" to guide deeper, cognition-aware fusion of multimodal features and to explicitly reason about semantic coherence and deviation between modalities (including user comments) to expose inconsistencies indicative of falsehood. The proposed Multi-Reading Habits Fusion Reasoning (MRHFR) network implements a cognition-aware fusion layer that learns dependencies among visual, textual, and other modal representations according to three distilled reading habits, and a coherence-constraint reasoning layer that measures semantic consistency between comments and each modality and constrains unimodal-induced deviations from the multimodal content. Experiments on two public datasets show MRHFR improves detection performance and offers a new paradigm for capturing multimodal inconsistencies.

result.text: The paper addresses the lack of realistic datasets for predicting hardware performance of complete tensor programs—i.e., full computational graphs of ML workloads—on accelerators, which limits the ability of compilers and autotuners to optimize end-to-end models. Its key insight is that using whole-program TPU graphs collected from real open-source models (ResNet, EfficientNet, Mask R-CNN, Transformer, etc.) yields a substantially more realistic and challenging prediction task than prior kernel- or block-level datasets, exposing scalability and learning-efficiency issues that matter in practice. The authors introduce TpuGraphs, a dataset of computational graphs paired with compilation configurations and measured execution times on TPUs, providing orders-of-magnitude more and much larger graphs than previous benchmarks to enable graph-level performance prediction research. By framing prediction at the graph level and supplying diverse, large-scale examples, TpuGraphs aims to drive development of scalable models and techniques for compiler/autotuner-informed optimization of real ML workloads.

result.text: The paper addresses the difficulty of systematically evaluating autonomous driving (AD) systems under rare, safety-critical conditions by pointing out that existing testing efforts are fragmented across different simulators, scenario types, and generation methods, making fair comparison and large-scale safety assessment infeasible. Its key insight is that a unified, extensible benchmarking platform that standardizes scenario types, generation algorithms, route and environment variations, and agent inputs enables apples-to-apples comparisons and more effective discovery of challenging test cases. The authors present SafeBench, a platform that integrates diverse safety-critical scenarios and generation techniques, implements four deep reinforcement learning–based AD agents with four input modalities, and provides tooling to generate and evaluate large-scale adversarial or distribution-shift test cases. Using SafeBench, they demonstrate that their generated scenarios are more challenging than baseline sets and reveal trade-offs between agent performance in benign versus safety-critical conditions, highlighting the need for improved testing and safer AD algorithms.

result.text: The paper addresses how to reliably predict the benefits of increasing model, dataset, or compute scale by revisiting empirical neural scaling laws and correcting weaknesses in prior fitting practices. Its key insight is that fitting scaling laws should minimize extrapolation loss—performance on held-out, larger-scale regimes—rather than merely optimizing interpolation to observed points, because that yields more trustworthy forecasts of performance at scales beyond the data. The authors propose a practical recipe for estimating scaling-law parameters from learning curves (including procedures for model selection, data splitting, and loss computation) and show across image classification, NMT, language modeling, and BIG-Bench tasks that their method extrapolates more accurately than previous approaches; they also release a 90-task benchmark to standardize future evaluations.

result.text: The paper addresses optimization for performative prediction, where deploying a model changes the future data distribution through agents' responses, distinguishing deployment from mere parameter updates. The key insight is that performativity creates a trade-off between updating frequently (which causes repeated distribution shifts) and updating lazily (which accumulates optimization error under a fixed distribution), and that this trade-off depends on the strength of performative effects. Under smoothness and strong convexity assumptions, the authors analyze two strategies—greedy deploy (deploy after every stochastic update) and lazy deploy (perform multiple updates per deployment)—and derive non-asymptotic convergence rates that interpolate to the standard O(1/k) rate as performativity vanishes, identifying regimes where each strategy is preferable; they validate these theoretical findings with synthetic and strategic-classification experiments.

result.text: The paper addresses defending against poisoning-based backdoor attacks when training data or models come from untrusted sources by identifying and removing poisoned samples. The key insight is that feature representations of poisoned (triggered) samples are more sensitive to input transformations than clean samples, so measuring feature consistency towards transformations (FCT) reliably distinguishes poisoned from clean data. Extensive experiments on coarse- and fine-grained target domains show substantial gains over prior methods, with average improvements up to 7.71% and 25.91% respectively.

result.text: Magic123 tackles single-image 3D object reconstruction by generating high-quality, textured meshes from an unposed image using both 2D and 3D diffusion priors. The method implements this “expert choice” routing within heterogeneous MoEs, compares it to prior top-1 and top-2 gating schemes under equal computational budgets, and demonstrates that expert choice yields over 2× faster pretraining convergence and better downstream fine-tuning performance on GLUE/SuperGLUE tasks, and even outperforms a dense T5 baseline on several tasks at lower activation cost.

result.text: The paper addresses whether standard Transformer architectures, without any graph-specific modifications, can serve as effective and expressive graph learners. The key insight is that by treating nodes and edges as independent tokens with appropriate token embeddings, a plain Transformer can match the expressivity of invariant graph networks (2-IGNs)—which are already strictly more powerful than message-passing GNNs—thereby overcoming perceived limitations of Transformers on graph-structured data. The method, called Tokenized Graph Transformer (TokenGT), converts each node and edge into tokens augmented with learned embeddings and feeds them to an unmodified Transformer; the authors prove theoretical expressivity equivalence to 2-IGNs and empirically validate TokenGT on the large-scale PCQM4Mv2 dataset, showing it outperforms GNN baselines and rivals specialized graph Transformer variants.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of efficient object-goal navigation in novel, visually realistic environments by learning semantic cues and layout regularities without access to action or goal labels, using only passive YouTube video data. The key insight is that off-policy Q-learning can be applied to pseudo-labeled transition quadruples (image, action, next image, reward) extracted from unannotated videos to discover useful semantic affordances and spatial priors for navigation despite suboptimal or unlabeled behavior. The method constructs approximate action and reward labels from video frame transitions, trains Q-functions on these passive transitions, and incorporates the learned semantic cues into a hierarchical navigation policy that selects subgoals and low-level controls. This approach yields much more efficient object-goal navigation in simulation—improving over end-to-end RL by 66% while requiring roughly 250× fewer environment interactions.

result.text: The paper tackles shortcomings in Composed Image Retrieval (CoIR), namely the scarcity and quality issues of existing datasets and the challenge of effectively fusing image and text queries. Its key insight is that scaling dataset size and diagnosing modality redundancy can substantially boost CoIR performance and that early cross-attention fusion with an auxiliary task yields stronger representations. To that end the authors introduce LaSCo, a new CoIR dataset an order of magnitude larger than prior sets, propose an analysis method to detect when image or text modalities are redundant or necessary in queries, and present CASE (Cross-Attention driven Shift Encoder), a baseline that fuses modalities early via cross-attention and uses an auxiliary training objective. Pretraining on LaSCo and using CASE leads to significant gains, including improved zero-shot performance and state-of-the-art results on benchmarks like FashionIQ and CIRR.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of detecting seizure events and the specific EEG channels involved without relying on scarce, costly labeled seizure data by formulating anomalous channel and clip detection as a self-supervised problem. Its key insight is that local structural and contextual patterns in EEG can be captured via sub-graphs, and contrasting positive (normal) and negative sub-graphs lets a model learn discriminative representations of normal brain activity so anomalies (seizures) stand out at test time. The method builds EEG graphs from channel relationships, samples local sub-graphs as positive and negative pairs, and trains a model with a combination of contrastive and generative losses to learn normal EEG dynamics; at inference, deviations from the learned normal manifold identify seizure channels and clips. Evaluated on the largest seizure dataset, this approach outperforms prior supervised and unsupervised methods while requiring no seizure examples during training.

result.text: The paper addresses the limitation of standard parameter-space regularization in neural network training, which makes it difficult to encode explicit preferences about the desired predictive functions and thus limits control over generalization and uncertainty. The key insight is to reinterpret parameter-space regularization as specifying an empirical prior over parameters and extend this view to directly regularize in function space via a function-space empirical Bayes (FSEB) approach, thereby allowing priors to express beliefs about predictive functions rather than only about parameters. Methodologically, FSEB combines parameter- and function-space regularization by constructing an empirical prior informed by observed function behavior (e.g., on inputs or pre-trained models) and incorporating it into optimization as a simple additional regularizer that is computationally light and easy to implement. Empirically, the paper shows that FSEB yields near-perfect semantic shift detection, better-calibrated uncertainties, improved adaptation from pre-trained models, and more robust generalization under covariate shift.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem that existing iterative preference-optimization methods improve general instruction following but fail to substantially boost multi-step reasoning performance; the authors aim to better select and refine Chain-of-Thought (CoT) traces that lead to correct answers. Their key insight is to directly optimize preferences over competing CoT candidates by emphasizing the winning versus losing reasoning steps that causally lead to the correct answer, and that combining a DPO-style preference loss with an additional negative log-likelihood term is crucial to steer the model toward correct reasoning trajectories. Methodologically, they iteratively generate multiple CoT samples, label winners and losers according to answer correctness, and train the model with a modified DPO objective plus an NLL term to increase probability of winning steps and decrease that of losing steps; repeated iterations yield steady reasoning improvements. Empirically, this procedure—applied to Llama-2-70B-Chat using only in-dataset examples—substantially raises accuracy on GSM8K, MATH, and ARC-Challenge (e.g., GSM8K from 55.6% to 81.6%, and 88.7% with 32-sample majority voting).

result.text: The paper addresses how to design a general, powerful, and scalable graph Transformer that overcomes the limited expressivity and quadratic cost of prior GTs and works across small and very large graphs. Its key insight is that decoupling local real-edge aggregation (message-passing) from a global fully-connected Transformer attention, combined with carefully chosen positional/structural encodings, yields a model that is both expressive (universal approximator on graphs) and can run in linear time O(N+E). Practically, the authors present a modular recipe—GraphGPS—comprising (i) local, global or relative positional encodings, (ii) a local message-passing module for sparse edge-based aggregation, and (iii) a global attention module for long-range interactions, and implement combinations of these components to achieve state-of-the-art or highly competitive results on 16 benchmarks.

Their results position kNN and rNN as simple, strong baselines for future certified defenses against poisoning and backdoor attacks.

result.text: The paper addresses the persistent problem of tuning SGD learning rates by proposing a parameter-free dynamic step size schedule called Distance over Gradients (DoG) that requires no hand-tuned "learning rate" hyperparameter. The key insight is that meaningful step sizes can be computed from simple, empirically available quantities—the distance from the current iterate to the initialization and the norms of observed gradients—yielding a scale-adaptive rule that automatically shrinks as optimization progresses. Methodologically, the authors derive a DoG formula (and a slight variant) and prove parameter-free convergence guarantees for stochastic convex optimization under only locally bounded stochastic gradients, then empirically evaluate DoG and a per-layer DoG on a wide range of vision and language transfer tasks to show performance close to tuned SGD and, in the per-layer case, often better than tuned SGD and approaching tuned Adam.

result.text: HateXplain addresses the need for interpretable and less biased hate speech detection by providing a multi-perspective benchmark that augments traditional 3-way labels (hate, offensive, normal) with target-community annotations and human rationales indicating text spans supporting each label. The key insight is that evaluating and training models with human-provided rationales reveals gaps between classification accuracy and explainability (plausibility and faithfulness), and that incorporating rationales can mitigate unintended bias toward protected communities. The authors collect and release the HateXplain dataset, evaluate state-of-the-art models on classification and explainability metrics, and show empirically that rationale-informed training improves explainability and reduces bias compared to models trained only on class labels.

result.text: The paper addresses the limited expressiveness and depth restrictions of standard Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), which typically use non-negative, channel-shared propagation operators and therefore can neither learn diverse channel-wise filters nor avoid over-smoothing as depth increases. result.text: The paper addresses fast, high-quality single-image 3D reconstruction, avoiding slow per-shape optimization and poor geometry/consistency of prior diffusion-guided NeRF approaches. The method runs in a single feed-forward pass: generate multi-view images from the input, feed them into the pretrained SDF reconstructor that enforces geometric consistency and surface priors, and produce a full textured mesh without per-shape optimization. result.text: The paper addresses fine-grained visual classification, where subtle inter-class differences make it hard to locate and exploit the truly discriminative object parts. The key insight is that a vision transformer's self-attention between the class token and patch tokens naturally indicates the importance of patches, so aggregating raw attention can guide selection of the most discriminative parts without complex region-detection pipelines. The authors propose TransFG, which augments a ViT with a Part Selection Module that fuses attention weights into an attention map to select informative patch tokens and model their relations, and they add a contrastive loss to push apart representations of confusing classes. Experiments on five fine-grained benchmarks show that this attention-guided patch selection and relational modeling yields state-of-the-art performance.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of making formal theorem proving—turning informal mathematical proofs into machine-checkable formal proofs—more practical by leveraging existing informal proofs to guide automation. The key insight is that informal proofs can be transformed into structured formal "sketches" that expose a high-level decomposition of the proof, and these sketches can effectively direct an automated prover’s search toward simpler subgoals rather than leaving it to unguided, costly exploration. The authors present Draft, Sketch, and Prove (DSP): a pipeline that maps informal proofs (authored by humans or generated by language models) into formal proof sketches and uses those sketches to constrain and prioritize the prover’s search, and they empirically show that LLM-derived sketches closely mirror informal reasoning and nearly double prover success on a benchmark of contest problems (20.9% → 39.3%).

result.text: This paper examines a novel security threat in reinforcement learning where an adversary subtly "poisons" the training environment—by altering rewards or transition dynamics—to coerce a learning agent into adopting a specific attacker-chosen policy. The key insight is that, for undiscounted infinite-horizon RL objectives, an attacker can formulate a constrained optimization problem that finds minimal-cost, stealthy perturbations that make the target policy uniquely optimal (or otherwise favored) under the learner’s objective, and that under mild structural conditions such attacks are often feasible with provable cost bounds. The authors develop an optimization framework that produces optimal stealthy attacks for different cost measures, derive sufficient conditions and lower/upper bounds on attack cost, and instantiate practical algorithms for both offline (planning in a poisoned model) and online (regret-minimizing learning with poisoned feedback) settings, demonstrating empirically and theoretically that an attacker can reliably teach arbitrary target policies.

result.text: The paper tackles the open problem of whether strongly fair allocations (EFX) of indivisible goods exist and can be computed, focusing on the restricted yet relevant domain of lexicographic preferences. Its key insight is that, unlike the additive-valuation setting where EFX existence and computability are unresolved, lexicographic preferences admit structural properties that guarantee existence and allow precise algorithmic characterization of allocations that are both EFX and Pareto optimal. The authors give polynomial-time algorithms that construct such EFX+PO allocations and fully describe the mechanisms that additionally satisfy strategyproofness, non-bossiness, and neutrality; they also show that strengthening efficiency to rank-maximality yields non-existence and hardness results, while relaxing fairness from EFX to MMS restores tractability.

result.text: The paper addresses the tendency of neural decomposition-based methods for multi-objective combinatorial optimization (MOCO) to produce repetitive, low-diversity Pareto sets. Its key insight is that combining indicator-informed guidance and explicit neighborhood exploration can both discourage duplicated solutions across subproblems and uncover multiple desirable optima per subproblem, yielding a richer Pareto front. The proposed Neural Heuristic with Diversity Enhancement (NHDE) implements this by integrating an indicator-enhanced deep reinforcement learning objective and a heterogeneous graph attention module that links instance graphs to Pareto-front graphs to guide solution generation, together with a multiple Pareto optima sampling-and-preservation strategy to explore and retain diverse nearby solutions. Experiments on standard MOCO benchmarks show NHDE produces significantly more diverse and higher-quality Pareto fronts and can be plugged into various neural MOCO frameworks.

result.text: The paper tackles unreliable conclusions in deep reinforcement learning evaluation that arise when researchers report aggregate point estimates (e.g., mean or median scores) from a small number of training runs, which hides statistical uncertainty and can produce misleading comparisons across algorithms. Its key insight is that the “few-run” regime common in modern, computationally expensive benchmarks substantially inflates uncertainty, so conclusions should be based on interval estimates and variability-aware metrics rather than point summaries alone. The authors demonstrate this with case studies on Atari 100k and other benchmarks, show that many published comparisons change under proper statistical analysis, and propose practical remedies—performance profiles, interquartile mean scores, and other robust aggregate metrics—along with an open-source library (rliable) and a recommended evaluation protocol to produce more reliable, uncertainty-aware comparisons.

result.text: The paper addresses the practical difficulty of choosing the per-example gradient clipping threshold R, a sensitive hyperparameter that critically affects accuracy in differentially private (DP) deep learning. Its key insight is that clipping can be automated in a DP-safe way so that no DP-specific tuning is required, enabling private optimizers to behave more like their non-private counterparts without sacrificing privacy or efficiency. The authors propose "automatic clipping" variants of common DP optimizers (e.g., DP-SGD, DP-Adam, DP-LAMB) that adapt clipping implicitly, provide a privacy-preserving and computationally cheap implementation, and come with a rigorous non-convex convergence analysis showing asymptotic rates comparable to standard SGD under a symmetric per-sample gradient noise assumption. Empirically, automatic clipping matches or outperforms prior state-of-the-art DP training on language and vision benchmarks and integrates into existing codebases with minimal changes.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of learning useful feature representations from unlabeled 3D medical images to reduce reliance on costly expert annotations for downstream tasks. The authors implement 3D versions of five methods—Contrastive Predictive Coding, Rotation prediction, Jigsaw puzzles, Relative patch location, and Exemplar networks—and show via experiments on brain MRI and pancreas CT segmentation (and transfer to 2D fundus images) that 3D pretraining improves data efficiency, accuracy, and convergence speed, and transfers well from large unlabeled 3D corpora to small task-specific datasets. They also release an open-source library containing their 3D and 2D implementations to facilitate adoption.

result.text: The paper tackles hyperspectral image restoration, where high spectral dimensionality and scarce ground-truth clean data make training large deep networks difficult and conventional denoising methods limited. Its key insight is to combine the interpretability and built-in priors of classical sparse coding with learnable components, yielding a compact, trainable model that leverages spectral–spatial structure without requiring massive datasets. Methodologically, the authors design a spectral-spatial sparse coding framework whose parameters are trained end-to-end—retaining handcrafted priors and sparse representations while optimizing filters and thresholds—resulting in a computationally efficient algorithm that substantially outperforms prior denoising approaches on multiple hyperspectral benchmarks.

The paper addresses how to make decentralized SGD both communication-efficient and fast-converging by choosing communication topologies that enable nearly-exact averaging with little per-iteration communication. The key insight is that exponential graphs—where each node links to O(log n) neighbors—and, notably, a schedule of log(n) one-peer exponential graphs (each node talks to a single neighbor per iteration) can together achieve exact or nearly-exact averaging while using much less communication than dense or fully synchronous topologies. The method proves theoretical bounds showing these graphs yield favorable spectral properties and consensus rates, integrates them into decentralized (momentum) SGD to balance per-iteration communication and iteration complexity, and validates the approach with experiments demonstrating faster, high-quality training compared to common topologies.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of high quantization error in post-training quantization (PTQ) for large language models by expanding the class of allowed transformations beyond simple per-weight scalings. Its key insight is that optimizing an equivalent affine transformation between pre- and post-quantized weights (and applying the inverse to preserve outputs) enlarges the optimization space and can substantially reduce quantization-induced error while retaining PTQ’s efficiency. The method, AffineQuant, directly optimizes an affine matrix for each layer subject to invertibility constraints enforced via a gradual mask optimization that starts with diagonal entries and progressively frees off-diagonal elements—leveraging the Levy–Desplanques theorem to maintain invertibility—and applies the corresponding inverse to keep pre- and post-quantization outputs equivalent. Empirically, this approach yields consistent improvements across LLMs and settings (e.g., better perplexity and zero-shot accuracy in 4/4-bit quantization) without runtime overhead.

result.text: The paper addresses improving time series forecasting by incorporating time-conditioned topological features into graph convolutional networks to better capture evolving geometric structure in data. The key insight is that zigzag persistence—a form of persistent homology that tracks topological features appearing, persisting, and disappearing across time—provides salient, stable descriptors of temporal shape that complement standard DL representations. The authors introduce a differentiable topological layer that computes zigzag persistence images as compact, theoretically stable summaries of time-varying topology and injects them into time-aware GCNs (Z-GCNETs), then evaluate this architecture on traffic and cryptocurrency price forecasting. Empirically, Z-GCNETs outperform 13 state-of-the-art baselines on four datasets, demonstrating that time-zigzag topological augmentation improves forecasting accuracy and robustness.

result.text: DeVRF addresses slow training of Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) methods for dynamic, non-rigid scenes by dramatically accelerating convergence while retaining high-fidelity novel-view synthesis. The key insight is to represent both the 3D canonical appearance and the 4D non-rigid deformation field with explicit, discrete voxel grids and to regularize the large parameter space by transferring knowledge from a separately learned multi-view static canonical volume. Methodologically, DeVRF first captures and trains a volumetric canonical radiance field from multi-view static images, then learns a voxelized 4D deformation field from few-view dynamic sequences under a static-to-dynamic learning paradigm and several implementation strategies to avoid overfitting; this yields comparable quality to prior dynamic NeRFs but trains roughly 100× faster.

result.text: The paper tackles automatic music transcription (AMT), specifically the challenge of transcribing multiple instruments simultaneously from audio—including low-resource instruments—while retaining precise pitch and timing. result.text: The paper addresses the limitation of Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM), observing that minimizing the perturbed-loss (maximum loss in a neighborhood) does not necessarily prefer flat minima because different curvature directions can yield similarly low perturbed loss. The key insight is that a compact mapping from the LLM’s hidden representations into the embedding space of pretrained image encoder/decoder and text-to-image models can ground the LLM for visual tasks without finetuning the core language model. Concretely, the method trains an efficient mapping network and a learned decision module: the mapping translates LLM hidden states into visual-model embeddings to drive an off‑the‑shelf text‑to‑image generator (or to match and retrieve images from a dataset), while the decision module uses LLM representations to choose retrieval versus generation at inference time. The resulting system outperforms baseline generation models on complex, context-dependent text‑to‑image tasks and supports coherent interleaved image–text inputs and outputs.

result.text: The paper addresses the need for reliable semantic similarity metrics to evaluate reformulation tasks like style transfer, paraphrase, and MT, noting that current metrics are widely used despite unclear fidelity to human judgment. Its key insight is that existing measures diverge substantially from human perceptions on reformulated texts, and that among many contenders a few newer metrics perform comparably while Word Mover’s Distance (WMD) aligns best with human similarity judgments in this setting. Methodologically, the authors compile a new dataset of 14,000 sentence pairs annotated for semantic similarity and use it to compare over a dozen automatic metrics, reporting correlations with human labels and demonstrating WMD’s superior, though still imperfect, reliability for measuring semantic equivalence in paraphrase/style-transfer scenarios.

The paper tackles the challenge of accurate multi-view image-based 3D object detection, where perspective images lack depth and thus struggle to localize objects precisely while lightweight image backbones are desired for deployment. Its key insight is to exploit the superior spatial cues of LiDAR by distilling cross-modal knowledge in a unified Bird’s-Eye-View (BEV) representation, enabling a student image-based detector to learn spatially rich features from a LiDAR-based teacher without requiring explicit depth prediction. The method, BEVDistill, aligns image and LiDAR features in BEV space and performs adaptive, cross-modal knowledge distillation within a teacher–student framework, transferring complementary localization and semantic information during training so that the student achieves LiDAR-like BEV understanding at inference cost identical to standard image-only models. Extensive experiments on nuScenes show that BEVDistill consistently improves a strong baseline (BEVFormer) and achieves state-of-the-art image-based 3D detection performance.

result.text: The paper tackles overfitting in graph classification when labeled graphs are scarce by leveraging unlabeled data through contrastive self-supervised learning (CSSL). Its key insight is that learning representations by contrasting different augmented views of the same graph teaches encoders to capture invariant, discriminative structure useful for downstream classification without labels. result.text: The paper tackles domain generalization, where models trained on multiple source domains must generalize to unseen target domains despite entangled common and domain-specific factors. Its key insight is that instead of forcing strict disentanglement, enforcing invariance of the semantic topology—the relational structure among category-relevant features—yields more robust, domain-agnostic representations. To do this, Mix and Reason (MiRe) combines Category-aware Data Mixing (CDM), which mixes pairs of cross-domain images guided by complementary activation maps so classifiers attend to semantic object regions, with Adaptive Semantic Topology Refinement (ASTR), which builds and progressively refines relation graphs through iterative local feature aggregation and global cross-domain relational reasoning to stabilize semantic topology across domains. Experiments on standard DG benchmarks show this approach improves robustness and generalization without relying on strong disentanglement assumptions.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of translating wearable photoplethysmography (PPG) into clinically useful electrocardiography (ECG) for continuous, low-cost cardiac monitoring, where standard diffusion models struggle to capture fine-grained ECG temporal features. The key insight is that indiscriminate noise injection across an entire signal hinders modeling of critical ECG regions (e.g., QRS complexes), so selectively treating regions of interest (ROI) during the forward and reverse diffusion processes can disentangle and preserve diagnostically important structure. They propose the Region-Disentangled Diffusion Model (RDDM), which applies targeted noise addition to ROIs in the forward process and performs separated denoising for ROI and non-ROI regions in the reverse steps, enabling high-fidelity PPG-to-ECG translation in as few as 10 diffusion steps. To validate clinical utility, they introduce CardioBench, a comprehensive benchmark of cardiac tasks, and show RDDM achieves state-of-the-art performance across heart rate and blood pressure estimation, stress classification, and detection of atrial fibrillation and diabetes.

result.text: The paper addresses the opaque mechanisms by which attention-based encoder–decoder networks produce alignment matrices across different sequence-to-sequence tasks and architectures. The key insight is that hidden states can be decomposed into a temporal component (position-dependent, input-independent) and an input-driven component (content-dependent, position-independent), and that the relative reliance on these components explains how attention patterns are formed. Methodologically, the authors propose and apply this decomposition to analyze attention behavior in both recurrent and feed-forward encoders/decoders, showing consistently that tasks requiring positional cues use the temporal component more while content-sensitive tasks leverage the input-driven component, illuminating a unified view of attention formation despite architectural differences.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of protecting a trained model’s functionality when it is deployed publicly, aiming to prevent adversaries from reconstructing or extracting the model while preserving useful responses for legitimate users. The key insight is to treat model protection as “information laundering”: instead of directly exposing deterministic model inputs and outputs, introduce probabilistic transformations that deliberately perturb or obfuscate queries and responses so that the information an adversary can glean about the original model is reduced while utility is retained. Methodologically, the authors formalize this idea with an information-theoretic framework that quantifies the tradeoff between utility and privacy leakage, derive optimal stochastic preprocessing and postprocessing mechanisms under that principle, and characterize how to balance perturbation strength to achieve desired privacy guarantees with minimal degradation in model performance.

result.text: The paper addresses improving transferability of adversarial examples in black-box attacks by rethinking why ensemble-based attacks work, noting prior methods merely average model outputs without analyzing underlying causes. The key insight is that ensemble transferability hinges on exploiting a "common weakness" across models, characterized by two properties: flatness of the loss landscape around adversarial examples and their closeness to each model’s local optima, both of which correlate with stronger cross-model transfer. result.text: The paper studies how lack of transparency about a principal’s decision rule (e.g., loan or college admissions) affects agents who must learn strategically by observing peers with heterogeneous information, addressing whether and when population subgroups can improve their true quality under such information disparities. The key insight is that when individuals infer an opaque rule from peers, group-specific information can create strong externalities: an optimal welfare-maximizing decision rule for the principal can perversely cause some groups’ true quality to worsen, while in many natural regimes one can design rules that guarantee simultaneous improvement across all sub-populations. Methodologically, the authors model strategic learning with inaccessible decision rules and heterogeneous informational groups, analyze equilibria to characterize welfare and improvement and introduce the “information overlap proxy” to quantify disparity in group improvements, derive conditions ensuring universal improvement with high predictive accuracy, and validate the theoretical findings with experiments on real-world datasets.

result.text: The paper addresses few-shot fine-grained recognition, where the challenge is to learn discriminative part-level representations from very few labeled examples of closely related subordinate categories. The key insight is that combining sparse, part-focused “hard” attention (selecting a few deep descriptors as a multi-instance bag) with dense, complementary “soft” attention (weighted activations over the whole feature map) yields richer, fine-grained embeddings that capture both salient local parts and broader contextual cues. The proposed Dual Attention Network builds two parallel branches—one that selects and aggregates a small set of informative deep descriptors via multi-instance learning and another that produces a soft-attended activation map—and fuses their outputs into a holistic image embedding that is trained via meta-learning in a metric space to generalize to novel classes. Empirical results on three fine-grained benchmarks show the method substantially outperforms prior state-of-the-art few-shot approaches.

result.text: The paper tackles autoformalization: automatically converting natural-language mathematics into formal specifications and proofs, a task important for formal verification and AI but long considered out of reach. The key insight is that large language models (LLMs) can already translate a substantial fraction (~25.3%) of competition-style math problems exactly into Isabelle/HOL formal statements, providing useful training data for downstream theorem proving. The authors use LLM-generated formalizations to augment training of a neural theorem prover and thereby improve performance on the MiniF2F benchmark, raising the proof success rate from 29.6% to 35.2%. This demonstrates that LLM-driven autoformalization can both produce high-quality formal statements and materially advance automated theorem proving.

result.text: The paper addresses the loss of geometric precision when extracting meshes from deep implicit surface representations implemented as ReLU MLPs, where standard discretized algorithms like marching cubes cannot exactly recover the learned geometry. The key insight is that a ReLU MLP partitions input space into linear regions whose boundaries yield analytic cells and faces that exactly characterize the zero-level isosurface, and that under specific theoretical conditions these analytic faces connect into a closed, piecewise-planar surface. Building on this, the authors prove connectivity conditions and develop a parallelizable "analytic marching" algorithm that traverses analytic cells to recover the exact mesh encoded by the MLP rather than an approximate discretized version. Empirical results in learned mesh reconstruction demonstrate improved fidelity and advantages over existing marching-cubes–based approaches.

result.text: The paper tackles open-vocabulary object detection, where models must detect novel categories but struggle because popular weak supervision sources—CLIP image-text pretraining and image-level labels—are misaligned with object-level localization. The key insight is that bringing language embeddings into an object-centric space and automatically grounding image-level labels to high-quality object proposals can close the gap between image- and object-level representations, yielding better transfer to novel categories. Methodologically, the authors perform object-centric alignment of CLIP embeddings and generate pseudo-labeled object proposals from image-level supervision to visually ground categories, then combine these complementary signals with a learned weight-transfer function that aggregates their strengths during detector training. This combined strategy substantially improves open-vocabulary detection, raising novel-class AP on COCO by 8.2 points and boosting LVIS rare and overall mask AP versus prior state-of-the-art.

result.text: The paper tackles fair allocation of indivisible goods when each agent faces individual feasibility constraints represented by matroids, aiming for envy-freeness up to one good (EF1) despite heterogeneity in both constraints and valuations. The key insight is that by exploiting structural properties of matroids (particularly partition and base-orderable matroids) together with restricted valuation classes (binary or small numbers of agents), one can avoid known impossibilities and design constructive EF1 procedures. Methodologically, the authors develop polynomial-time algorithms tailored to specific combinations of matroid types and valuation restrictions—yielding EF1 complete allocations for (i) any number of agents with heterogeneous partition matroids and binary valuations, (ii) two agents with arbitrary valuations and heterogeneous partition matroids, and (iii) up to three agents with binary valuations and identical base-orderable matroids—while also delineating negative results for other settings.

result.text: The paper addresses the limitation of standard RLHF that trains a single reward model from aggregated preference data, which cannot faithfully represent diverse and potentially conflicting human preferences and can systematically disadvantage minority tastes. The key insight is that modeling preference heterogeneity explicitly—by learning a mixture of preference distributions—and optimizing policies with a MaxMin (egalitarian) objective yields more equitable alignment than a single aggregated reward, connecting naturally to distributionally robust optimization and general-utility RL. Methodologically, the authors fit a mixture of preference models via expectation-maximization, then train policies to maximize the minimum expected utility across inferred preference components, and validate this approach on both small (GPT-2) and large (Tulu2-7B) models, showing large gains in overall win-rate and substantial improvements for minority groups without harming majority performance.

The paper addresses how differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DPSGD), while protecting privacy, can amplify disparate impact across groups in trained models. The key insight is that inequitable gradient clipping in DPSGD causes gradient misalignment between groups—small or underrepresented groups have their gradients disproportionately clipped, steering optimization toward objectives that favor majority groups and thus increasing unfairness. To mitigate this, the authors propose a method that prevents gradient misalignment by adjusting the clipping/aggregation process (e.g., group-aware or adaptive clipping strategies) so that per-group gradient contributions are preserved more faithfully before noise addition, thereby reducing the disparate impact introduced by standard DPSGD.

result.text: The paper addresses the limitations of post-training quantization (PTQ) methods that quantize neural networks in isolated sub-net blocks, neglecting inter-layer dependencies which leads to suboptimal low-bit performance and brittleness. Methodologically, the authors combine empirical trajectory analysis across phases with theoretical arguments: they trace how output-layer norm and other quantities change in each phase, provide empirical evidence for these mechanisms, and, under simplifying assumptions, give a proof of the EOS sharpness behavior for two-layer fully connected linear networks while discussing limitations and additional empirical observations.

result.text: The paper addresses scalable, efficient inference of continuous-time normalizing flows that transform between any chosen base and target probability densities without the heavy cost of backpropagating through ODE solvers. The key insight is to define a time-dependent stochastic interpolant density between base and target and infer the flow’s velocity directly from its probability current, which yields a simple quadratic loss on the velocity expressed as expectations that can be estimated empirically rather than via likelihood-based ODE backpropagation. The method trains a velocity field by minimizing that quadratic objective (and optionally a path-length regularizer for near-optimal transport), then integrates the resulting ordinary differential equation to sample or evaluate densities at any time; when the base is Gaussian the same velocity gives a diffusion-model-like sampler and score estimator, but the approach generally sidesteps SDEs and achieves competitive or superior density estimation and image generation while scaling ODE-based flows to much larger resolutions.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of automatically discovering jailbreak prompts for black-box large language models (LLMs), aiming to expose and bypass safety guardrails without access to model internals. The key insight is to treat jailbreak generation as a search over prompt variants guided by a separate attacker LLM that iteratively proposes and refines candidate attacks while using a lightweight pruning stage to discard low-promise candidates before querying the target, thereby reducing query cost. The proposed method, Tree of Attacks with Pruning (TAP), builds a tree of prompt refinements where an attacker LLM expands nodes into refined prompts, a learned evaluator prunes unlikely branches, and surviving prompts are tested against the target LLM; empirically TAP jailbreaks state-of-the-art models (including GPT-4 variants) on over 80% of cases and outperforms prior black-box approaches in success rate and query efficiency, even circumventing advanced guardrails like LlamaGuard.

Its key insight is that explicitly inducing diversity in ensemble predictions via an information-bottleneck-style latent representation and an adversarial diversity objective yields the multimodality and prediction variability needed for better generalization and OOD detection. The method trains stochastic latent variables for each ensemble member with a diversity-inducing adversarial loss combined with an information bottleneck constraint, producing diverse output behaviors without sacrificing accuracy; experiments on MNIST, CIFAR100, TinyImageNet and MIT Places 2 show substantial gains in classification accuracy, robustness to dataset shift, and out-of-distribution detection compared to strong baselines.

result.text: The paper addresses the security and safety risks introduced when large language models are extended with visual inputs, showing that vision-integrated LLMs create a new, high-dimensional attack surface that can be exploited to bypass alignment guardrails. The key insight is that continuous visual inputs both are easier to perturb adversarially and allow attackers to realize a far broader set of harmful objectives than simple classification attacks, so a single carefully crafted visual adversarial example can universally “jailbreak” an aligned multimodal model. The authors demonstrate this by constructing visual adversarial examples optimized against aligned VLMs (e.g., Flamingo, GPT-4 variants) that, when presented as images, cause the models to ignore safety constraints and follow a wide variety of harmful instructions beyond the narrow training cues used to produce the perturbation. Their results link classical adversarial vulnerability to alignment failures in multimodal models and highlight a fundamental challenge for safe deployment of vision-enabled foundation models.

result.text: MERLOT addresses the problem of learning multimodal “script” knowledge—temporal, commonsense reasoning about events—from raw video and speech without supervision. Its key insight is that combining both frame-level (spatial) and video-level (temporal) self-supervised objectives over large-scale narrated video enables a single model to learn alignments between visual frames and corresponding words while also building global, time-aware contextual representations. The method pretrains a Transformer-based multimodal encoder on millions of YouTube videos with transcribed speech using a mix of objectives that include matching images to temporally corresponding words and predicting broader video-level context, then finetunes this representation for downstream tasks. The resulting model yields strong out-of-the-box temporal commonsense, state-of-the-art performance across many video QA benchmarks, and improved transfer to static-image commonsense tasks.

The key insight is that a single-pixel, class-consistent perturbation—setting the same pixel location to the same atypical value across images of a class—acts as a strong, stable shortcut that derails learning much more effectively than distributed noise yet is harder to eliminate. result.text: The paper addresses the problem that standard GAN discriminators lose sensitivity to high-frequency image content—largely due to downsampling layers—causing generators to produce images with deficient spectral detail and a notable spectrum discrepancy from real data. The key insight is that because the Fourier transform is bijective, explicitly measuring and penalizing spectral discrepancies alongside spatial realism will incentivize generators to reproduce high-frequency details and reduce the spectrum gap. To implement this, the authors propose SSD-GAN, which augments the discriminator with a frequency-aware classifier that evaluates input realness in both spatial and spectral domains, thereby providing spectral feedback to the generator; the module is lightweight, plug-and-play with common GAN architectures and objectives, and is empirically shown to improve fidelity across architectures and datasets.

result.text: The paper addresses unreliable and inconsistent reporting of reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm performance, which impedes reproducibility and fair comparison. Its key insight is that much of this inconsistency arises from flawed or incomplete evaluation metrics rather than inherent algorithmic variability, so improving the evaluation methodology can yield more reliable and comparable results. The authors propose a comprehensive evaluation methodology that standardizes measurement procedures, combines robust single-environment metrics with principled aggregation across environments, and applies statistical practices to reduce noise and bias. They validate the approach by re-evaluating a broad class of RL algorithms on standard benchmarks, showing that the new protocol produces more consistent, reproducible, and interpretable performance assessments.

result.text: The paper tackles the bottleneck in column generation (CG) caused by repeatedly solving an NP-hard pricing problem, using graph coloring as a testbed. Its key insight is that a machine learning model can predict near-optimal pricing solutions which, when used to guide a targeted sampling procedure, yields many high-quality columns much more quickly than repeatedly solving the hard subproblem exactly. The proposed Machine-Learning-based Pricing Heuristic (MLPH) integrates an ML predictor into each CG iteration to estimate the optimal pricing solution and then drives a sampling-based generator to produce multiple promising columns, which are added to the restricted master problem. Empirical results on graph coloring show that MLPH substantially improves CG efficiency compared to six state-of-the-art methods and translates into notably better performance for branch-and-price exact algorithms.
