result.text: The paper addresses how to learn accurate predictors when training data contain missing values, questioning the common two-step practice of imputing first and then fitting a predictor. The key insight is that for nearly all imputation functions, an impute-then-regress strategy with a sufficiently flexible learner is asymptotically Bayes-optimal for prediction across any missingness mechanism, so perfect conditional imputation is unnecessary and can even produce discontinuous regression targets that are hard to learn; this motivates jointly learning imputation and prediction instead of treating them as separate problems. Methodologically, the authors adapt NeuMiss—a neural architecture designed to model conditional relationships between observed and missing components under arbitrary missingness patterns—and train it end-to-end to perform imputation and regression together, showing empirically that this joint approach outperforms various two-step procedures on finite-sample experiments.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of high-fidelity audio synthesis from low-bitrate discrete representations, where existing autoregressive and token-based models can produce impressive results but suffer audible artifacts when conditioning is imperfect. result.text: The paper addresses the overlooked supply-chain risk that pretrained models downloaded from untrusted repositories can be tampered with to compromise the privacy of downstream finetuning data. The authors demonstrate concrete constructions of such backdoors across architectures (including transformers), show attack algorithms that reconstruct training examples from the finetuned weights or outputs, and empirically and theoretically analyze their effectiveness and limitations, highlighting how loose DP guarantees do not protect against untrusted pretrained initializations.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of deploying high-performing hyperspectral image (HSI) reconstruction models for snapshot compressive imaging (SCI) on resource-constrained devices by dramatically reducing model size and computation while retaining accuracy. Its key insight is that a carefully redesigned base network can be binarized without large performance loss if activations are adaptively redistributed before binarization and the gradient approximation during training closely matches the sign function. Concretely, the authors propose the Binarized Spectral-Redistribution Network (BiSRNet) built from a novel Binarized Spectral-Redistribution Convolution (BiSR-Conv) that adaptively reshapes HSI representations, employs a scalable hyperbolic tangent surrogate for Sign in backpropagation, and integrates four specialized binarized convolutional modules to handle dimensional mismatches and propagate full-precision information. Extensive experiments show BiSRNet outperforms existing binarization approaches and achieves reconstruction quality comparable to full-precision methods while being far more efficient and hardware-friendly.

Its key insight is that the changing consensus distance—the divergence among device models during training—is a primary factor explaining this performance gap, and that if consensus distance stays below a critical threshold, decentralized training matches centralized convergence rates. Methodologically, the authors provide theoretical analysis linking consensus distance to convergence, empirically validate the relationship between consensus distance and generalization across settings, and derive practical training guidelines and scheme adjustments that keep consensus distance small to mitigate performance degradation in data-center and on-device setups.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of accelerating and reducing memory use in sparse neural network training by eliminating the dense computation that previous methods still required during backward propagation when estimating gradients for structural (sparsity) parameters. result.text: The paper addresses the problem of minimizing regret in finite-horizon tabular Markov decision processes while guaranteeing differential privacy, considering both joint DP (centralized protection) and local DP (user-side protection) settings. result.text: The paper addresses the tendency of large sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models to overfit and suffer from sparse, imbalanced data allocation as the expert count grows, which caps performance especially on limited-data tasks. The key insight is that routing should encourage variance-aware, cluster-level diversity among experts so that experts learn more distinct and appropriate knowledge rather than redundant or undertrained behaviors. The authors propose Mixture of Expert Clusters (MoEC), which groups experts into clusters and imposes variance-based constraints during routing to promote balanced activation and diversity, together with a cluster-level expert dropout mechanism tailored to the clustered structure. Empirical results on machine translation and NLU show that MoEC mitigates overfitting and sparse allocation, unlocking better performance from large-scale sparse models.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of detecting and explaining multi-modal fake news by uncovering the implicit deceptive patterns behind fabrications rather than providing only superficial saliency-based explanations. Its key insight is that typical fabrications can be characterized by a small set of interpretable deceptive patterns—image manipulation, cross-modal inconsistency, and image repurposing—whose presence can be modeled as discrete latent variables and used both for prediction and explanation. result.text: The paper tackles the problem of learning causal graph structure from data, specifically extending continuous, differentiable formulations of the combinatorial causal discovery problem to exploit interventional data which improves identifiability. Its key insight is that the continuous-constrained optimization paradigm can naturally incorporate interventions and benefit from expressive neural architectures, enabling end-to-end differentiable learning that handles perfect and imperfect interventions and even cases where intervention targets are unknown. result.text: The paper tackles the open question of existence of EFX (envy-free up to any item) allocations of indivisible goods, focusing on extending positive existence results beyond very restricted cases. The key insight is a set of new combinatorial and allocation-construction techniques that nearly close the gap for four agents by showing that one can always achieve an EFX allocation while leaving at most a single item unallocated, and that these techniques naturally generalize beyond additive utilities via a broader valuation class. Methodologically, the authors develop and analyze procedures that manipulate bundles and carefully exchange or discard at most one item to eliminate envy, introduce the "nice cancelable" valuation class (encompassing additive, unit-demand, budget-additive, multiplicative, etc.), and prove that their constructive arguments yield the almost-full EFX existence result for four agents and extend earlier existence theorems to this wider class.

The paper addresses the challenge of learning policies for multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) that must adapt to changing, potentially continuous preference vectors without training and storing separate policies for every preference. The key insight is to train a single universal network conditioned on preference vectors that can represent the Pareto front across the entire preference space, using preferences to directly guide parameter updates and a parallelized data-collection scheme to boost sample efficiency. The method, called Preference-Driven MORL (PD-MORL), conditions a single policy network on preference inputs, updates network parameters with preference-weighted objectives, and employs a novel parallelization strategy to improve learning efficiency in continuous control tasks. Empirically, PD-MORL yields substantially larger hypervolume (up to 25% improvement) while using an order of magnitude fewer trainable parameters than prior approaches.

The paper tackles the challenge of improving data-efficiency and generalization in reinforcement learning from visual (pixel) and state observations, where current methods struggle to learn quickly and transfer to new environments. The key insight is that applying standard, well-chosen data augmentations during RL training—such as random translate, crop, color jitter, patch cutout, random convolutions, and a new random amplitude scale—can substantially improve representation learning and policy robustness without complex architectural changes. The method, called RAD, is a simple plug-and-play module that augments inputs before they are passed to existing RL algorithms and is evaluated extensively across pixel- and state-based benchmarks; empirically RAD achieves state-of-the-art data-efficiency and final performance on DeepMind Control Suite and OpenAI Gym and markedly better test-time generalization on ProcGen.

result.text: The paper addresses how multiple parties can collaboratively improve machine learning models when data sharing is legally or ethically constrained by both confidentiality (no explicit dataset pooling) and privacy (no implicit leakage via models or gradients), a setting where existing approaches like federated learning or differential privacy fall short. result.text: AdaFuse addresses efficient video action recognition by selectively retaining useful temporal information while eliminating redundant computation across frames. The key insight is that strong temporal modelling can be achieved by adaptively fusing only the necessary channels from historical convolutional feature maps with pruned current-frame features, rather than processing all temporal data uniformly. The method implements an adaptive temporal fusion module that learns per-channel fusion weights between past and present features, combined with a skip operation that bypasses computation when frames are redundant, yielding a lightweight network that reuses past features to save work. Experiments on Something-Something V1/V2, Jester, and Mini-Kinetics demonstrate that AdaFuse achieves about 40% computation reduction with accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art methods.

The authors introduce DeepSpeed-MoE, an end-to-end library extension that combines new MoE architectural designs, model compression techniques that shrink models up to 3.7×, and a highly optimized inference engine that yields up to 7.3× better latency/cost versus prior MoE solutions and up to 4.5× faster or 9× cheaper inference versus quality-equivalent dense models. By integrating these methods into a production-ready system, DeepSpeed-MoE demonstrates a practical path to scale and deploy next-generation sparse models more efficiently.

result.text: The paper investigates whether safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) holds when users communicate in non-natural languages (ciphers), addressing the risk that current defenses—trained primarily on natural language—may be bypassed. The key insight is that LLMs can understand and respond to ciphered prompts, and in fact exhibit a latent "secret cipher" behavior that can be triggered via role play and enciphered demonstrations, enabling stealthy jailbreaks even against strong models like GPT-4. The authors introduce CipherChat, a framework that sends system-role descriptions and few-shot enciphered examples to LLMs to systematically evaluate 11 safety domains across English and Chinese, showing that many human-designed ciphers and the proposed SelfCipher can nearly completely bypass GPT-4’s safety in several domains. Their results reveal a pressing need to extend alignment methods beyond natural languages and provide code and data for reproducibility.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of protecting proprietary training data from being used to train high-performance models by adding imperceptible perturbations that disrupt the entire training process rather than just one model. The key insight is that gradients from intermediate training checkpoints behave like an ensemble of diverse models—their cross-model gradients are nearly orthogonal—so optimizing perturbations to fool all checkpoints yields examples that are "always unrecognized" during training and thereby poison learning robustly. The method, called Self-Ensemble Protection (SEP), computes gradients from multiple saved checkpoints of a single training run to craft perturbations that maximize misclassification across those snapshots, producing small ℓ∞-bounded perturbations that severely degrade downstream model accuracy; extensive experiments across datasets, architectures, and baselines show SEP substantially outperforms prior data-protection techniques.

result.text: The paper tackles GAN training under limited-data regimes, where discriminators overfit and synthesis quality drops when few real images are available. Its key insight is to replace or augment the usual binary real-vs-fake discriminator task with instance discrimination—forcing the discriminator to distinguish every individual image (real or synthesized)—so it can continually learn from the effectively infinite set of generated samples and thus avoid overfitting. Methodologically, InsGen augments the discriminator objective with an instance-level contrastive loss plus a noise perturbation strategy to strengthen discrimination, and it uses the discriminator’s learned instance representations to encourage the generator toward more diverse outputs; this simple modification yields substantial empirical gains (e.g., a 23.5% FID improvement on 2K FFHQ).

result.text: The paper addresses shortcomings in cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning under the common CTDE framework, specifically examining how the widely used Individual Global Max (IGM) decomposition can be a lossy representation whose approximation errors accumulate in hypernetwork-based value factorization methods. The key insight is that treating IGM as an exact consistency constraint is problematic because its decomposition error compounds through Bellman updates, and separating the lossy decomposition from value learning via an imitation-learning objective can prevent that error accumulation. Concretely, the authors introduce an imitation-learning-based strategy that decouples the lossy local-to-global mapping from Bellman iterations—training a policy or mixer to imitate target joint actions rather than repeatedly propagating decomposed value errors—and provide theoretical justification plus empirical validation on the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge with limited observability, showing improved performance over state-of-the-art IGM-based approaches.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of task-agnostic inverse design for complex fluid-structure interaction problems, where traditional ML-based design methods struggle when faced with distributions or dynamics different from their training tasks. Its key insight is that general-purpose graph network simulators—trained even on single-step data—can be composed with gradient-based optimization to backpropagate through long multi-step physical trajectories, enabling effective design updates despite model mismatch. The method couples a pretrained graph neural network simulator of fluid-structure dynamics with gradient descent on design parameters, propagating gradients through hundreds of simulated steps to optimize shapes and surfaces (e.g., tools for manipulating flow and airfoil geometries) and demonstrating superior performance to sampling-based optimizers and parity with specialized solvers. Overall, this simple, fast, and reusable framework shows that learned simulators can support high-dimensional, long-horizon design optimization across diverse fluid-structure interaction tasks.

result.text: The paper tackles the high computational cost and limited flexibility of existing neural operators for solving forward and inverse PDE problems defined on large geometric domains. Its key insight is that mapping input functions into a learned latent space, performing the operator learning there, and decoding back to the geometric space via a physics-aware cross-attention yields a compact, efficient representation that still permits continuous-space decoding for interpolation and extrapolation. The proposed Latent Neural Operator (LNO) implements this by introducing a Physics-Cross-Attention (PhCA) module to transform geometric representations into latent tokens, learning the operator entirely in latent space, and applying the inverse PhCA to recover values at arbitrary spatial locations; this architecture reduces memory and training time while improving accuracy, achieving substantial speedups and competitive or state-of-the-art results on multiple forward and inverse PDE benchmarks.

The paper addresses semi-supervised learning in realistic “open-world” scenarios where unlabeled data at test time may contain novel classes absent from the labeled training set, requiring a system to both classify known classes and detect/initialize new ones. Its key insight is that standard semi-supervised training biases models toward seen classes because discriminative features for seen classes are learned faster, so reducing this bias by adaptively widening decision margins for uncertain examples can equalize intra-class variance between seen and novel classes. The proposed method, ORCA, is an end-to-end deep model that uses an uncertainty-adaptive margin mechanism to adjust classification boundaries based on sample uncertainty, enabling simultaneous classification of known classes and identification/initialization of novel classes; experiments on image and single-cell datasets show substantial gains over baselines, notably large improvements on both seen and novel classes.

result.text: The paper tackles scalable detection of backdoor attacks in deep neural networks, where existing optimization-based defenses become prohibitively slow as the number of classes grows because they try to find minimal triggers for every possible target label. The key insight is to frame label selection as a K‑arm optimization problem akin to multi‑armed bandits: by stochastically and iteratively focusing optimization effort on a small set of promising target labels guided by an objective, the method both cuts complexity and reduces uncertainty about which labels are likely poisoned. The proposed K‑Arm scanning algorithm alternates between selecting candidate labels according to estimated rewards and running trigger‑finding optimizations on those labels, refining selections over iterations; this yields much faster scanning and higher detection accuracy, outperforming prior techniques on thousands of IARPA TrojAI models.

result.text: The paper tackles the memory inefficiency and expert redundancy of sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) models, which arise from duplicating layers into many experts and from representational collapse in learned routing. The key insight is that routing statistics reveal expert importance and relationships, so aligning neuron permutations and merging experts guided by activation frequency can consolidate knowledge while suppressing insignificant experts, and that merged experts exhibit low-rank structure amenable to further compression. The proposed M-SMoE first permutes neurons to align experts, groups dominant experts with their "group members" using routing-derived affinities, and merges each group by weighting expert parameters by activation frequency; MC-SMoE then decomposes these merged experts into low-rank and structurally sparse forms for additional compression. Experiments across eight benchmarks show MC-SMoE can cut memory by up to ~80% and reduce FLOPs by ~20% with negligible performance loss.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of learning causal DAGs via continuous optimization, addressing the instability and scalability limits of prior Differentiable Causal Discovery (DCD) methods that fail beyond small variable sizes. The key insight is that replacing the standard acyclicity constraint with a theoretically and empirically more stable alternative, combined with a training regime designed for sparse graphs, yields far better numerical behavior and scalability. The method, Stable Differentiable Causal Discovery (SDCD), derives and proves properties of the new acyclicity constraint, integrates it into a differentiable optimization framework, and employs sparsity-aware training to recover structure from observational and interventional data. result.text: The paper addresses the challenging problem of fusing separately trained neural networks that solve different tasks into a single multi-task model without any further training. Its key insight is that naive permutation-and-average merging fails when networks have task-specific, non-overlapping features, so merging should allow selective combination of features and support partial merging to preserve task-specific heads. The proposed method, ZipIt!, introduces a general "zip" operation that merges corresponding features across models (rather than simply averaging entire weights) and permits partial zipping up to a chosen layer to produce a shared backbone with separate heads. Empirically, these modifications yield substantial gains (20–60% over prior merging methods), making zero-shot combination of disjoint-task models much more practical.

result.text: The paper addresses how to design decision policies and counterfactual explanations when individuals can strategically change features in response to explanations to improve their chances of favorable decisions. The key insight is that while optimizing explanations for a given policy is NP-hard, the utility objective is nondecreasing and submodular (and the joint policy-plus-explanations objective is a non-monotone submodular maximization), which enables efficient approximation via greedy and recent randomized algorithms with provable guarantees. The authors therefore cast explanation selection as a submodular optimization problem, apply a greedy algorithm for the constrained (monotone) case and a randomized algorithm for the joint (non-monotone) case, and introduce matroid constraints to promote diversity of explanations across the population. Experiments on synthetic and real lending and credit-card datasets confirm that their algorithms produce explanation sets and policies that yield higher utility than several baselines.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of inducing effective sparsity in deep neural networks by learning where to prune parameters rather than relying on uniform or heuristic layer-wise budgets that hurt accuracy or increase FLOPs. The key insight is to reparameterize weights using a differentiable soft-threshold operator that both smoothly drives weights to zero and makes the pruning thresholds themselves learnable, enabling automatic discovery of non-uniform sparsity budgets. The key insight is that "unstable convergence" arises from interactions between sharp directions of the loss landscape, stochastic noise, and iterative dynamics—so that transient or bounded oscillations around minima can still yield overall descent despite violating smoothness-based step-size limits. result.text: The paper addresses discriminator overfitting in GANs and the unclear question of which and how strongly data augmentations can be applied during GAN training. Its key insight is that integrating contrastive representation learning into the discriminator (ContraD) lets the discriminator tolerate much stronger augmentations while simultaneously producing and leveraging more discriminative features for both contrastive learning and adversarial training. Methodologically, ContraD augments discriminator training with a contrastive loss that pulls together differently augmented views of the same example and pushes apart real and fake features, enabling stable training with stronger augmentations and yielding improved FID/IS and linear evaluation performance. As a practical bonus, the learned features enable simple unsupervised conditional generation via latent sampling.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of detecting post-training backdoor attacks on classifiers when the defender lacks the training data or clean reference models, focusing particularly on challenging two-class settings and cases with multiple simultaneous attacks. The key insight is that reverse-engineered candidate backdoor patterns can be evaluated by an expected transferability (ET) statistic that quantifies how consistently a recovered pattern causes inputs from other classes to be misclassified to the same target, and that this ET score yields a domain- and attack-configuration–agnostic separation between attacked and clean models. The method reverse-engineers potential backdoor patterns from the deployed classifier, computes the ET statistic for these candidates (using the classifier’s responses on held-out inputs rather than any training labels), and flags models as backdoored when ET exceeds a fixed threshold; experiments on six benchmarks show the approach reliably detects both two-class and multi-attack scenarios across different reverse-engineering algorithms.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of performing scalable Bayesian inference with deep learning so practitioners can specify priors and obtain calibrated uncertainty without costly posterior computations. Its key insight is that a large transformer can be trained via in-context learning to approximate the Bayesian posterior predictive distribution by treating posterior approximation as a supervised task: sample tasks from a prior, draw datasets, mask one label, and train the model to predict the masked label conditional on the rest. The method, called Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs), thus learns to map a set-valued training set and query input to a probabilistic prediction in a single forward pass, and the authors show PFNs can closely emulate Gaussian processes and enable efficient approximate Bayesian inference (often hundreds-fold faster) across Gaussian process regression, Bayesian neural nets, tabular classification, and few-shot image tasks.

Its key insight is that universal, stealthy trigger tokens and poisoned discrete prompts can be discovered and optimized solely through API queries and few-shot examples, enabling reliable, transferable manipulation without white-box access. The proposed TrojLLM framework combines a trigger-discovery algorithm that searches for universal input-level triggers via black-box queries and a progressive Trojan poisoning algorithm that iteratively crafts poisoned prompts to maximize attack efficacy and transferability across models. Experiments show TrojLLM can successfully implant Trojans in real-world LLM APIs such as GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 while preserving performance on clean inputs, highlighting practical risks and suggesting avenues for defense.

result.text: The paper tackles scalable representation learning on very large graphs, observing that existing graph Transformers are overcomplicated and costly because they inherit deep multi-head attention designs from NLP/vision despite the heavy all-pair computation on massive node sets. Based on this, the authors propose SGFormer, a Simplified Graph Transformer that uses an efficient single-layer attention mechanism (no positional encodings, no preprocessing or auxiliary losses) to propagate information among arbitrary nodes, which empirically matches or surpasses deeper models while scaling to web-scale graphs and achieving large inference speedups.

result.text: The paper tackles shortcomings in Composed Image Retrieval (CoIR), namely the scarcity and quality issues of existing datasets and the challenge of effectively fusing image and text queries. Its key insight is that scaling dataset size and diagnosing modality redundancy can substantially boost CoIR performance and that early cross-attention fusion with an auxiliary task yields stronger representations. To that end the authors introduce LaSCo, a new CoIR dataset an order of magnitude larger than prior sets, propose an analysis method to detect when image or text modalities are redundant or necessary in queries, and present CASE (Cross-Attention driven Shift Encoder), a baseline that fuses modalities early via cross-attention and uses an auxiliary training objective. Pretraining on LaSCo and using CASE leads to significant gains, including improved zero-shot performance and state-of-the-art results on benchmarks like FashionIQ and CIRR.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of decoding natural images from noisy, non-invasive EEG recordings to enable object recognition directly from brain signals. Its key insight is that self-supervised contrastive learning can align representations learned from paired image stimuli and EEG responses, allowing useful image features to be inferred from EEG despite low signal-to-noise ratios. The method uses separate image and EEG encoders trained with a contrastive objective to pull matching image–EEG pairs together in feature space, augmented by attention modules to capture spatial correlations and extensive analyses across temporal, spatial, spectral, and semantic EEG dimensions. Evaluated on a large EEG–image dataset, the approach achieves substantially above-chance zero-shot recognition (15.6% top-1, 42.8% top-5 on 200-way tasks) and offers biologically plausible insights for neural decoding and BCI applications.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of designing an acquisition function (AF) for Bayesian optimization that generalizes across diverse black-box functions, avoiding the large performance variation seen with handcrafted AFs. The key insight is to treat AFs as Q-functions and learn a distribution over Q-networks (a Bayesian DQN) in a few-shot meta-learning framework, which provides the sampling uncertainty needed for BO while reducing overfitting that plagues direct DQN approaches. result.text: The paper addresses long-term music-conditioned dance generation, where autoregressive models tend to accumulate prediction errors and fail to maintain rhythmic and stylistic consistency with music over extended sequences. Its key insight is that treating the task as a sequence-to-sequence problem and training with a gradual curriculum that transitions from full teacher forcing to predominantly autoregressive generation reduces error accumulation and improves music–dance alignment. The authors propose a novel seq2seq architecture that processes long music feature sequences and captures fine-grained correspondence between music and motion, combined with a curriculum learning strategy that progressively replaces ground-truth past motions with model-generated ones during training. Experiments show this combination yields more stable, longer, and musically coherent dance sequences, outperforming prior methods on automatic metrics and human judgments.

The key insight is that medical time series contain meaningful consistency at multiple nested levels—observation, sample, trial, and patient—and that jointly contrasting across these levels yields more informative, generalizable representations. The authors propose COMET, a hierarchical contrastive framework that formulates and optimizes contrastive losses at each of the four levels to preserve multi-scale consistencies in a self-supervised manner, and evaluate it in a patient-independent regime on ECG and EEG datasets. result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of finding compact, high-performing sparse neural networks without the costly multi-stage pipeline of traditional pruning methods. Its key insight is to jointly learn both network weights and a trainable, layer-wise pruning threshold via backpropagation so that the sparse structure is adapted dynamically during standard training rather than imposed afterward. The method introduces masked layers with learnable thresholds that push small-magnitude activations/weights to zero and are optimized alongside weights, enabling the model to reach high sparsity with little performance loss in the same number of epochs as dense training. Empirical results show competitive or superior sparsity–accuracy tradeoffs across architectures and reveal that dynamic, fine-grained thresholding exposes limitations of three-stage pruning and offers guidance for designing inherently compact networks.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of making neural architecture search (NAS) fast and broadly applicable to diverse, under-explored domains beyond computer vision, where AutoML could have the most impact. The key insight is that fixing a standard CNN topology but searching only over operation choices—specifically kernel sizes and dilations—gives rich multi-resolution feature extraction while dramatically reducing the search space, and that leveraging the Fourier diagonalization of convolution lets one efficiently compute mixtures of these operations. result.text: The paper tackles the high computational cost of self-consistency (SC) decoding for chain-of-thought multi-step reasoning, which boosts accuracy by aggregating many sampled reasoning traces but requires expensive, fixed-size sampling. The key insight is that SC’s consensus often emerges long before the preset number of samples, so dynamically stopping sampling once the answer distribution stabilizes preserves accuracy while cutting cost. They propose Early-Stopping Self-Consistency (ESC), a simple scalable procedure that monitors sampled outputs and halts further sampling when a confidence or stability criterion is met, plus a control scheme to trade off performance and cost per task/model. Empirical evaluation across arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic benchmarks with diverse model scales shows ESC dramatically reduces average sample counts (e.g., GSM8K -80.1%, MATH -33.8%) while maintaining comparable reasoning performance.

result.text: The paper addresses why deterministic gradient descent (GD) — without any explicit stochastic gradient noise — can nonetheless display random-like long-time behavior when optimizing multiscale objective functions. The key insight is that using a learning rate large enough to smooth over microscopic (fast) oscillations but small enough to resolve macroscopic structure effectively induces chaotic, noise-like dynamics so that GD does not settle at a single local minimizer but instead samples a statistical steady state. The authors formalize this by constructing a stochastic map with bounded noise that approximates the coarse-grained GD iterates, prove a sufficient condition under which the long-time distribution is well approximated by a rescaled Gibbs measure, and support the theory with numerical experiments showing convergence to statistical distributions rather than point minima.

result.text: The paper addresses inefficient and imbalanced token-to-expert routing in sparsely-activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, where fixed top-k routing can leave experts under- or over-trained and tokens unfairly limited in expert access. The key insight is to reverse the selection direction—have experts choose the top-k tokens to serve rather than forcing tokens to pick a fixed number of experts—so each expert maintains a fixed bucket size while tokens can be routed to a variable number of experts, improving load balance and utilization. The method implements this “expert choice” routing within heterogeneous MoEs, compares it to prior top-1 and top-2 gating schemes under equal computational budgets, and demonstrates that expert choice yields over 2× faster pretraining convergence and better downstream fine-tuning performance on GLUE/SuperGLUE tasks, and even outperforms a dense T5 baseline on several tasks at lower activation cost.

result.text: The paper tackles inefficient exploration in cooperative value-based multi-agent RL under centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE), where monotonic mixing of individual utilities into a joint-action value harms performance on tasks with nonmonotonic returns. The key insight is to use universal successor features (USFs) to learn policies for related auxiliary tasks with simpler reward structures, and to interleave those policies during exploration so the learned monotonic joint-value for the target task better recognizes and prioritizes useful coordinated joint actions. UneVEn implements this by sampling related tasks, training USFs to obtain task-conditioned exploration policies, and applying novel action-selection schemes that switch between these sampled-task policies during exploration while still learning the target joint-action value for decentralized execution. Empirically, this approach yields substantially better coordination and higher returns than state-of-the-art baselines on a challenging predator–prey benchmark.

result.text: The paper addresses the high computational cost and potential instability of decision-focused learning, where an optimization problem with unknown parameters is embedded in the prediction-training loop and must be solved and differentiated through at each iteration. Its key insight is that a compact, quality-aware surrogate of the original optimization—built by representing the feasible space with a small set of meta-variables that are linear combinations of the original variables—can both speed up training/inference and smooth the learning landscape by concentrating capacity on the most decision-relevant directions. The method jointly trains a low-dimensional surrogate optimization model and the predictive model end-to-end, replacing the full problem with the surrogate during training and inference so gradients and solves are cheaper and better behaved; experiments on adversary modeling, submodular recommendation, and portfolio optimization show large runtime reductions and improved decision quality.

result.text: The paper tackles operator learning for solving PDEs by approximating the inverse map from input coefficients/forcing to solution functions in a resolution-independent way. The key insight is that PDE solution operators have kernels that are efficiently compressible in a multiwavelet basis, so explicitly projecting and learning the kernel’s multi-scale multiwavelet coefficients lets the model capture dependencies across scales while remaining numerically compact. Methodologically, the authors embed inverse multiwavelet filters into a neural operator architecture that computes repeated multiwavelet transforms to train projected kernel components at multiple scales, and they demonstrate this scheme on KdV, Burgers’, Darcy, and Navier–Stokes problems, achieving substantially lower relative L2 errors and the ability to generalize from coarse training data to high-resolution inference.

result.text: The paper addresses Generalized Category Discovery (GCD), where a dataset has both labeled and unlabeled images and the goal is to cluster the unlabeled images into both known and novel classes consistent with the taxonomy implied by the labeled set. The key insight is that existing benchmarks often admit a single natural partition, so models can succeed by unsupervised grouping rather than by extrapolating the labeled taxonomy; to reveal this, the authors introduce Clevr-4, a synthetic dataset with four equally valid mutually orthogonal partitions (shape, texture, color, count) that forces methods to follow the labeled taxonomy. They show strong unsupervised methods fail on Clevr-4 and identify weaknesses in prior GCD algorithms, then propose μGCD, a simple mean-teacher–based method that leverages consistency regularization from representation learning to align unlabeled clustering with the labeled taxonomy; μGCD substantially outperforms baselines on Clevr-4 and achieves state-of-the-art results on the real-data Semantic Shift Benchmark.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of removing backdoor triggers implanted in deep neural networks—poisoned training-time manipulations that leave clean accuracy intact but force targeted misclassification when a trigger appears. Its key insight is that backdoored models exhibit altered intermediate-layer attention patterns that can be corrected by aligning the compromised model’s attention with that of a cleanly fine-tuned teacher, thereby erasing the trigger’s effect without degrading normal performance. The proposed method, Neural Attention Distillation (NAD), obtains a teacher by independently fine-tuning on a small clean subset and then distills its intermediate attention maps into the backdoored student during further fine-tuning on that same clean data, using attention-alignment losses to guide the student toward the teacher’s behavior. Empirically NAD removes backdoors from models infected by multiple state-of-the-art attacks using only 5% clean data while preserving accuracy on clean examples.

result.text: The paper addresses the poor generalization of supervised learning models for the traveling salesman problem (TSP), aiming to apply a model trained on small instances to arbitrarily large graphs. The key insight is to reuse a small pre-trained model as a localized feature extractor: by sampling and converting subgraphs from a large instance, producing heat maps that indicate promising edges or nodes, and then merging these heat maps to obtain a global guidance signal. args.text: We propose Structure-Conditioned Prompt Distillation (SCPD) for text-attributed graphs: an LLM teacher consumes subgraph textualizations whose encoding is automatically selected per task and per graph topology, while a compact graph transformer student learns from the teacher. Concretely, we use an SGFormer-style one-layer global-attention backbone equipped with structure-aware G-Adapters, and distill multi-granularity signals (node, motif, graph) from the LLM—including hidden states and attention patterns—via contrastive/alignment losses, with TokenGT-style token bridges to map textual evidence onto node/edge tokens. A small controller chooses among graph-to-text encoders based on topology statistics and validation feedback, ensuring the LLM sees the most informative context for each task and regime. We additionally fuse neighborhood signals during training in a GraphFormers-like interleaving schedule to stabilize semantics, hypothesizing that SCPD matches LLM-level semantic understanding in a highly efficient student while improving robustness under heterophily and long-range dependencies.

We propose Offline Language-Conditioned Active Neural SLAM: a modular navigator that learns from passive roaming videos to build predictive, uncertainty-aware semantic maps and a subgoal value function defined in a shared image–text embedding space. Using offline RL with a conservative Q-learning regularizer, we train the global policy to choose exploration subgoals that trade off predicted goal likelihood and epistemic uncertainty while avoiding out-of-distribution overestimation; pseudo-actions and rewards are derived from video via action inference and hindsight goal relabeling. At test time, free-form language or image goals are projected into the embedding to produce semantic likelihood heatmaps that are fused with the predictive map, while a classical planner and learned local policy execute short-horizon motion as in Active Neural SLAM. We hypothesize strong zero-shot ImageNav/ObjectNav performance and improved sim-to-real transfer, with gains scaling with passive data and robust under noisy state estimation.

result.text: The paper addresses improving variational inference for Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) and deep Gaussian processes (DGPs) by capturing inter-layer posterior dependencies that standard factorized approximations miss. The key insight is that the optimal posterior over top-layer weights depends strongly on lower-layer weights, so defining a correlated posterior via inducing inputs only at the network input and propagating them through the network—so-called global inducing points—can model those cross-layer dependencies compactly. Methodologically, the authors derive the optimal top-layer posterior for regression BNNs, use that structure to construct a correlated variational family across all layers, extend the approach to DGPs by unifying inference via propagated inducing inputs rather than independent per-layer inducing sets, and learn the global inducing points jointly with model parameters to achieve strong empirical performance (e.g., 86.7% on CIFAR-10) without augmentation or tempering.

args.text: Compute-Optimal Granularity Scheduling (COGS) for MoE. Instead of fixing expert size and k throughout training, we derive and implement a training-time schedule for expert granularity and activation that follows asymmetric compute-optimality, allocating more FLOPs to additional steps early and shifting to larger experts later. We combine the MoE granularity scaling law with solvable training dynamics that explain time-vs-width exponents to predict phase boundaries and a two-stage policy: begin with many small experts and higher routing entropy to harvest step-driven gains under data reuse, then merge/swell experts and reduce activation as capacity/embedding limits dominate. A DynMoE-style controller prunes and grows experts online to track the schedule, and theory predicts lower loss per FLOP and smaller train–test gaps than any static granularity under fixed-day budgets.

result.text: The paper addresses improving complex problem-solving with large language models by overcoming limitations of static chain-of-thought prompts and the need for effective exploration and self-evaluation. Its key insight is that iteratively generating many trial reasoning traces, using the model to evaluate and extract error patterns, and then bootstrapping revised prompts from that ensemble produces stronger reasoning behavior than single-shot exemplars. The method, called Boosting of Thoughts (BoT), starts from a simple prompt, repeatedly explores large trees of candidate reasoning steps, solicits model self-evaluations to identify and analyze errors, uses those analyses to automatically revise and refine prompting, and repeats this loop until a final answer is produced. Experiments with GPT-4 and Llama2 on challenging math problems show BoT yields higher or comparable solve rates versus prior advanced prompting techniques.

result.text: The paper tackles offline reinforcement learning, where the challenge is to learn reliable policies from fixed logged data without environment interaction, focusing on avoiding overoptimistic behavior in regions poorly covered by the dataset. Its key insight is to cast model-based offline RL as a two-player zero-sum game in which an adversarial dynamics model is trained to both fit the dataset and minimize the policy’s estimated value, thereby inducing pessimism where the data is scarce. The method, RAMBO, alternates between policy optimization inside the learned model and adversarial model updates that trade off data likelihood with value minimization, yielding a conservative value estimate that provably lower-bounds true performance under PAC-style guarantees. result.text: The paper addresses communication bottlenecks in distributed/federated optimization by unifying two previously separate approaches for gradient compression—variance-reduced unbiased compressors (DIANA) and error-feedback for biased contractive compressors (EF21)—into a single framework that can handle both. The key insight is that compressors can be characterized by two parameters (bias and variance), and by designing an algorithm that exploits both error feedback and variance-reduction ideas one can recover DIANA and EF21 as special cases while enabling a broader class of compressors. The proposed method introduces a new algorithm (EF-BV) that operates with this generalized compressor class, combines independent randomness across workers with an error-correction mechanism, and leverages variance reduction to improve convergence as the number of workers grows. The authors prove linear convergence under suitable conditions, showing that EF-BV inherits the practical benefits of biased compressors like top-k and the theoretical scaling advantages of randomized unbiased schemes.

Its key insight is that standard distillation misses the ensemble’s functional diversity, particularly when members have near-zero training error, so the student must be exposed to regions where ensemble members disagree. The proposed method augments distillation with a perturbation strategy that searches for inputs that elicit disagreement among ensemble members and uses those perturbed samples during training so the student can absorb diverse behaviors. Empirically this approach yields distilled models with enhanced captured diversity and improved accuracy and calibration, narrowing the gap to full ensembles.

The key insight is that deterministic, learned routing is not necessary and that forcing diverse experts to behave consistently via mutual supervision can make randomly activated experts both robust and parameter-efficient. The authors propose THOR, which stochastically activates a random expert per input during training and inference and trains experts with a consistency-regularized loss so each expert learns from ground-truth labels and from other experts as teachers, encouraging aligned predictions across experts. result.text: LongVideoBench addresses the lack of public benchmarks for evaluating large multimodal models (LMMs) on long, interleaved video-language inputs by introducing a question-answering dataset that tests long-term multimodal understanding up to hour-long videos. The key insight is that the central challenge is not only locating relevant segments but performing "referring reasoning"—answering questions that include references to specific video contexts (referred contexts) and require retrieving and reasoning over detailed multimodal evidence from those segments. To operationalize this, the authors collect 3,763 web videos with subtitles and create 6,678 human-annotated multiple-choice questions across 17 fine-grained categories that force models to find and reason over relevant frames and language; evaluation shows current top commercial LMMs still struggle and that performance improves when models can process more frames, highlighting LongVideoBench’s value for next-generation long-context LMM development.

result.text: The paper tackles protecting open-source image datasets from unauthorized model training by improving “unlearnable examples” — imperceptibly perturbed images that poison downstream training — to be robust against adversarially trained attackers. The key insight is that prior robustness gains mainly came from strengthening the surrogate model used to craft defensive noise, while the noise itself was unstable and even negatively correlated with protection, so replacing expensive adversarial perturbations with randomized perturbations can stabilize and improve noise effectiveness. The authors propose Stable Error-Minimizing (SEM) noise, which trains defensive perturbations against random (stochastic) perturbations rather than iterative adversarial ones, yielding more stable and efficient noise generation. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and an ImageNet subset show SEM outperforms prior methods in both protection effectiveness and computational efficiency.

result.text: CAGroup3D tackles accurate 3D object detection in point-clouds by addressing limitations of bottom-up grouping methods that ignore class consistency and lose voxels due to segmentation errors. The key insight is to form class-aware local groups on surface voxels that share the same semantic prediction to create higher-quality proposals, and then to recover missed fine-grained geometry by pooling directly from the sparse backbone. Concretely, the method is a two-stage fully sparse-convolutional detector: a first stage generates proposals via class-aware grouping of voxels, and a second stage refines them with a memory- and computation-efficient sparse RoI pooling module that aggregates backbone features for each proposal, yielding substantial mAP gains on ScanNetV2 and SUN RGB-D.

result.text: The paper examines why physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), which impose PDE constraints as soft losses, often fail on nontrivial PDEs despite expressive architectures, attributing failures to ill-conditioning and an extremely challenging loss landscape created by PDE-based regularization rather than model capacity. The key insight is that the standard simultaneous enforcement of complex differential operators across space-time makes optimization hard, so training struggles even when the network can represent the solution. result.text: The paper tackles the gap between neural combinatorial optimization methods that produce good single-shot solutions and classical hand-crafted heuristics that effectively exploit available compute via search, aiming to give neural methods a search procedure that leverages solving time. The method, simulation-guided beam search (SGBS), performs beam search where candidate ordering uses both neural-policy probabilities and rollout evaluations, and is integrated with efficient active search (EAS) by using SGBS outputs to update the policy and using the improved policy to drive better SGBS exploration. result.text: The paper investigates how commonly used baselines in policy gradient methods affect optimization beyond merely reducing gradient variance, showing that baseline choice can change the optimization dynamics and even harm learning despite lower variance. The key insight is that baselines influence the update direction and curvature of the expected update—so two baselines with identical variance can lead to different trajectories and convergence properties, and some baselines can cause natural policy gradient to converge to suboptimal policies for any stepsize when sampling is tied to the current policy. The authors analyze simple illustrative examples and theoretical conditions, and propose decoupling the sampling policy from the current policy to restore robust convergence for a much broader set of baselines, arguing for treating stochasticity in updates more carefully than by variance reduction alone.

args.text: We propose Cross-Modal Semantics-Augmented Sampling (CM-SAS) for point-based LiDAR detectors: instead of deriving per-point foreground scores purely from 3D features, we project points into an image branch trained for spatially aware cues (e.g., local coordinate maps) and fuse its 2D foreground/boundary logits with 3D evidence to produce calibration-aware per-point sampling weights. A lightweight point-to-pixel aligner with a learned reliability gate down-weights visual cues under occlusion or low light, and the fused scores jointly drive both set-abstraction down-sampling and loss weighting so that more object-relevant and contour points are retained. This cross-modal sampling is especially beneficial for far or small objects where LiDAR is sparse, improving recall with negligible overhead and complementing image-to-point gradient coupling. The module is plug-and-play and can replace standard or semantics-only sampling in point-based backbones.

result.text: The paper studies whether ordering training examples by difficulty (curriculum) or by difficulty-reverse (anti-curriculum) actually improves neural network learning compared to standard i.i.d. training. The authors observe that networks exhibit strong implicit curricula from architecture and optimization biases—samples are learned in a highly consistent order—and then run extensive experiments across thousands of explicit orderings (curriculum, anti-curriculum, and a random-curriculum that grows dataset size over time) to isolate effects. They find that on standard benchmarks explicit curricula yield only marginal gains and that random ordering with a dynamically increasing dataset performs as well or better, implying most apparent benefits come from changing dataset size rather than ordering; however, curriculum (not anti-curriculum) does provide meaningful gains under limited training time budgets or when labels are noisy. The method combines empirical analysis of implicit learning order with large-scale controlled comparisons across ordering strategies and varied training conditions to pinpoint when curricula are truly beneficial.

result.text: The paper addresses efficient and expressive parameterization of the bounded linear operators that define neural operators for learning mappings between function spaces (e.g., solutions of PDEs), noting that previous architectures rely on costly lifting/projection layers and can struggle with training or overfitting. The key insight is that these inter-neuron linear operators can be compactly and effectively represented using multigrid-style hierarchies, which both satisfy the required operator-theoretic properties and provide practical inductive biases for multiscale structure and boundary conditions. The proposed MgNO architecture implements this insight by replacing per-neuron linear maps with multigrid parameterizations that operate across scales, eliminating separate lifting/projecting layers and naturally handling various boundary conditions. Empirically, MgNO trains more easily than CNN-based baselines, generalizes better than spectral neural operators, and achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and efficiency on a range of PDE benchmarks.

result.text: The paper tackles semi-supervised learning by asking how to effectively leverage plentiful unlabeled data with minimal labeled examples. Its key insight is that combining consistency regularization (make predictions invariant under strong augmentation) with confidence-thresholded pseudo-labeling (use only high-confidence predictions from weakly-augmented inputs as targets) yields a simple yet powerful training signal. The FixMatch method generates pseudo-labels from weakly-augmented unlabeled images, keeps only those above a confidence threshold, and trains the model to predict those labels on corresponding strongly-augmented versions, alongside standard supervised loss on labeled data. This straightforward approach achieves state-of-the-art results on standard SSL benchmarks and the paper includes extensive ablations showing which design choices drive its success.

args.text: We propose Factorized Riemannian Diffusion: a generative model that learns a product-of-submanifolds latent geometry for controllable generation without labeled factors. It combines Riemannian score-based diffusion with a variational likelihood on product manifolds and a weak pairwise constraint that two samples share at least one factor, aligning the corresponding submanifold coordinates while letting others vary. A de Rham–style prior encourages diffusion-invariant subspaces and we add an isometric regularizer to preserve local distances within each factor; optionally, factor flows are parameterized by learned Lie-algebra generators to capture continuous symmetries. The result is a model that jointly learns metrics and scores per factor, enabling linear factor editing, targeted conditional sampling, and improved inversion across image and sequential domains.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of producing interpretable natural language explanations for model predictions without requiring large amounts of costly human-annotated explanations. Its key insight is to treat explanations as latent variables that capture the model’s reasoning and can be learned jointly with prediction, so a small set of labeled explanations can bootstrap explanation generation for much more data. The method is a variational EM framework that alternately trains an explanation-generation module and an explanation-augmented prediction module so they mutually improve, and it extends to semi-supervised learning via explanation-based self-training that assigns pseudo-labels to unlabeled examples and iteratively generates explanations to refine both modules. Experiments on two NLU tasks show the approach yields effective predictions and coherent natural language explanations in both supervised and semi-supervised settings.

result.text: The paper addresses why linear graph convolutional networks (GCNs)—which replace nonlinear transforms with repeated linear feature propagation—fail to improve when using many propagation steps despite their efficiency. The key insight is to view linear propagation as a continuous graph diffusion process and recognize that tying the number of discrete propagation steps to the terminal diffusion time limits expressiveness and leads to over-smoothing or ineffective diffusion. To fix this, the authors introduce Decoupled Graph Convolution (DGC), which separates the terminal diffusion time from the number of propagation iterations so that the model can control diffusion strength independently of computational steps, enabling effective exploitation of many propagation steps and substantially improving performance of linear GCNs to rival nonlinear variants.

args.text: Active Diffusion-Assisted Triplane Refinement: start with a feed-forward large reconstruction model that predicts a triplane NeRF from a single image, and attach a lightweight adapter that applies a low-rank delta to the triplane features conditioned on a small set of synchronized novel views synthesized by a multi-view diffusion prior. At test time, the base model also outputs per-ray/voxel uncertainty; these uncertainties drive an active view selection loop that queries the diffusion prior for the most informative viewpoints, then refines the field via one or two adapter updates, yielding improved back-view geometry and sharper textures in seconds. We train the system end-to-end with multi-view photometric and cycle-consistency losses, distilling geometry-aware denoising signals from the diffusion prior to encourage calibrated uncertainty and minimal corrections. This combines the speed and generalization of single-shot 3D prediction with probabilistic modeling of unseen parts and multi-view synchronization, enabling controllable quality–compute tradeoffs.

result.text: The paper addresses the under-explored problem that high variance in model predictions makes many binary classification decisions effectively arbitrary, which confounds evaluation and intervention in algorithmic fairness. The key insight is that prediction variance—captured by a proposed self-consistency metric—can both quantify arbitrariness and reveal that many benchmark datasets already appear close-to-fair once arbitrary decisions are accounted for. Methodologically, the authors introduce self-consistency as a variance-derived proxy, design an ensemble-based abstention algorithm that refuses to classify examples with high arbitrariness, run the largest empirical study to date on variance and fairness across HMDA benchmarks, and release a toolkit to facilitate future work; their experiments show that ignoring prediction variance can lead to misleading conclusions about fairness and the value of fairness interventions.

result.text: The paper addresses the high computational cost of vision transformers (ViTs), particularly the quadratic scaling with token count and limitations of existing token-reduction methods that either break spatial structure or require costly pretraining. Its key insight is to perform dynamic, instance-wise token selection using the transformer’s native global class attention and then treat retained (“informative”) and dropped (“uninformative”) tokens differently through a slow-fast updating scheme that preserves spatial structure and information flow. The method, called Evo-ViT, selects tokens via class-attention-based scoring and routes selected tokens through more frequent, heavier updates while routing unselected tokens through lighter, less frequent updates, enabling compatibility with both flat and deep-narrow ViT architectures from training start. Experiments show Evo-ViT greatly reduces FLOPs and increases throughput (e.g., >60% speedup on DeiT-S) with minimal accuracy loss (~0.4% top-1 on ImageNet-1K), outperforming prior pruning approaches in efficiency and accuracy.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of reconstructing accurate continuous surfaces from 3D point clouds by learning signed distance functions (SDFs). result.text: The paper addresses scalable solution of robust Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), where transition model uncertainty makes standard dynamic programming computationally expensive and poorly scalable in the number of states S and actions A. args.text: We propose a Distributional Projection-Robust Wasserstein (DPRW) discrepancy that replaces the single worst-case k-dimensional subspace in PRW with a learned probability measure over the Grassmann manifold, penalized by entropy or an f-divergence to interpolate between max-projection and sliced/averaged regimes. This smooths the objective and improves conditioning, enabling efficient algorithms that combine Riemannian block-coordinate updates (for transport vs. subspace distribution) with corrected Riemannian extragradient steps, while parameterizing the distribution sparsely via a small atomic mixture learned by a Grassmannian Frank–Wolfe. With entropic OT in the inner problems, the distributional and entropic regularization can induce local geodesic strong convexity–concavity, suggesting last-iterate linear rates and better complexity than max-only PRW. Empirically, DPRW should be less brittle and lower-variance than PRW on high-dimensional generative modeling and robust shift benchmarks, while retaining robustness absent from uniform sliced approaches.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of combining client-level differential privacy with communication-efficient federated learning, noting that existing compression techniques and privacy mechanisms have not been jointly optimized. Its key insight is that by unifying compression operators with a flexible family of local gradient estimators (including variance-reduced methods and shifted compression schemes), one can design algorithms that preserve local differential privacy while improving communication complexity without degrading utility. The proposed method, SoteriaFL, first analyzes the pitfalls of naively compressing differentially private SGD and then introduces a general framework that integrates noise-adding for local differential privacy with tailored compressed gradient estimators and variance-reduction/shift strategies. The authors provide theoretical characterizations of the trade-offs among privacy, utility, and communication, showing SoteriaFL attains strictly better communication complexity than prior private federated learning methods that do not use compression while maintaining comparable privacy and utility.

result.text: The paper addresses the high computational cost of vision transformers (ViTs), particularly the quadratic scaling with token count and limitations of existing token-reduction methods that either break spatial structure or require costly pretraining. Its key insight is to perform dynamic, instance-wise token selection using the transformer’s native global class attention and then treat retained (“informative”) and dropped (“uninformative”) tokens differently through a slow-fast updating scheme that preserves spatial structure and information flow. The method, called Evo-ViT, selects tokens via class-attention-based scoring and routes selected tokens through more frequent, heavier updates while routing unselected tokens through lighter, less frequent updates, enabling compatibility with both flat and deep-narrow ViT architectures from training start. Experiments show Evo-ViT greatly reduces FLOPs and increases throughput (e.g., >60% speedup on DeiT-S) with minimal accuracy loss (~0.4% top-1 on ImageNet-1K), outperforming prior pruning approaches in efficiency and accuracy.

args.text: We propose cage-conditioned deformation priors for NeRF editing that combine a category-agnostic cage with a learned library of local deformation fields anchored to cage vertices/faces, trained from diverse non-rigid mesh deformations to enforce plausible, spatially coherent motion. At edit time, text or handle inputs select and weight these cage-local codes under a ViCA-NeRF–style latent consistency objective to maintain cross-view alignment, while the induced 4D warp is realized with a voxelized deformation grid for real-time feedback. args.text: We propose MoTEx-TKG, a contrastively gated temporal mixture-of-experts that routes each query to the most suitable forecasting mechanism. A CENET-style history-vs-nonhistory detector selects among (i) a TEILP-like interpretable temporal-rule walker with interval PDFs for time prediction, (ii) a neural embedding expert (e.g., ChronoR/BoxTE) for novel, pattern-disruptive links, and (iii) a CyGNet-style copy-generation head to exploit recurrences; for cold-start entities, a MetaTKGR-inspired meta-adapter rapidly personalizes the gate and experts from few observations. Joint training alternates expert-specific losses with a routing objective that maximizes contrastive separability of history-driven vs non-history queries and adds a calibration head for uncertainty-aware rankings. This yields accuracy across regimes (repetitive, novel, cold-start) while preserving rule-based explanations when the rule expert is chosen.

args.text: We propose Dual-Space Curvature Smoothing (DSCS), a fast adversarial training regime that prevents catastrophic overfitting by jointly flattening the loss in input- and weight-space at near single-step cost. Concretely, we couple diversified, non-maximal FGSM perturbations with a small-radius SAM step enhanced by a GSAM-style surrogate-gap reduction and random weight smoothing, and add a light GradAlign penalty to explicitly reduce input-loss curvature; a FOSC-based schedule gradually increases these regularizers and adversary fidelity over training. This dual smoothing blunts boundary concentration and stabilizes the inner maximization, yielding robust accuracy competitive with multi-step PGD while maintaining clean accuracy via flatter minima. We evaluate with a parameter-free attack ensemble to ensure no gradient obfuscation and analyze improvements via reduced dominant Hessian eigenvalues and lower variance of adversarial directions.

Its key insight is that every calibration error can be paired with a proper scoring rule, yielding a "proper calibration error" that upper-bounds the original error and admits estimators with optimal (unbiased and consistent) properties. The authors propose a framework that constructs these proper calibration errors from proper scores, derive estimators and theoretical guarantees, and empirically show that common calibration estimators perform worse than the proposed approach. Because proper scores exist beyond classification, the method naturally extends recalibration techniques to broader prediction tasks.

args.text: We propose segmented control-variate hybrid gradients for nonsmooth differentiable physics. Long-horizon rollouts are partitioned at detected nonsmooth events (contacts, plastic yielding), and exact simulator gradients are used only within smooth segments as a control variate for a global likelihood-ratio estimator, with a learned per-segment alpha blending based on local smoothness/stiffness metrics estimated via small randomized smoothing probes; this preserves unbiasedness while sharply reducing variance and avoids the structural bias of reparameterization gradients at discontinuities. Event detection and segmentation leverage localized mesh-based contact solvers, and the alpha-scheduler is meta-learned across tasks. We evaluate on PlasticineLab and long-horizon tool-use sequences composed from short-horizon skills, demonstrating improved sample efficiency and stability over prior hybrid estimators.

The key insight is that this behavior is not chaotic but driven by a self-stabilization mechanism: instability pushes iterates along the top eigenvector, and the cubic term in the local Taylor expansion reduces curvature in that direction until stability is restored, causing GD to oscillate around the sharpness cutoff. The key insight is that moderate mutual distillation among experts can broaden each expert's effective training signal by sharing useful features and predictions learned by other experts, improving individual expert competence on their assigned inputs without collapsing specialization. The proposed method, MoDE, implements mutual distillation regularization across experts during training—encouraging them to mimic useful aspects of each other’s outputs while preserving gating-driven specialization—and is validated across tabular, NLP, and CV benchmarks, with an "expert probing" analysis that empirically shows distilled knowledge improves per-expert and overall MoE performance.

args.text: We propose replacing heuristic selection in theorem proving and branch-and-bound with an exact solution to a regularized policy optimization computed at each search node over a sampled subset of candidate expansions, using learned priors and value/effort estimates; this yields a principled alternative to PUCT and greedy/RL branching. Concretely, we maximize estimated downstream return (or minimize search cost) plus an entropy/KL regularizer to a prior policy over a Sampled MuZero–style action subset, and expand according to the exact optimizer rather than an approximation. We integrate this with an operator-style policy improvement–projection loop to update the parameterized policy online from search trajectories, applying the framework to HyperTree Proof Search and MCS BnB branching. We hypothesize tighter exploration control and reduced tree sizes versus HTPS/PUCT and RL-only branching, especially in high-branching regimes where subset sampling preserves structure while keeping per-node optimization tractable.

result.text: The paper addresses reliable off-policy estimation of the stationary-state density ratio between a target policy and the sampling distribution, pointing out that prior GenDICE formulations become non–convex-concave when enforced positivity via nonlinear parameterizations, breaking convergence guarantees despite being necessary for consistency. args.text: I propose Position-Aware Capacity Reservation (PACR) for Mixture-of-Experts routing to mitigate the observed drop-towards-the-end effect in MoE LLMs. PACR augments expert-choice routing with a lightweight admission controller that forecasts per-position token load within each microbatch (via sequence length and running position-conditioned load histograms) and reserves a fraction of each expert’s bucket for later positions; unused reservations decay within the step so early tokens can backfill idle capacity. args.text: We propose VectorTextDiff, a layered text-to-image/editing pipeline that couples a standard diffusion backbone with a differentiable vector-text renderer to produce crisp, multilingual, typographically correct text at arbitrary resolution. result.text: We propose Offline Language-Conditioned Active Neural SLAM: a modular navigator that learns from passive roaming videos to build predictive, uncertainty-aware semantic maps and a subgoal value function defined in a shared image–text embedding space. Using offline RL with a conservative Q-learning regularizer, we train the global policy to choose exploration subgoals that trade off predicted goal likelihood and epistemic uncertainty while avoiding out-of-distribution overestimation; pseudo-actions and rewards are derived from video via action inference and hindsight goal relabeling. At test time, free-form language or image goals are projected into the embedding to produce semantic likelihood heatmaps that are fused with the predictive map, while a classical planner and learned local policy execute short-horizon motion as in Active Neural SLAM. We hypothesize strong zero-shot ImageNav/ObjectNav performance and improved sim-to-real transfer, with gains scaling with passive data and robust under noisy state estimation.

result.text: The paper addresses the gap between fast but sometimes suboptimal chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning and the more deliberative but computationally expensive tree-of-thought (ToT) search, aiming to retain ToT-quality reasoning without its inference cost. The key insight is that the preference information implicitly generated during ToT search—i.e., which partial reasoning branches lead to better final solutions—can be used as supervision to teach a model to prefer those better reasoning steps during standard CoT decoding. The method, called Chain of Preference Optimization (CPO), fine-tunes LLMs by aligning each step of generated CoT traces with the preferred steps extracted from ToT trees, effectively distilling the tree search’s selection signals into the model so it produces higher-quality reasoning chains at inference time. Empirical results across QA, fact verification, and arithmetic tasks show that CPO yields substantial improvements in problem-solving accuracy while avoiding the heavy inference overhead of running ToT.

args.text: We propose LF-ODE-ECG, a generative model that evolves a low-dimensional cardiac source state with a neural ODE and renders multi-lead ECG via a fixed or lightly personalized biophysical lead-field matrix, enforcing cross-lead consistency by construction. result.text: Compute-Optimal Granularity Scheduling (COGS) for MoE. Instead of fixing expert size and k throughout training, we derive and implement a training-time schedule for expert granularity and activation that follows asymmetric compute-optimality, allocating more FLOPs to additional steps early and shifting to larger experts later. We combine the MoE granularity scaling law with solvable training dynamics that explain time-vs-width exponents to predict phase boundaries and a two-stage policy: begin with many small experts and higher routing entropy to harvest step-driven gains under data reuse, then merge/swell experts and reduce activation as capacity/embedding limits dominate. A DynMoE-style controller prunes and grows experts online to track the schedule, and theory predicts lower loss per FLOP and smaller train–test gaps than any static granularity under fixed-day budgets.

result.text: The paper addresses real-time, high-fidelity novel view rendering for dynamic scenes, where prior NeRF-based approaches rely on slow per-scene MLP deformation models and yield limited quality. The key insight is to replace implicit deformation networks with an explicit, clustered Gaussian representation: grouping 3D Gaussians that share similar properties (rotation, translation, location) into compact "superpoints" so motion can be modeled and rendered efficiently. The method reconstructs the scene with explicit 3D Gaussians, forms superpoints by clustering based on Gaussian attributes, and uses superpoint-driven Gaussian splatting to render dynamic frames with minimal extra computation.
