result.text: The paper tackles the overlooked safety problem that instruction-tuned LLMs do not reliably distinguish between user instructions and data, leaving them vulnerable to manipulations like indirect prompt injection and unsuitable for safety-critical use. The key insight is that this vulnerability can be formalized and measured: by defining a principled notion of instruction–data separation and deriving an empirical estimator based on model outputs, one can quantify how much a model treats parts of its input as executable instructions versus inert data. The authors operationalize this idea by creating the SEP dataset and evaluation protocol to compute the empirical separation measure on real models, and they evaluate multiple LLMs to show that all exhibit poor separation and that typical mitigations (prompt engineering, fine-tuning) offer little improvement or trade off utility. Their released code and dataset provide a foundation for benchmarking and developing methods to improve instruction–data separation in future work.

The paper addresses the limitation of current Video-LLMs that can only grasp coarse-grained video semantics and thus fail at tasks requiring comprehension or localization of specific temporal segments. The key insight is that training a Video-LLM on large-scale, segment-level instruction data enables fine-grained temporal reasoning and grounding rather than just global video understanding. To realize this, the authors build an automatic data-generation engine to create Moment-10M, a massive dataset of videos paired with segment-level instructions, and train Momentor on this data so it can reason about, locate, and answer questions about precise moments in videos; zero-shot evaluations show strong performance on temporally grounded comprehension and localization tasks.

result.text: The paper addresses inverse problems for partial differential equations that are naturally posed as mappings from operators (e.g., coefficient or boundary-condition maps) to solution functions, a setting that standard operator-learning frameworks—which map functions to functions—do not directly handle. The key insight is that by composing operator- and function-level neural architectures one can learn inverse operators directly: specifically, combining DeepONet’s branch/trunk structure for learning operator-to-function mappings with Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) components captures both local and global structure needed for stable inverse recovery. The proposed Neural Inverse Operator (NIO) architecture composes DeepONet and FNO modules in a mathematically motivated way to approximate operator→function maps, and is trained end-to-end on paired operator-function data; experiments show NIOs outperform baselines in accuracy and robustness while being orders of magnitude faster than traditional direct or PDE-constrained optimization methods.

result.text: The paper addresses shortcomings of Neural Processes (NPs)—notably underfitting and intractable likelihoods—that limit their ability to provide reliable uncertainty estimates for sequential decision-making tasks. The key insight is to reformulate uncertainty-aware meta-learning as a sequence modeling problem and train a likelihood-based autoregressive model that can capture richer predictive distributions while honoring NP symmetries (invariance to observed context points and equivariance to target inputs). args.text: Unify learned branching in branch-and-bound (BnB) with AlphaZero-style search-as-optimization by solving, at each node, an exact regularized policy optimization that minimizes predicted remaining tree size under a learned cost-to-solve model. Concretely, choose a branching distribution via a convex program that balances predicted pruning gains and bound tightening against exploration bonuses derived from epistemic uncertainty, with a regularizer anchoring to classical heuristic priors; expand branches by sampling from this optimized distribution. Train the cost-to-solve and uncertainty models online from BnB rollouts, analogous to AlphaZero self-play but with a BnB-specific objective, and show that under calibrated predictions the exact optimizer monotonically reduces expected tree size relative to heuristic selection. Evaluate on MCS/MCCS and related BnB tasks to demonstrate consistent runtime reductions over both traditional and RL-learned branching heuristics.

result.text: We propose Cross-Modal Semantics-Augmented Sampling (CM-SAS) for point-based LiDAR detectors: instead of deriving per-point foreground scores purely from 3D features, we project points into an image branch trained for spatially aware cues (e.g., local coordinate maps) and fuse its 2D foreground/boundary logits with 3D evidence to produce calibration-aware per-point sampling weights. A lightweight point-to-pixel aligner with a learned reliability gate down-weights visual cues under occlusion or low light, and the fused scores jointly drive both set-abstraction down-sampling and loss weighting so that more object-relevant and contour points are retained. This cross-modal sampling is especially beneficial for far or small objects where LiDAR is sparse, improving recall with negligible overhead and complementing image-to-point gradient coupling. The module is plug-and-play and can replace standard or semantics-only sampling in point-based backbones.

result.text: The paper tackles the difficulty of training GANs reliably and efficiently—specifically the need for heavy regularization, large compute, and long hyperparameter searches to reach high-quality image synthesis. Its key insight is that projecting real and generated images into a fixed, pretrained feature space (and importantly mixing features across channels and resolutions) gives the discriminator more useful, multi-scale information that it otherwise fails to exploit from deeper pretrained layers. The method, called Projected GAN, feeds both real and fake samples through a frozen feature extractor and supplies mixed, multi-resolution feature maps to the discriminator while keeping the generator trained adversarially; this change improves sample efficiency, stability, and convergence speed, scales to very high resolutions, and achieves state-of-the-art FID on many benchmarks—often matching prior best scores up to 40× faster.

result.text: We propose Structure-Conditioned Prompt Distillation (SCPD) for text-attributed graphs: an LLM teacher consumes subgraph textualizations whose encoding is automatically selected per task and per graph topology, while a compact graph transformer student learns from the teacher. Concretely, we use an SGFormer-style one-layer global-attention backbone equipped with structure-aware G-Adapters, and distill multi-granularity signals (node, motif, graph) from the LLM—including hidden states and attention patterns—via contrastive/alignment losses, with TokenGT-style token bridges to map textual evidence onto node/edge tokens. A small controller chooses among graph-to-text encoders based on topology statistics and validation feedback, ensuring the LLM sees the most informative context for each task and regime. We additionally fuse neighborhood signals during training in a GraphFormers-like interleaving schedule to stabilize semantics, hypothesizing that SCPD matches LLM-level semantic understanding in a highly efficient student while improving robustness under heterophily and long-range dependencies.

result.text: We propose Offline Language-Conditioned Active Neural SLAM: a modular navigator that learns from passive roaming videos to build predictive, uncertainty-aware semantic maps and a subgoal value function defined in a shared image–text embedding space. Using offline RL with a conservative Q-learning regularizer, we train the global policy to choose exploration subgoals that trade off predicted goal likelihood and epistemic uncertainty while avoiding out-of-distribution overestimation; pseudo-actions and rewards are derived from video via action inference and hindsight goal relabeling. At test time, free-form language or image goals are projected into the embedding to produce semantic likelihood heatmaps that are fused with the predictive map, while a classical planner and learned local policy execute short-horizon motion as in Active Neural SLAM. We hypothesize strong zero-shot ImageNav/ObjectNav performance and improved sim-to-real transfer, with gains scaling with passive data and robust under noisy state estimation.

Its key insight is to represent program transformation choices as a domain-specific probabilistic programming abstraction, enabling modular, stochastic specification of transformations that experts can analyze and extend. The method, MetaSchedule, implements this abstraction and pairs it with an end-to-end, learning-driven search framework to explore the rich, expert-extendable space and select optimized programs. args.text: We propose GW-TopoGCD, a topology-preserving prototype alignment framework for generalized category discovery under domain shift that aligns source and target prototype graphs via Gromov–Wasserstein transport, preserving semantic relations while permitting unmatched and many-to-one mappings to naturally accommodate novel target classes. We initialize and refine target prototypes with semantic-weighted soft assignments and decoupled optimization for known vs. novel groups, replacing brittle one-to-one bipartite matching with structure-aware transport that is robust to class splits/merges and unknown-class emergence. To prevent style cues from confounding alignment, we disentangle high-level semantics from low-level domain factors and minimize their mutual information, coupled with style-mixing augmentations to expand domain coverage. The joint objective minimizes GW distance between prototype graphs, enforces semantic–domain independence, and regularizes pseudo-labels, with an optional hierarchical split criterion (e.g., code-length/stability) to recover multi-granularity categories when warranted by target data.

result.text: The paper addresses slow and sometimes brittle inference in pretrained language models by enabling dynamic early stopping to save computation while maintaining or improving accuracy. The key insight is that attaching simple internal classifiers to each layer and stopping when their predictions stop changing for a fixed number of consecutive layers (a “patience” threshold) prevents overthinking and unnecessary deeper computation. The method—Patience-based Early Exit—therefore runs the model sequentially, checks intermediate predictions at each layer, and halts inference once the same class is predicted for a preset number of steps, yielding fewer average layers evaluated; experiments with ALBERT show this plug-and-play approach improves efficiency and robustness and gives a better accuracy-speed trade-off than prior early-exit strategies.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of offline model-based optimization, where a learned proxy model is used to optimize designs but performs poorly on out-of-distribution candidates; the key challenge is generating reliable labels for unseen designs to fine-tune the proxy. The key insight is that symmetric co-teaching among multiple proxies, driven by a rotating pseudo-labeler and reinforced by importance weighting via meta-learning, can selectively harvest high-quality pseudo-labeled samples near the current optimization trajectory and transfer trustworthy knowledge while mitigating label noise. The proposed method, Importance-aware Co-Teaching for Offline Model-based Optimization (ICT), maintains three symmetric proxies whose mean forms the final ensemble, repeatedly selects one proxy as a pseudo-labeler to generate local pseudo-data, uses a co-teaching scheme between the other two proxies to exchange small-loss (low-noise) samples for fine-tuning, and finally applies meta-learning-based sample reweighting to assign importance weights to pseudo-samples; this combination yields state-of-the-art performance across multiple design benchmarks.

args.text: We propose Meta-episodic Trigger-Invariant Few-Shot Learning (MTIF): a bi-level training scheme that hardens few-shot learners against hidden attractive/repulsive backdoors by combining an inner-loop input-conditioned perturbation adversary with outer-loop invariance learning. The adversary maximizes the feature gap on support sets (generalizing recent FSL backdoors), while the learner enforces prototype and representation consistency across clean/perturbed/augmented support–query views via contrastive and feature-shift regularization, targeting the transformation sensitivity characteristic of triggered samples. At meta-test, we attach a kNN/rNN head on the learned embedding to obtain instance-wise certificates on how many poisoned support examples per episode are required to flip predictions. This focuses on trigger-agnostic stability rather than visible artifacts and makes explicit the assumption that task-relevant features are stable across tasks/augmentations, addressing limits of general-purpose detection.

result.text: We propose Factorized Riemannian Diffusion: a generative model that learns a product-of-submanifolds latent geometry for controllable generation without labeled factors. It combines Riemannian score-based diffusion with a variational likelihood on product manifolds and a weak pairwise constraint that two samples share at least one factor, aligning the corresponding submanifold coordinates while letting others vary. A de Rham–style prior encourages diffusion-invariant subspaces and we add an isometric regularizer to preserve local distances within each factor; optionally, factor flows are parameterized by learned Lie-algebra generators to capture continuous symmetries. The result is a model that jointly learns metrics and scores per factor, enabling linear factor editing, targeted conditional sampling, and improved inversion across image and sequential domains.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem that making predictions can change the very outcomes they predict—“performative” effects—so standard supervised learning that treats data as fixed can fail as the prediction-decision loop induces distribution shift. The key insight is to formalize this feedback by treating the data-generating distribution as a function of the deployed predictor and introducing the equilibrium concept of performative stability, which requires predictions to be calibrated to the future outcomes that arise when decisions are made using those predictions. Methodologically, the authors develop a risk-minimization framework that models performative effects, derive necessary and sufficient conditions under which repeated retraining converges to performatively stable predictors with near-minimal loss, and show that this framework generalizes strategic classification, providing the first sufficient conditions for retraining to succeed in the presence of strategic feedback.

args.text: We propose Gradient-Calibrated Token Routing (GCTR) for fine-grained recognition: augment a ViT with a sub-pixel gradient-consistency prior computed from early features to flag high-frequency, part-discriminative regions, as in context-aware attentional pooling. This prior modulates class-attention-based token importance to produce a joint discriminativeness score, which drives an Evo-ViT-style slow–fast routing where high-priority tokens receive frequent heavy updates and low-priority/background tokens are updated lightly, while adding register tokens to prevent background artifacts from being co-opted. We further condition deformable token merging on the saliency prior so tokens do not merge across fine boundaries, preserving subtle cues at similar FLOPs. The result should improve the accuracy–efficiency trade-off on fine-grained benchmarks by retaining truly discriminative micro-structure while aggressively pruning redundant context.

We propose utility-driven lemma invention for neural theorem provers: instead of opportunistically adding any verified lemma, the system learns to conjecture, select, and prune lemmas based on their expected marginal utility across future problems. During expert-iteration and tree-search, we collect subgoal traces, embed and cluster recurring subgoals, and train a predictor of lemma utility (e.g., expected proof-length reduction and success lift) using retrieval signals and hard negatives from annotated premise datasets; an LLM then proposes cluster-conditioned candidate lemmas that are verified and scheduled via a contextual bandit to allocate proof/verification budget. The prover retrieves from a continually pruned library prioritized by predicted utility, with periodic compression (merging near-duplicates, removing dominated lemmas) to keep the library small and high-impact. Evaluations on miniF2F and novel-premise splits measure gains in generalization and sample efficiency, with ablations on clustering, bandit scheduling, and pruning showing that explicit utility estimation outperforms prior purely opportunistic lemma growth.

We propose Analytic Hybrid Differentiable Marching (AHDM) for open and closed surfaces: exploit the exact linear-region decomposition of ReLU MLPs to analytically traverse the zero set of a learned unsigned distance field, while a learned auxiliary sign field gates which facets constitute the target (possibly open) surface. Within each analytic cell, we derive closed-form vertex and face Jacobians with respect to network parameters, yielding end-to-end gradients that match the exact piecewise-planar geometry rather than a discretized approximation. To control watertightness when desired, we add a soft Poisson consistency layer that solves a differentiable indicator field with Dirichlet constraints where the sign is confident and Neumann boundaries elsewhere, providing flux regularization without forcing closure. This hybrid yields high-fidelity, topology-agnostic meshes with stable surface-level training signals, improving single-view reconstruction and point-cloud fitting for shapes with thin structures and mixed topology.

result.text: The paper addresses improving human alignment of large language models by avoiding the complexity and instability of reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and the information loss of reducing multi-sample comparisons to pairwise contrasts. Its key insight is that alignment can be framed as matching the model’s probability ranking over multiple candidate responses to human preference rankings, and that extending pairwise contrasts to full preference rankings yields richer supervisory signal. The proposed method, Preference Ranking Optimization (PRO), is a supervised fine-tuning algorithm that iteratively contrasts candidates within n-length preference lists so the model both prioritizes the best reply and progressively orders the remaining responses, thereby aligning output probabilities with human judgments. Empirically, PRO outperforms baselines and achieves performance comparable to ChatGPT and human responses across automatic, reward-based, GPT-4, and human evaluations.

args.text: We propose a Degradation-Conditioned Deep Equilibrium Reconstructor for CASSI that jointly amortizes scene-specific degradation estimation and performs implicit fixed-point reconstruction. A lightweight estimator infers per-scene coding-mask misalignment, spectral response, and noise scale from the measurement, which conditions a nonexpansive, measurement-aware Half-Shuffle Transformer used as the implicit operator; we solve for its fixed point with Anderson acceleration and train end-to-end via implicit differentiation. This merges the stability and constant-memory benefits of deep equilibrium models with the accuracy gains of degradation-aware unfolding, and further integrates binarized spectral-redistribution blocks in later layers to enable efficient edge deployment without major quality loss. result.text: The paper addresses the trade-off in decentralized learning between minimizing per-iteration communication (by contacting few neighbors) and maintaining fast network-wide information mixing, noting that common topologies either require high node degrees or mix poorly as network size grows. The key insight is that one can design sparse, communication-efficient topologies whose consensus (mixing) rate does not degrade with network size, by balancing node degrees and using time-varying neighbor selections so that information spreads rapidly despite low per-iteration connectivity. Concretely, the authors propose EquiTopo, a family including EquiStatic—an almost-regular static graph with degree Θ(log n)—and EquiDyn—a time-varying one-peer topology generated by a random sampling procedure; both achieve an n-independent consensus rate and are plugged into decentralized SGD and gradient-tracking algorithms to yield provably faster communication and improved convergence, corroborated by experiments and a BlueFog implementation.

Using a small calibration set, we estimate layerwise curvature (e.g., K‑FAC/diagonal Hessian) and learn a stack of structured rotations (butterfly/Givens blocks) that equilibrate inverse‑Hessian diagonals to suppress outlier directions; on top, we learn per-channel piecewise/nonuniform codebooks with a loss proxy weighted by this curvature. The rotations are folded into weights (as in rotation/affine equivalence) and the learned grids target standard integer formats, preserving kernel compatibility; beyond weights/activations, we extend to KV caches by learning key rotations pre‑RoPE and sensitivity‑weighted grids for sub‑4‑bit storage. Compared to rotation‑only or grid‑only PTQ, HEROQ aligns quantizer capacity with true sensitivity, aiming for near‑QAT accuracy at 4/4‑bit without custom kernels and modest extra compute.

result.text: We propose segmented control-variate hybrid gradients for nonsmooth differentiable physics. Long-horizon rollouts are partitioned at detected nonsmooth events (contacts, plastic yielding), and exact simulator gradients are used only within smooth segments as a control variate for a global likelihood-ratio estimator, with a learned per-segment alpha blending based on local smoothness/stiffness metrics estimated via small randomized smoothing probes; this preserves unbiasedness while sharply reducing variance and avoids the structural bias of reparameterization gradients at discontinuities. Event detection and segmentation leverage localized mesh-based contact solvers, and the alpha-scheduler is meta-learned across tasks. We evaluate on PlasticineLab and long-horizon tool-use sequences composed from short-horizon skills, demonstrating improved sample efficiency and stability over prior hybrid estimators.

args.text: I propose a sharpness-mediated account of broken neural scaling: the kinks, delayed gains, and double-descent behaviors captured by smoothly broken power laws emerge when training transitions into a self-stabilized edge-of-stability regime and the time-averaged fraction of unstable (η·λmax>2) steps crosses a scale-dependent threshold. Mechanistically, as model/data/compute scale, λmax grows and constant–step-size GD/SGD undergoes a ballistic-to-diffusive transition at a critical step size; EOS self-stabilization via cubic curvature reduces λmax along the top mode, changing the effective capacity and noise temperature in a non-monotonic way that reshapes performance vs. scale. This yields concrete predictions: the break location is determined by early-training estimates of η·λmax and the cubic coefficient along the top eigendirection; at fixed η it should shift with batch-size–controlled noise and with architectural choices that alter curvature, and large constant step sizes can mimic stochasticity to smooth or delay the break. Empirically, logging sharpness, EOS occupancy, and cubic-term proxies across scales should enable fitting a two-regime scaling model whose boundary is predicted from these dynamics, providing prescriptive levers (LR, batch size, architecture) to induce, move, or avoid scaling breaks.

args.text: We propose Adaptive Off-Policy Proximal Policy Optimization, which calibrates the width and shape of the proximal surrogate to the measured off-policyness of each batch. Using DEON to estimate off-policyness, we decouple a dedicated proximal policy from the behavior policy and set a per-batch temperature for a smooth sigmoid surrogate (or per-sample clipping coefficients) via an off-policy improvement bound, shrinking the trust region under high DEON and relaxing it when data are near on-policy. result.text: I propose Position-Aware Capacity Reservation (PACR) for Mixture-of-Experts routing to mitigate the observed drop-towards-the-end effect in MoE LLMs. PACR augments expert-choice routing with a lightweight admission controller that forecasts per-position token load within each microbatch (via sequence length and running position-conditioned load histograms) and reserves a fraction of each expert’s bucket for later positions; unused reservations decay within the step so early tokens can backfill idle capacity. result.text: The paper tackles the gap in evaluating multimodal agents on realistic, open-ended computer tasks by introducing OSWorld, a scalable, interactive benchmark that simulates real operating systems (Ubuntu, Windows, macOS) and arbitrary applications to reflect diverse, real-world computer use. The authors implement OSWorld with 369 real-world tasks, each paired with reproducible initial-state configurations and custom evaluation scripts, and they evaluate current LLM/VLM-based agents, finding a large performance gap (human 72.36% vs. best model 12.24%) driven by failures in GUI grounding and operational knowledge. OSWorld, along with code, data, and baselines, is released to facilitate development and analysis of more capable multimodal generalist agents.

result.text: We propose LF-ODE-ECG, a generative model that evolves a low-dimensional cardiac source state with a neural ODE and renders multi-lead ECG via a fixed or lightly personalized biophysical lead-field matrix, enforcing cross-lead consistency by construction. Unlike prior GAN-based dynamics that operate directly in signal space, the latent ODE produces dipole/activation coefficients whose linear projection yields all 12 leads, while disease conditioning modulates the vector field to inject localized pathology; a view-structure discriminator and ROI-weighted losses further shape morphology at diagnostically critical intervals. Training couples adversarial objectives with simulator-informed regularization on simple electrophysiology priors and a brief calibration step to adapt the lead-field to a patient, enabling disease-faithful, patient-adaptable, physics-consistent synthesis that improves downstream diagnosis and privacy-preserving data sharing.

args.text: To counter latency-raising adversarial inputs in camera-based AD perception, I propose Budgeted Randomized Early-Exit with Latency Regularization (BREELR). During training, optimize a joint objective that penalizes task error and a differentiable runtime proxy while performing adversarial augmentation that explicitly maximizes runtime, so the model learns latency-insensitive features and robust exit gating. At inference, enforce a hard deadline via patience-based early exits and randomized, functionally-equivalent operator/route choices (e.g., kernel variants, feature downsampling paths) to decorrelate attacker gradients from realized compute and to fall back to an anytime, conservative action as the deadline approaches. Evaluate within SlowTrack-style pipelines and SafeBench to show bounded tail-latency and reduced crash rates under white- and black-box slowdown attacks compared to vanilla early-exit and standard adversarial training.

result.text: The paper tackles the reliance of chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting on labeled exemplars for steering large language models through complex reasoning tasks. Its key insight is that models can autonomously perform analogical reasoning by first self-generating relevant exemplars or background knowledge tailored to the current problem, which then serve as in-context guides for the subsequent solution—thus removing the need for externally labeled or retrieved exemplars while adapting to each instance. The proposed method, analogical prompting, structures prompts so the model first produces analogous examples or supportive knowledge conditioned on the target problem and then uses those self-created exemplars to generate a chain-of-thought and final answer. Experiments show this approach improves performance over zero-shot CoT and manually curated few-shot CoT across diverse benchmarks including GSM8K, MATH, Codeforces, and BIG-Bench tasks.

Its key insight is that without prior structural knowledge of the data distribution, backdoor patterns can be indistinguishable from legitimate predictive features—making general-purpose detection impossible—and thus defenses implicitly rely on latent assumptions. Leveraging an alternative, explicit assumption that the backdoor corresponds to the single strongest feature in the training data, the authors formalize this setting and derive a detection primitive and algorithm with theoretical guarantees. result.text: The paper addresses fair allocation of indivisible items among agents with unequal entitlements (weights), aiming to extend and relate standard fairness concepts to the weighted setting. Its key insight is that weighted fairness admits a rich family of parameterized relaxations—where parameters control whether allocations favor smaller- or larger-weight agents—and that while every single relaxation in these families is always attainable, different relaxations may be mutually incompatible, so tradeoffs are inherent; similarly, a natural weighted generalization of maximin share fairness can be approximated only up to a provably optimal factor. Instead of fixing expert size and k throughout training, we derive and implement a training-time schedule for expert granularity and activation that follows asymmetric compute-optimality, allocating more FLOPs to additional steps early and shifting to larger experts later. args.text: Vision–language models often treat image-embedded text and subtle adversarial visual cues as executable instructions, enabling typographic-image jailbreaks and cross-modal perturbations that bypass text-only safety. We propose Modality-Scoped Instruction Separation (MSIS): a training objective and routing module that only permits instruction execution from trusted input channels by (i) surfacing OCR-extracted imperatives from images, (ii) learning an instruction-origin classifier, and (iii) applying conflict-aware supervision with counterfactual pairs where image-embedded commands contradict user text, combined with gradient-blocked control tokens so the vision encoder cannot steer policy tokens. We add a token-level modality-attribution head and safety loss that penalize generations attributed to the vision channel when they violate policy, yielding a measurable instruction–data separation score adapted to VLMs. Trained by augmenting safe instruction datasets with synthetic typographic prompts and adversarial-image cases, MSIS is expected to sharply reduce FigStep-style and compositional adversarial jailbreak success while preserving helpfulness.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem that practitioners face when selecting large multimodal language models (MLMs): existing benchmarks are numerous and general-purpose, so they do not reliably indicate which model will perform best for a specific application. The key insight is that a programmatic, customizable benchmark engine—built around an extendable taxonomy of visual assets and tasks—can generate targeted, scalable evaluations that reveal nuanced, application-relevant strengths and weaknesses of MLMs. The authors present Task-Me-Anything, a pipeline containing a huge inventory of images, videos, and 3D assets (with rich category, attribute, and relationship annotations) that can synthesize hundreds of millions of image/video QA pairs and, under computational budgets, algorithmically answer user queries about model performance; using this resource they show systematic patterns (e.g., open-source models are strong on objects/attributes but weak on spatial/temporal reasoning, larger models tend to do better with exceptions, and GPT4o struggles with motion/rotation and color discrimination).

args.text: I propose Factorized Mutual-Information Discovery (F-MID) for universal/open-set domain adaptation with novel-category discovery: learn a representation explicitly split into semantic and domain factors, enforce their independence, then maximize mutual information between pseudo-labels and the semantic factor while minimizing it with the domain factor. Pseudo-labels are produced via prototype-based clustering that can dynamically spawn new prototypes when local density and MI gains justify it, avoiding the single-unknown collapse. A mean-teacher consistency path aligned to the labeled taxonomy stabilizes known-class assignments, while an attract-and-disperse neighborhood objective in the semantic space sharpens cluster boundaries. This combination prevents clusters from binding to domain cues, enabling fine-grained discovery of novel classes across universal DA and source-free settings.

result.text: The paper addresses defending black-box models against backdoor attacks—where poisoned training samples cause misclassification—when only query access to the model is available and no clean/poison labels or model internals are known. The key insight is that deliberately destroying potential trigger patterns via a simple linear transformation (e.g., blur) and then restoring semantic content with a powerful pre-trained diffusion model can remove backdoor signals while preserving class-relevant features, enabling zero-shot purification without retraining or access to clean data. The method, called ZIP, first applies a transformation to incoming images to disrupt backdoor triggers and then runs a novel guided reverse diffusion process that uses the transformed image as guidance to generate high-fidelity purified images; this purified output is used for model queries, and evaluations show ZIP outperforms prior black-box backdoor defenses across datasets and attack types.

args.text: Mixture-of-Experts Neural Processes improve expressiveness but learned routers add routing overhead and can violate translation-equivariant inductive biases needed for stationary spatio-temporal tasks. We propose Hash-Equivariant Neural Processes (Hash-ENP): build a ConvNP feature map and route each query location to k experts via a balanced, local hash of the convolutional features, yielding translation-equivariant, permutation-invariant expert selection without auxiliary load-balancing losses. Experts are lightweight equivariant decoders specialized to modes or regions; their predictions are aggregated to preserve exchangeability, with a neighborhood-consistency regularizer to avoid fragmented assignments. This hash-routed MoE decoder scales like sparse FFNs while improving spatial coherence and few-shot generalization on image and spatio-temporal completion.

result.text: The paper addresses the gap in understanding why AlphaZero-style Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) heuristics work and how to improve them by framing them as optimization rather than ad-hoc rules. Its key insight is that common MCTS selection rules (including AlphaZero's PUCT and UCT) can be interpreted as approximate solutions to a specific regularized policy optimization problem, so replacing the approximation with the exact optimizer should yield better search policies. Methodologically, the authors derive the underlying regularized optimization formulation, design a variant of AlphaZero that computes the exact solution to that optimization at each node (instead of using the heuristic selection formula), and empirically demonstrate that this principled variant consistently outperforms the original AlphaZero across multiple domains.

args.text: We propose TRiBe-DR: a decoupled-behavior, off-policy proximal policy gradient method that jointly learns a state-dependent control-variate baseline and adapts clipping radii to the measured off-policyness of each batch. Per-batch clipping widths are set by upper bounds on the bias of a three-way doubly robust off-policy policy-gradient estimator, computed from nuisance error estimates and confidence sets for density ratios learned with a stable Perron–Frobenius–based estimator, while the sampling policy is decoupled to maintain benign expected-update curvature. The baseline is trained to temper update aggressiveness and prevent action-probability collapse subject to an off-policy improvement bound, yielding high-probability monotonic improvement with large replay buffers and recovering O(1/t) on-policy convergence (accelerated with entropy). We hypothesize TRiBe-DR matches or exceeds the sample efficiency of off-policy PPO variants without sacrificing their stability.

result.text: The paper addresses whether expressive neural networks can learn structural causal models (SCMs) and make valid causal inferences from data, pointing out the gap between function approximation and causal learnability. Its key insight is that universal approximability does not overcome fundamental limits from the causal hierarchy—neural nets, no matter how expressive, cannot identify effects of interventions from purely observational data without additional structural constraints. result.text: We propose Offline Language-Conditioned Active Neural SLAM: a modular navigator that learns from passive roaming videos to build predictive, uncertainty-aware semantic maps and a subgoal value function defined in a shared image–text embedding space. result.text: Meta-Active Function-Space PAC-Bayes couples function-space meta-regularization with active data and task selection to explicitly reduce uncertainty in the meta-learned stochastic-process prior. args.text: Permutation-aligned masked Fisher merging: first align each task model to an elected base via a symmetry-equivariant aligner to resolve neuron permutations, then attach EMR-style lightweight modulators. args.text: We propose Parse-to-Act, a dual-head VLM that jointly reconstructs simplified HTML/DOM from screenshots and predicts goal-conditioned pixel-level action affordance maps for generic mouse/keyboard control. result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of enabling agents to explore and evaluate actions in rich, open-ended environments without prior task-specific knowledge. The key insight is that a Large Language Model (LLM) can provide useful, human-aligned preference signals over short trajectory captions that serve as intrinsic rewards, allowing decision-making guidance without having the LLM interact with the environment. The method, called Motif, elicits pairwise preferences from an LLM on captioned snippets of agent behavior, converts those preferences into a scalar intrinsic reward, and trains reinforcement-learning agents on that reward (optionally combined with environment reward); experiments in the procedurally generated NetHack domain show that optimizing this intrinsic signal improves exploration and performance—sometimes exceeding direct environment-reward training—and produces steerable, interpretable behaviors that scale with LLM size and prompt information.

result.text: We propose GW-TopoGCD, a topology-preserving prototype alignment framework for generalized category discovery under domain shift that aligns source and target prototype graphs via Gromov–Wasserstein transport, preserving semantic relations while permitting unmatched and many-to-one mappings to naturally accommodate novel target classes. We initialize and refine target prototypes with semantic-weighted soft assignments and decoupled optimization for known vs. novel groups, replacing brittle one-to-one bipartite matching with structure-aware transport that is robust to class splits/merges and unknown-class emergence. To prevent style cues from confounding alignment, we disentangle high-level semantics from low-level domain factors and minimize their mutual information, coupled with style-mixing augmentations to expand domain coverage. The joint objective minimizes GW distance between prototype graphs, enforces semantic–domain independence, and regularizes pseudo-labels, with an optional hierarchical split criterion (e.g., code-length/stability) to recover multi-granularity categories when warranted by target data.

result.text: The paper addresses the gap between theoretical FLOPs reductions of spatial-wise dynamic convolution and the actual runtime speedup on multi-core hardware by targeting practical inference latency rather than just computation counts. Its key insight is that latency depends not only on algorithmic complexity but also on scheduling strategies and hardware characteristics, so a latency prediction model can guide both network design and execution to achieve real speedups. The method, called LASNet, performs coarse-grained spatially adaptive inference while using an efficient latency predictor that jointly models algorithm, scheduler, and hardware effects; this predictor is used to optimize where and how to allocate computation and to choose scheduling strategies across platforms. Empirical results on classification, detection, and segmentation show substantial real-world latency reductions (e.g., 36% on Tesla V100 and 46% on Jetson TX2 for ResNet-101) without accuracy loss.

result.text: The paper addresses the gap between fast but sometimes suboptimal chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning and the more deliberative but computationally expensive tree-of-thought (ToT) search, aiming to retain ToT-quality reasoning without its inference cost. The key insight is that the preference information implicitly generated during ToT search—i.e., which partial reasoning branches lead to better final solutions—can be used as supervision to teach a model to prefer those better reasoning steps during standard CoT decoding. The method, called Chain of Preference Optimization (CPO), fine-tunes LLMs by aligning each step of generated CoT traces with the preferred steps extracted from ToT trees, effectively distilling the tree search’s selection signals into the model so it produces higher-quality reasoning chains at inference time. Empirical results across QA, fact verification, and arithmetic tasks show that CPO yields substantial improvements in problem-solving accuracy while avoiding the heavy inference overhead of running ToT.

result.text: The paper addresses a novel deployment-stage threat to deep neural networks: stealthily flipping a small number of stored weight bits to force a chosen input to be misclassified into a target class while preserving overall accuracy. The key insight is to treat bit-flip selection as a binary integer programming problem over the model’s memory bits and then use an equivalent continuous reformulation to enable efficient, principled optimization rather than ad hoc heuristics. The authors solve the reformulated problem with an ADMM-based optimizer that identifies the minimal set of critical bit flips, and experiments show this method reliably induces targeted misclassification with few flips and little impact on other predictions.

args.text: We propose an Interaction-Bounded Fusion Curriculum (IBFC) for in-the-wild affective mental health detection that estimates per-clip audio–visual interaction strength from unlabeled co-occurring data via information-theoretic bounds and uses these estimates to guide training and inference. Training starts on high-interaction segments to teach a cross-attention fusion module stable synergistic patterns, while jointly learning unimodal experts and a routing gate that defers to unimodal predictions when interaction is low or modalities disagree. We evaluate on D-Vlog for depression and StressID for stress, and assess cross-dataset and longitudinal robustness using GLOBEM-style splits, expecting improved generalization, calibration, and reduced overfitting to spurious correlations. By turning interaction estimation into a practical signal for when and how to fuse, IBFC yields adaptive, reliable multimodal decisions in the wild.

result.text: The paper addresses detecting input-level backdoor attacks in fully black-box ML-as-a-service settings where users can only query models and receive labels. Its key insight is that poisoned inputs exhibit markedly higher prediction consistency than benign inputs when all pixel values are progressively amplified—an effect the authors call scaled prediction consistency and for which they provide theoretical justification. The proposed method, SCALE-UP, flags malicious test samples by repeatedly amplifying pixels and measuring label consistency across amplified versions, filtering those with unusually stable predictions; experiments on benchmarks show this label-only defense is effective, efficient, and robust to adaptive attacks.

args.text: We propose an intrinsic-rate thermostat for normalized networks: a per-layer control loop that maintains a target intrinsic learning rate by jointly adjusting weight decay and occasional norm projection, using observed rotation speed of weights as the control signal. The target is chosen to sit at the edge-of-stability yet follow a sharpness-reduction flow; a simple PID rule updates decay to keep per-layer rotation near setpoint, suppressing the batchnorm–weight-decay destabilization cycles while preserving their generalization benefits. This removes most learning-rate tuning by tying effective step size to geometry (akin to parameter-free schedules) and can optionally correct finite-step distortions by modestly adapting the nominal step when stationary variance inflates. We predict faster, stabler equilibration and better test accuracy across BN/LayerNorm ResNets and transformers, with ablations comparing decay-only, projection-only, and joint control.

result.text: The paper addresses improving rationalization for NLP models by identifying true causal rationales rather than spurious features that correlate with labels under the conventional maximum mutual information (MMI) criterion. The key insight is that causal rationales d-separate non-causal input parts from the target label, so selecting a rationale that minimizes the conditional dependence between the unselected input and the label will force the model to include all causal features. Methodologically, the authors formalize this Minimum Conditional Dependence (MCD) criterion and implement it by minimizing a practical dependence measure (KL-divergence) between the unselected text and the label conditioned on candidate rationales, showing substantial empirical gains (up to 13.7% F1) over MMI-based baselines.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of "over-squashing" in graph neural networks, where information from distant nodes gets compressed and distorted during message passing, limiting GNN performance on tasks needing long-range interactions; this is commonly attributed to graph bottlenecks but lacked a precise formulation. The key insight is that over-squashing corresponds to negatively curved edges in the graph: such edges act as combinatorial bottlenecks that concentrate and distort many incoming messages, and can be detected via a novel edge-based discrete curvature measure. The authors define this new curvature, prove a formal relationship between negative curvature and the deterioration of information flow in message passing, and propose a curvature-driven graph rewiring algorithm that adds or reweights edges to reduce negative curvature; experiments show that this rewiring alleviates over-squashing and improves GNN performance on long-range tasks.

result.text: The paper tackles single-image novel view synthesis where severe occlusion makes projecting 2D features into a NeRF insufficient, producing blurry or inconsistent novel views. Its key insight is to leverage a 3D-aware conditional diffusion model (CDM) as a teacher that can hallucinate plausible, multi-view-consistent virtual views, and to distill that knowledge into a NeRF to resolve uncertainty in occluded regions. Methodologically, NerfDiff generates many candidate views from the CDM at test time, uses a novel NeRF-guided distillation loop that selects and refines 3D-consistent virtual views, and finetunes the NeRF on these improved samples so the radiance field learns richer geometry and appearance priors. result.text: The paper addresses strategic classification when agents do not observe the classifier (opaque setting) and thus try to learn and manipulate it, contrasting this with the standard transparent model where the classifier is known. Its key insight is that opacity changes agents’ strategic behavior and can increase overall prediction error, so one should quantify the “price of opacity” — the performance gap between optimal robust classifiers under opaque versus transparent interaction. Methodologically, the authors formalize a generalized strategic classification model that incorporates agent learning under opacity, define and analytically characterize the price of opacity, provide a sufficient condition guaranteeing a strictly positive price (implying transparency is preferable), and empirically evaluate how existing robust classifiers (e.g., Hardt et al.) are impacted when agents are kept in the dark.

result.text: The paper addresses the limited granularity of existing visual transformers, which split images into relatively large patches and thus may miss fine-scale, within-patch structure important for recognizing objects at different scales and locations. Its key insight is that modeling attention not only between coarse patches (sentences) but also inside each patch among smaller subpatches (words) yields richer representations with little extra cost. The proposed Transformer in Transformer (TNT) embeds each large patch as a sequence of smaller patch tokens, applies an inner transformer to compute “word” attention within each patch and an outer transformer to model “sentence” attention across patches, and aggregates word- and sentence-level features end-to-end. Experiments on ImageNet and other benchmarks show TNT improves accuracy (e.g., +1.7% top-1 over similar-cost visual transformers) while maintaining comparable computational complexity.

result.text: We propose utility-driven lemma invention for neural theorem provers: instead of opportunistically adding any verified lemma, the system learns to conjecture, select, and prune lemmas based on their expected marginal utility across future problems. During expert-iteration and tree-search, we collect subgoal traces, embed and cluster recurring subgoals, and train a predictor of lemma utility (e.g., expected proof-length reduction and success lift) using retrieval signals and hard negatives from annotated premise datasets; an LLM then proposes cluster-conditioned candidate lemmas that are verified and scheduled via a contextual bandit to allocate proof/verification budget. The prover retrieves from a continually pruned library prioritized by predicted utility, with periodic compression (merging near-duplicates, removing dominated lemmas) to keep the library small and high-impact. Evaluations on miniF2F and novel-premise splits measure gains in generalization and sample efficiency, with ablations on clustering, bandit scheduling, and pruning showing that explicit utility estimation outperforms prior purely opportunistic lemma growth.

result.text: We propose Analytic Hybrid Differentiable Marching (AHDM) for open and closed surfaces: exploit the exact linear-region decomposition of ReLU MLPs to analytically traverse the zero set of a learned unsigned distance field, while a learned auxiliary sign field gates which facets constitute the target (possibly open) surface. Within each analytic cell, we derive closed-form vertex and face Jacobians with respect to network parameters, yielding end-to-end gradients that match the exact piecewise-planar geometry rather than a discretized approximation. To control watertightness when desired, we add a soft Poisson consistency layer that solves a differentiable indicator field with Dirichlet constraints where the sign is confident and Neumann boundaries elsewhere, providing flux regularization without forcing closure. This hybrid yields high-fidelity, topology-agnostic meshes with stable surface-level training signals, improving single-view reconstruction and point-cloud fitting for shapes with thin structures and mixed topology.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of over-smoothing in deep graph neural networks, which prevents deeper models from improving performance on graph-structured data. Its key insight is to view graph convolutions as discrete approximations to partial differential equations (PDEs) on manifolds, and to use numerical PDE solvers’ principles to design architectures that control smoothing and stability. Concretely, the authors propose a family of GNN layers inspired by explicit and implicit time-stepping schemes and reaction-diffusion PDEs, combining diffusion-like propagation, learnable reaction terms, and adjustable time-step/implicitness to prevent over-smoothing while retaining expressive propagation; experiments across vision, biology, and chemistry show these PDE-GCNs match or outperform state-of-the-art models.

result.text: The paper addresses open-vocabulary video instance segmentation (OpenVIS), i.e., detecting, segmenting, and tracking instances of arbitrary categories in video without being limited to training-time classes. Its key insight is that strong open-vocabulary capabilities can be achieved by combining class-agnostic, recall-focused mask proposals with instance-centric open-vocabulary token encoders and a tracking formulation that predicts future instance tokens rather than relying on closed-set identity labels. The proposed InstFormer framework implements this by (1) using an open-world mask proposal network trained with a contrastive instance margin loss to exhaustively propose class-agnostic masks, (2) adapting CLIP into InstCLIP with Instance Guidance Attention to produce compact open-vocabulary instance tokens for classification and tracking, and (3) introducing universal rollout association that casts tracking as next-frame instance token prediction; together these components enable lightweight fine-tuning on limited-category data and achieve state-of-the-art OpenVIS performance while remaining competitive on supervised VIS.

The key insight is that masked modeling can be reframed as a form of knowledge distillation: frozen, pretrained 2D/language transformers can provide informative latent targets (dark knowledge) that guide a 3D student model to learn foundational geometry. Their method, Autoencoders as Cross-Modal Teachers (ACT), first trains discrete variational autoencoders to convert pretrained transformer features into latent codes while keeping the teacher frozen with prompt tuning, then uses those latent features as targets for masked point modeling to distill semantics into a 3D transformer student. result.text: The paper addresses the theoretical foundations of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), specifically when humans provide pairwise or K-wise preferences and the true reward is linear; it aims to explain when and why common practice (MLE-based reward learning followed by policy optimization) succeeds or fails. The key insight is that while the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) for the reward converges under both the Bradley–Terry–Luce and Plackett–Luce preference models, using that learned reward naively to train a policy can fail, whereas a pessimistic variant of MLE yields better policies under suitable coverage assumptions; additionally, under Plackett–Luce the true K-wise MLE and a split-into-pairs MLE both converge but the true K-wise MLE is asymptotically more efficient. Methodologically, the authors analyze convergence and sample complexity for linear rewards under BTL/PL models, prove consistency and efficiency results for different MLE formulations, derive a pessimistic training approach that improves policy performance given limited coverage, and unify RLHF with max-entropy inverse reinforcement learning by providing the first sample complexity bound for that IRL setting.

result.text: Propose a language-conditioned 3D foundation segmenter for volumetric medical imaging that unifies semantic, spatial, and text prompts to enable open-vocabulary, report-driven segmentation of both anatomy and pathology. The model is pretrained with a joint objective that combines fully volumetric self-supervision with contrastive alignment between radiology reports/MeSH terms and 3D token grids via multi-projection renderings (MIPs and orthogonal slice stacks) and a lifting module that fuses 2D text–image alignments back into the 3D latent volume; at inference, zoom-out–zoom-in processing and optional point/box seeds disambiguate location. Ontology-aware prompt expansion maps free text to controlled medical terms and attributes, while weak labels mined from reports are denoised by cross-view and inter-slice consistency constraints to supervise voxel masks at scale. This yields zero-/few-shot, language-driven volumetric segmentation with better controllability than semantic-only prompting and improved generalization on AMOS-style multi-organ and lesion benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses inductive representation learning for temporal networks, aiming to capture universal dynamic laws (e.g., triadic closure) so models trained on some systems can generalize to unseen ones without relying on node identities or rich edge attributes. The key insight is that temporal dynamics can be represented by collections of short temporal random walks that act as implicit, automatically retrieved temporal motifs, and that replacing explicit node identities with anonymized hitting-count statistics preserves inductivity while retaining motif correlations. Methodologically, the authors introduce Causal Anonymous Walks (CAWs)—temporal random walks anonymized via counts over sampled walks—and a neural encoder CAW-N that learns representations from CAWs, coupled with a constant-time/memory CAW sampling strategy for online training and inference. Empirically CAW-N yields substantial gains in inductive link prediction (≈10% average AUC) and strong transductive performance across multiple real-world temporal networks.

result.text: The paper addresses artifacts and poor geometry/normals in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), where individual Gaussian primitives collapse into highly anisotropic, needle-like shapes that degrade reconstruction quality. The key insight is that this collapse can be quantified by the Gaussians’ effective rank—which often approaches 1—so constraining effective rank will discourage degenerate anisotropy and preserve meaningful shape information. The authors propose an effective-rank regularizer applied to each Gaussian during optimization, which penalizes overly low-rank covariance structures and thereby yields more accurate normals and geometry while reducing needle artifacts; the regularizer is lightweight and modular, making it easy to add to existing 3DGS variants without harming rendering fidelity.

args.text: We propose SCA-BV-PP: a memoryless compressed FL protocol for arbitrary partial participation that embeds the induced-unbiased transform of contractive compressors into a stochastic controlled averaging reformulation, so clients keep no persistent residuals while the server maintains a single global control variate. Each round, sampled clients transmit updates using the induced-unbiased transform with seeded independent randomness; the server aggregates them via EF-BV–style variance-reduced error correction and compresses the downlink using a DoCoFL-compatible scheme. This design targets linear convergence under smoothness/PL assumptions, inherits EF-BV’s favorable scaling with cohort size, supports any contractive compressor without per-client state, and preserves the SCA half-uplink-cost advantage. Practically, it tolerates heterogeneous data and sporadic clients while avoiding the instability of classic error feedback for biased compressors.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of Catastrophic Overfitting (CO) in single-step adversarial training—where models trained with FGSM suddenly become vulnerable to multi-step attacks—seeking a reliable and efficient remedy that scales to large perturbation radii. The key insight is that stronger random noise injected around the clean input combined with deliberately not clipping the perturbed example prior to the FGSM step prevents CO even for large epsilons, contradicting prior beliefs that mild noise or clipping were sufficient or necessary. result.text: I propose a sharpness-mediated account of broken neural scaling: the kinks, delayed gains, and double-descent behaviors captured by smoothly broken power laws emerge when training transitions into a self-stabilized edge-of-stability regime and the time-averaged fraction of unstable (η·λmax>2) steps crosses a scale-dependent threshold. Mechanistically, as model/data/compute scale, λmax grows and constant–step-size GD/SGD undergoes a ballistic-to-diffusive transition at a critical step size; EOS self-stabilization via cubic curvature reduces λmax along the top mode, changing the effective capacity and noise temperature in a non-monotonic way that reshapes performance vs. scale. This yields concrete predictions: the break location is determined by early-training estimates of η·λmax and the cubic coefficient along the top eigendirection; at fixed η it should shift with batch-size–controlled noise and with architectural choices that alter curvature, and large constant step sizes can mimic stochasticity to smooth or delay the break. Empirically, logging sharpness, EOS occupancy, and cubic-term proxies across scales should enable fitting a two-regime scaling model whose boundary is predicted from these dynamics, providing prescriptive levers (LR, batch size, architecture) to induce, move, or avoid scaling breaks.

args.text: We propose Disagreement-Guided Adversarial MoE Distillation: a single student with K lightweight expert branches in late layers that preserves ensemble diversity while keeping a single forward pass via a shared trunk and post-training consolidation. Each expert is trained with a per-expert discriminator to adversarially match the feature distribution of different teacher members or subgroups, while a conditional mutual-information penalty discourages experts from being predictable from one another given the label, preserving complementary modes. Training interleaves standard distillation with a disagreement-seeking perturbation search that surfaces inputs where teachers diverge and routes them to different experts to encourage specialization. After training, the experts are merged into a compact head via learned gates or linear consolidation to limit inference overhead, yielding a student that better captures ensemble multimodality and improves calibration and shift robustness over naive distillation.

result.text: The paper addresses a representational limitation of QMIX, a cooperative multi-agent Q-learning algorithm whose monotonic mixing constraint prevents representing value functions where an agent’s action ordering depends on other agents’ actions, causing projection errors that can misidentify optimal policies. args.text: To robustly detect out-of-context and repurposed multimedia news, I propose Evidence-Guided Contradiction Reasoning (EGCR): beyond modeling intra-post cross-modal consistency, the system retrieves near-duplicate images and semantically related reports from a large news/web index and reasons about contradictions in time, place, and entity attributes between the claim, the image, and the retrieved evidence. A vision–language model generates multiple pseudo-captions and attribute tags for the image, specialized predictors estimate geo/temporal cues, and an evidence selector builds a compact, content-relevant evidence set for each post. A hybrid neural–symbolic head infers discrete deception patterns (e.g., image repurposing vs. cross-modal inconsistency) from these structured signals and user comments, and the final decision is reweighted by view-specific fidelity/consistency scores. result.text: The paper tackles reliable causal structure learning from observational data when latent confounders and selection bias may be present, aiming to recover the correct Markov equivalence class under causal Markov and faithfulness assumptions. The key insight is to iteratively refine a complete graph by restricting the size of conditional independence (CI) conditioning sets according to their graph-theoretic distance from the tested node pair, so earlier iterations use smaller, higher-power conditioning sets and later iterations expand the search only as needed. The method—Iterative Causal Discovery (ICD)—starts with a complete graph and in successive iterations identifies and removes edges using CI tests whose conditioning sets are bounded by iteration-specific distances, guaranteeing that independence and causal relations discovered at any stage are sound and enabling an anytime algorithm that is both statistically stable and computationally more efficient; empirical results show ICD requires far fewer CI tests and yields more accurate graphs than FCI, FCI+, and RFCI.

args.text: We propose a unified, amortized compiler-optimization framework that learns a multi-task, graph-level performance surrogate to score schedules and device placements on full computation graphs, trained on realistic graph-performance data. We represent transformation and placement choices with a probabilistic program and use a conditional Generative FlowNet to sample diverse decision sequences proportional to the surrogate’s predicted speedup, while a GO-style non-autoregressive head produces globally consistent one-pass assignments. We hypothesize this yields superior end-to-end speedups and sample efficiency versus pure RL or heuristic search, especially for pipelined multi-device workloads.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem that existing foundation agents fail to generalize across diverse virtual environments because each environment exposes highly varied observation and action interfaces. Its key insight is to standardize interaction via a unified General Computer Control (GCC) setting—using screenshots as input and keyboard/mouse actions as output—so a single agent architecture can operate any software without bespoke APIs. args.text: We propose Performatively Stable Bayesian Optimization (PS-BO), an acquisition strategy that jointly seeks improvement while steering the optimizer’s induced query distribution toward the oracle’s effective training distribution to avoid out-of-distribution hallucinations. Concretely, we alternate autofocused oracle reweighting with acquisition updates that penalize regions of high calibration mismatch, estimated via posterior-sample disagreement and hyperparameter uncertainty, and optimize a Lagrangian trade-off between gain and stability. We frame multi-step query-distribution evolution as an MDP and train a policy to reach performatively stable fixed points where the deployed acquisition and the retrained oracle are calibrated to each other. We hypothesize PS-BO reduces failure cases in protein/small-molecule design versus standard BO or pure autofocusing by explicitly optimizing for calibration-stability alongside utility.

result.text: WILDS addresses the lack of realistic evaluation benchmarks for distribution shift by assembling a diverse suite of "in-the-wild" datasets where training and test distributions differ in ways that occur in real applications (e.g., hospitals, cameras, countries, time periods, demographics, molecular scaffolds). Its key insight is that progress on robust, generalizable ML requires standardized, real-world shifts rather than synthetic or retrofitted perturbations, so methods should be evaluated across many modalities and domains to reveal common failure modes. WILDS provides unified data loaders, metrics, and train/test splits for tasks such as tumor identification, wildlife monitoring, and poverty mapping, and demonstrates that baseline models suffer substantial performance drops under these authentic shifts. By cataloging promising but missing datasets and reporting where shifts do and do not harm performance, WILDS aims to catalyze development of broadly effective robustness methods grounded in practical deployment scenarios.

result.text: CoDet tackles the challenge of obtaining reliable region-word alignments from image-caption pairs for open-vocabulary object detection, avoiding reliance on pre-aligned vision-language models that can mislocalize or fail to generalize. The key insight is to reframe alignment as a co-occurring object discovery task: images whose captions mention the same concept will contain objects of that concept that repeatedly co-occur across the image group, so discovering visually similar regions across such groups yields robust region-word correspondences. Methodologically, CoDet groups images by shared caption concepts, mines visually similar regions across each group to identify co-occurring objects, and aligns these discovered regions with the concept to train an object detector; this approach scales effectively with larger backbones and achieves state-of-the-art open-vocabulary detection performance on benchmarks like OV-LVIS.

result.text: We propose Factorized Riemannian Diffusion: a generative model that learns a product-of-submanifolds latent geometry for controllable generation without labeled factors. It combines Riemannian score-based diffusion with a variational likelihood on product manifolds and a weak pairwise constraint that two samples share at least one factor, aligning the corresponding submanifold coordinates while letting others vary. args.text: We propose EoS-guided Intrinsic Rotation Control: a closed-loop scheduler that maintains per-layer scale-invariant rotation rates near a target chosen from the Edge-of-Stability regime while keeping the intrinsic learning rate (step size × weight decay) stable. Concretely, at each step we estimate per-layer rotation (angle between successive normalized weights) and a scale-invariant sharpness proxy, then use a simple PI controller to adjust decoupled weight decay and/or layerwise step sizes so that rotation equilibrates across layers and sharpness tracks an EoS-setpoint—thereby preventing BN+weight-decay–induced effective-LR spikes and cyclic destabilizations. This unifies intrinsic-rate theory with rotational equilibrium and replaces ad‑hoc warmup or hand-tuned decay schedules with automatic feedback control; it predicts flattened BN cycles, more uniform rotation, and improved convergence/generalization relative to constant or gradient-norm–driven decay. We will benchmark against tuned SGD/AdamW, SWD, and DoG, and ablate rotation-only vs sharpness-coupled control to isolate the contribution of EoS targeting.

args.text: We propose Register-stabilized Coarse-to-fine Part Routing (RCPR) for fine-grained recognition: append register tokens to ViTs to prevent background tokens from serving as scratch space, yielding cleaner, more faithful attention for part discovery. We fuse class-to-patch attention with a CAP-style spatial–semantic consistency prior computed from sub-pixel image gradients to score candidate parts and add a consistency loss that encourages contiguous, high-gradient regions to align with attention-selected tokens. RCPR then performs coarse-to-fine token processing, restricting TNT-style inner-patch refinement and heavy updates to the top-K regions while routing remaining tokens through lightweight paths, reducing compute via hierarchical, sparse attention. This unifies TransFG’s attention-guided part selection with coarse-to-fine sparsification to improve accuracy/efficiency trade-offs and interpretable part localization on fine-grained benchmarks.

We propose Boosted Diffusion GNNs: a stagewise training scheme that couples implicit graph diffusion with an error-driven reaction term. Each boosting round applies a stable implicit (PDE-inspired) diffusion step while injecting a sparse, learnable source at misclassified nodes via an elastic L1/L2 smoothing operator to achieve local adaptivity and avoid over-smoothing. The boosting perspective yields weak-learning conditions and transductive Rademacher bounds that improve with depth/rounds, while the diffusion backbone inherits stability to topology perturbations; jointly, this provides principled depth, robustness, and performance on both homophilous and heterophilous graphs. Practically, we learn the time-step and source strength per round by line search, yielding a multi-scale schedule that targets hard regions without globally oversmoothing.

result.text: The paper addresses the high computational cost of estimating Shapley values for explaining black-box models, which typically require many model evaluations per input. The key insight is that the Shapley value can be approximated by a learned explainer that amortizes computation across inputs by framing Shapley estimation as a weighted least-squares problem and training a neural explainer to predict contributions in one forward pass. The method trains this explainer with standard stochastic gradient optimization to minimize a loss derived from the Shapley characterization, yielding a model that produces near-Shapley attributions dramatically faster than sampling-based estimators. Empirically, FastSHAP delivers high-quality explanations with orders-of-magnitude speedups, making real-time Shapley-style explanations practical.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of reducing the computational and data costs of sparse neural network training without sacrificing accuracy, noting that simply increasing sparsity can severely degrade performance at extreme levels. The key insight is that complementary techniques—selectively freezing layers during training and sieving the dataset to train on only informative subsets—can substantially cut training work while preserving model quality, and that these strategies are feasible and effective even in the unique context of sparse training. The authors analyze when and how layer freezing can be applied to sparse models and introduce a data-sieving procedure that maintains dataset representativeness while using only a fraction of examples, then integrate both into a unified sparse-training framework called SpFDE. Extensive experiments show SpFDE reduces training cost across three axes (weight sparsity, layer freezing, dataset sieving) with little to no accuracy loss.

result.text: The paper tackles the high computational cost of Vision Transformers (ViTs) at inference and training time by reducing the number of tokens processed without retraining or with minimal training. The key insight is that many tokens are redundant (e.g., multiple tokens representing parts of the same object or across frames) and can be merged into representative tokens with little accuracy loss, so selectively combining similar tokens yields large speedups. The proposed method, Token Merging (ToMe), uses a lightweight, general matching algorithm to pair and merge similar token embeddings during forward passes (optionally applied during training), thereby cutting token count and compute while preserving information; empirically ToMe doubles throughput for large ViTs on images, videos, and audio with only ~0.2–0.4% accuracy/mAP drops and can also accelerate MAE fine-tuning.

result.text: Introduce a per-user, per-attribute privacy odometer for LLM agents that composes leakage risk across multi-turn trajectories using adaptive RDP/GDP accounting and enforces individualized budgets at runtime. The agent wraps decoding and tool calls with an attribute-mention detector calibrated to a local-DP mechanism (e.g., randomized response over attribute presence), using the odometer to decide when to redact, paraphrase, or abstain so that each sensitive attribute’s cumulative loss stays within its budget while honoring user-specific tolerances. This bridges contextual privacy evaluation to formal guarantees by treating attribute mentions as events with calibrated sensitivity, composing them with Rényi filters/odometers and GDP supermartingale bounds under fully adaptive interaction, and yields a tunable helpfulness–privacy frontier. We will evaluate on PrivacyLens-style scenarios and report leakage/helpfulness trade-offs under heterogeneous budgets.

result.text: We propose CLAP-EM Transcribe: a scalable weakly supervised AMT pipeline that constructs pseudo-aligned training pairs by retrieving candidate scores for raw audio at web scale, then jointly refining alignments and a seq2seq transcriber. We first use DISCO-10M’s publicly released CLAP embeddings to retrieve top-k symbolic candidates for each audio clip, initialize the audio encoder with MERT to inject pitch/tonal priors, and run an EM procedure akin to NoteEM where a differentiable alignment module produces soft score–audio alignments that supervise an MT3-style transcriber. The transcriber in turn re-ranks candidates and improves alignments across EM iterations with augmentation (pitch-shift/time-stretch) and confidence-weighted pseudo-labeling, yielding large, diverse training signal without any manually aligned pairs. We evaluate across MAPS, Slakh, GuitarSet, and cross-dataset generalization, with ablations on retrieval quality and alignment confidence, and expect especially strong gains on low-resource instruments.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of poor calibration in survival analysis—i.e., when predicted event counts within time intervals differ from observed counts—and the lack of a way to directly optimize calibration during model training. The key insight is that distributional calibration (D-CALIBRATION), which measures squared differences between predicted and observed event counts across time intervals, can be converted into a differentiable objective and jointly optimized with standard losses. The proposed method, X-CAL, incorporates this differentiable D-CALIBRATION term into the training objective (alongside maximum likelihood or other goals) so practitioners can explicitly trade off calibration versus predictive performance. Experiments on simulated data, an MNIST-based survival task, MIMIC-III length-of-stay prediction, and TCGA brain cancer data show that X-CAL substantially improves calibration with minimal loss in concordance or likelihood.

result.text: The paper tackles efficient, symmetry-preserving prediction of quantum Hamiltonian matrices for molecular systems, where maintaining SE(3) equivariance typically conflicts with computational and memory efficiency.
