args.text: We propose speed-aware movement-adaptive global pruning for fine-tuning large pretrained models: compute per-weight importance from movement scores during fine-tuning, then rescale them with L2-distortion-aware layer normalization to reflect each layer’s global impact, and finally allocate layerwise sparsities via a speed-constrained optimizer using target-hardware timing. This unifies movement-based importance (robust in transfer) with LAMP-style global sensitivity and SPDY’s DP-based layer budget selection, yielding guaranteed end-to-end speedups while preserving accuracy at high sparsity. Practically, we update layer budgets periodically as movement statistics evolve, prune the least important weights under the allocated per-layer caps, and optionally rewind or distill during the final recovery phase. We expect strong gains in LLM and vision fine-tuning where unstructured sparsity is acceptable but must meet strict latency targets.

result.text: The paper tackles novel view synthesis from unstructured photo collections where varying illumination and transient occluders create artifacts and slow, costly training for prior NeRF-based solutions. The key insight is that 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) can be adapted to this wild setting by explicitly assigning appearance to each Gaussian via material-like attributes, per-image global illumination and camera factors, and local reflectance variance, while directly aligning high-frequency reference image features to Gaussians through triplane sampling rather than image-space proxies. The method—Wild-GS—uses this per-Gaussian appearance model plus triplane-sampled feature transfer, 2D visibility maps to downweight or remove transient objects, and depth regularization to stabilize geometry, yielding much faster training and rendering. Building on this, the authors propose ASAM (Adaptive Sharpness-Aware Minimization), an optimizer that, at each step, computes worst-case normalized perturbations within a scaled neighborhood and updates parameters to minimize the resulting robust loss; experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that ASAM improves generalization over prior sharpness-aware methods.

result.text: We propose Adaptive Off-Policy Proximal Policy Optimization, which calibrates the width and shape of the proximal surrogate to the measured off-policyness of each batch. Using DEON to estimate off-policyness, we decouple a dedicated proximal policy from the behavior policy and set a per-batch temperature for a smooth sigmoid surrogate (or per-sample clipping coefficients) via an off-policy improvement bound, shrinking the trust region under high DEON and relaxing it when data are near on-policy. To preserve reliability and enforce constraints, we integrate a CUP-style constrained update projection that triggers only when the DEON-calibrated step would violate improvement or safety conditions. This design targets replay-driven sample efficiency with batch-size invariance and stronger stability than static off-policy PPO, and provides a monotonic improvement guarantee under bounded DEON.

args.text: We propose Diffusion Mixture Neural Processes (DMNP), which combine diffusion-based neural processes with mixture-of-experts to capture multimodal, heterogeneous function families in meta-learning. Each expert is a symmetry-aware diffusion generator with ConvNP-style equivariant encoders/decoders; a differentiable k-selection gate maps the context set to a sparse mixture over experts while preserving exchangeability. Training jointly maximizes context-conditioned likelihood of finite marginals via diffusion denoising losses and encourages expert diversity; at inference DMNP yields calibrated, multimodal posteriors and scales with sparse compute. We evaluate on nonstationary meta-regression and image completion, ablating gating (top-k vs DSelect-k), expert symmetry choices, and adding light mutual-distillation between experts to mitigate narrow-vision effects.

args.text: We propose Counterfactual Cross-Modal Probing (CCMP) for multimodal fake news detection: rather than only measuring observed consistency, CCMP learns from minimally edited counterfactuals that selectively perturb one modality (e.g., attribute-level image edits, caption paraphrases that flip entities/relations, or audio–lip desynchronization in short videos) while holding others fixed, training the detector to be maximally sensitive to targeted inconsistencies and invariant to spurious social cues. A conditional editor guided by structured scene/attribute graphs from text–image–audio produces semantically plausible counterfactuals, and a causal multi-view objective (risk extrapolation across sources/publishers) encourages invariance to distribution shifts. Compared to reweighting-based multimodal fusion, CCMP supplies targeted supervision aligned with inconsistency types and naturally extends to short-video settings, yielding robustness and edit-based explanations. At inference, generation is not used; the model predicts veracity and reports which probe types would flip its decision as human-understandable evidence.

result.text: The paper addresses uncertainty quantification in causal discovery from observational data, noting that maximum-likelihood point estimates of DAGs can be misleading when graphs are non-identifiable or data are scarce. Its key insight is that a scalable variational Bayesian treatment over DAGs—rather than a single point estimate—better captures posterior uncertainty and improves structure recovery in low-data regimes, provided the variational family, relaxation, and priors are chosen appropriately. The authors introduce BCD Nets, which parametrize distributions over adjacency matrices with an expressive variational family, use a continuous relaxation of discrete graph variables to enable low-variance stochastic gradients for variational inference, and incorporate suitable priors for linear–Gaussian SEMs; experiments on synthetic and real datasets show improved structural Hamming distance compared to maximum-likelihood baselines.

result.text: Compute-Optimal Granularity Scheduling (COGS) for MoE. Instead of fixing expert size and k throughout training, we derive and implement a training-time schedule for expert granularity and activation that follows asymmetric compute-optimality, allocating more FLOPs to additional steps early and shifting to larger experts later. We combine the MoE granularity scaling law with solvable training dynamics that explain time-vs-width exponents to predict phase boundaries and a two-stage policy: begin with many small experts and higher routing entropy to harvest step-driven gains under data reuse, then merge/swell experts and reduce activation as capacity/embedding limits dominate. A DynMoE-style controller prunes and grows experts online to track the schedule, and theory predicts lower loss per FLOP and smaller train–test gaps than any static granularity under fixed-day budgets.

args.text: We propose Token-Cascade Autoregression, a unified multimodal LLM that reasons and generates with a nested, semantic visual token hierarchy while dynamically allocating an instance-wise token budget. Images (and video frames) are discretized into coarse lexical-aligned semantic tokens plus progressively finer residual groups; during decoding, a learned policy inside the LLM uses its hidden states and the prompt to decide where to stop at coarse tokens, where to request finer tokens, and when to route to retrieval versus generative refinement under a latency-aware cost. Training couples left-to-right multimodal next-token learning with a budget regularizer and distills an oracle that reveals ideal per-sample allocations from a Matryoshka-style tokenizer and dynamic semantic grouping, enabling frozen- or lightly-tuned LLM variants via mapping modules. This yields a single model that trades off speed and fidelity on-the-fly, improves localized generation/editing, and scales to video by allocating motion/detail tokens only where needed.

result.text: The paper addresses the security risk that Large Language Models (LLMs) can be covertly manipulated via Trojan-style prompt attacks in realistic black-box settings. Its key insight is that universal, stealthy trigger tokens and poisoned discrete prompts can be discovered and optimized solely through API queries and few-shot examples, enabling reliable, transferable manipulation without white-box access. The proposed TrojLLM framework combines a trigger-discovery algorithm that searches for universal input-level triggers via black-box queries and a progressive Trojan poisoning algorithm that iteratively crafts poisoned prompts to maximize attack efficacy and transferability across models. Experiments show TrojLLM can successfully implant Trojans in real-world LLM APIs such as GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 while preserving performance on clean inputs, highlighting practical risks and suggesting avenues for defense.

result.text: GlyphControl tackles the challenge of generating coherent, accurately rendered visual text with diffusion-based text-to-image models without retraining large text encoders or the base model. The method encodes glyph instructions as additional conditioning signals and trains a lightweight controller on a new LAION-Glyph benchmark so the diffusion model respects glyph geometry and content; evaluation with OCR accuracy, CLIP score, and FID shows GlyphControl yields better legibility and fidelity than prior approaches like DeepFloyd IF.

args.text: We propose an online, coverage-aware sampling and augmentation curriculum for GANs defined in a frozen, pretrained projected feature space. During training, we estimate per-instance undercoverage by contrasting kNN densities of generated vs. real samples and by tracking per-instance discriminator discrepancy statistics; we then sample real images with probability proportional to undercoverage while softly downweighting extreme outliers to avoid capacity waste. In tandem, we apply differentiable augmentations with strength inversely proportional to undercoverage to curb discriminator overfitting on overrepresented regions, and add a generator regularizer to match cluster occupancy in the projected feature space. This unified scheme maintains fidelity by ignoring spurious tails while actively steering learning toward underrepresented modes, and is architecture-agnostic.

result.text: The paper tackles improving representation learning on text-attributed graphs (TAGs) by better leveraging rich textual signals from large language models (LLMs) to boost graph neural network (GNN) performance without heavy engineering or cost. Its key insight is that LLM-generated explanations—textual rationales for zero-shot classifications—contain structured, informative cues that can be transformed into compact, discriminative features for downstream graph learning. The method prompts an LLM to produce zero-shot labels and accompanying explanations for node texts, then uses an LLM-to-LM interpreter to convert those explanations into feature vectors which are fed into a GNN for training; this pipeline yields state-of-the-art accuracy on benchmarks (Cora, PubMed, ogbn-arxiv, and a new tape-arxiv23) while substantially reducing training time compared to prior LM-enhanced TAG approaches.

result.text: The paper addresses the limitation of standard Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) that assume homophily and therefore perform poorly on graphs with heterophily where connected nodes often belong to different classes. The key insight is to replace the fixed homophily-based propagation with an adaptive propagation mechanism that learns a per-edge homophily degree from both topology and node attributes, allowing the model to modulate aggregation strength between node pairs according to their learned similarity. Methodologically, the authors introduce two learnable measurements of homophily (topological and attribute-based), incorporate them into the convolutional propagation so that messages are scaled adaptively, train the whole architecture end-to-end, and provide theoretical guarantees that the mechanism constrains representation similarity by homophily degree; experiments on seven datasets show superior performance on heterophilous graphs and competitive results on homophilous ones.

args.text: Riemannian Masked Graph Pretraining (RMGP) for EEG seizure localization unifies manifold-aware EEG features, instance-adaptive connectivity, and foundation-style tokenization. For each short segment, we map channels or band-limited signals to SPD covariance embeddings, build an instance-adaptive inter-channel graph, and discretize SPD features with a geodesic VQ tokenizer; a graph transformer is then pretrained with joint masked node/edge modeling plus short-horizon next-step prediction in token space, augmented by an imbalance-aware SSL regularizer to capture rare dynamics. Fine-tuning attaches a subgraph anomaly head for zero/semi-shot seizure and channel detection and a supervised classifier for seizure-type recognition, with quantitative localization metrics. We hypothesize RMGP improves cross-dataset transfer, rare-type recall, and focal localization by combining GNN pretraining for seizures, large-scale masked-token learning, SPD-robust EEG encoding, dynamic graph structure, and imbalance-robust SSL.

result.text: We propose an SE(3)-equivariant Mamba for point clouds that preserves linear-time global modeling while guaranteeing rotation/translation consistency. Features are expressed in irreducible representations within local canonical frames per patch (from anisotropic neighborhood PCA), and degree-wise MIMO state-space scans are run along multiple space-filling traversal orders with shared, equivariance-constrained parameters; the traversal streams are fused via order-prompted, permutation-invariant mixing. A multi-order consistency loss aligns hidden states across traversals to remove ordering bias, yielding SE(3)-robust global context without quadratic attention. This bridges the efficiency of 1-D SSM serializations in point-cloud Mamba with the geometric guarantees of SE(3)-Transformers, and is expected to excel under arbitrary rotations and sparse sampling.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of low-quality training data in LLM self-training, where naively using model-generated responses often yields incorrect or unhelpful intermediate reasoning traces. Its key insight is to infer per-step "process rewards" from oracle final answers via Monte Carlo tree search, estimating how likely each step is to lead to a correct solution and using those inferred rewards both as value targets and as a filter for selecting high-quality traces. The proposed method, ReST-MCTS*, integrates process-reward-guided MCTS* to search for high-accuracy reasoning traces under a fixed search budget, uses the search-derived per-step values to refine a process reward model, and iteratively self-trains policy, reward, and value models on the selected traces to progressively improve reasoning performance over alternate self-training baselines.

The key insight is to combine a low-rank latent-factor structure (Probabilistic PCA) with separate marginal transformations per column via a Gaussian copula, so that the latent Gaussian structure captures dependence while flexible marginals match heterogeneous data types (real, ordinal, binary). The method fits this Low Rank Gaussian Copula model by estimating column-wise monotonic transforms and a shared low-rank covariance in the copula space, yielding a scalable (linear-time in rows and columns) probabilistic imputer that produces point estimates and well-calibrated uncertainty measures; experiments show state-of-the-art accuracy and uncertainty that correlates strongly with actual error.

result.text: The paper tackles the puzzle of why simple optimization methods reliably find good solutions in highly non-convex neural network training by asking whether independently trained models actually lie in the same basin up to permutation symmetries of hidden units. The key insight is that many apparent distinct minima are equivalent under unit permutations, so by reordering hidden units one can align two models into a shared, approximately convex basin enabling direct weight-space merging. They introduce three algorithms that permute units of one model to match a reference model and empirically show this “re-basin” yields functionally equivalent weights with near-linear mode connectivity across architectures and datasets (including zero-barrier connectivity for ResNets on CIFAR-10), while also exploring how width and training time affect connectivity and presenting a counterexample that highlights limits of the single-basin hypothesis.

args.text: Plug-and-Play Video-to-Music: turn a strong text-to-audio latent diffusion prior into a video-conditioned generator by doing posterior sampling with a differentiable multiscale visual–audio alignment objective, avoiding any paired video–music training. Concretely, we extract a visual rhythm map (onsets/tempo/sections from motion and shot-change features) and optimize a constraint that combines Earth-Mover’s-Distance between this map and a differentiable audio-onset distribution (from spectral-flux on the model’s mel latents) with a temporal contrastive term from a CAVP encoder, backpropagating through the frozen denoiser across noise levels. An optional lightweight joint discriminator provides cross-modal guidance, while a text prompt steers musical style so that video controls timing/structure; the base prior (e.g., a timing-aware latent audio diffusion) preserves fidelity and length control. We hypothesize state-of-the-art long-horizon rhythmic lock and semantic sync on dance/sports/film benchmarks, rivaling end-to-end V2A systems with far less training, and validate with multiscale AV alignment and human preference studies.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of hallucinations and accumulated errors in Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting for large language models, which undermine trustworthiness and accuracy on complex reasoning tasks. Its key insight is that full-proof verification of an entire deductive chain is intractable, but breaking verification into local, stepwise subprocesses with minimal necessary context lets models perform rigorous self-checking and reduces error propagation. The authors introduce Natural Program, a natural-language deductive format that structures reasoning into precise steps grounded on explicit premises, and they implement a step-by-step self-verification procedure that verifies each deduction before proceeding. result.text: The paper addresses detection of backdoor attacks in convolutional neural networks, where a model is trained to respond to a specific trigger without degrading normal performance by poisoning a small fraction of training data. The key insight is that neurons that mediate the backdoor exhibit distinct pre-activation distributional differences between benign and poisoned inputs—differences in moments that are invariant across attack types—so these “backdoor neurons” can be exposed by statistical measures. Building on mild assumptions about activation distributions, the authors propose two practical detection methods: ranking neurons by their differential entropy and by the Kullback–Leibler divergence between the empirical benign pre-activation distribution and a poisoned-statistics-based hypothetical distribution; experiments show these strategies efficiently and effectively locate backdoor neurons across various attacks.

result.text: The paper addresses why Graph Neural Networks struggle to propagate and preserve useful information across graphs—manifesting as over-smoothing (node features becoming indistinguishable) and over-squashing (long-range signals being compressed and lost). Its key insight is that both pathologies are governed by local graph geometry expressed via Ollivier-Ricci curvature: positive curvature regions promote feature mixing and thus over-smoothing, while negative curvature regions concentrate and distort flows, causing over-squashing. Building on this, the authors derive theoretical links between curvature and message-passing dynamics and introduce Batch Ollivier-Ricci Flow, a curvature-aware graph rewiring algorithm that iteratively adjusts edges to normalize local curvature and thereby mitigate both over-smoothing and over-squashing simultaneously.

result.text: We propose utility-driven lemma invention for neural theorem provers: instead of opportunistically adding any verified lemma, the system learns to conjecture, select, and prune lemmas based on their expected marginal utility across future problems. During expert-iteration and tree-search, we collect subgoal traces, embed and cluster recurring subgoals, and train a predictor of lemma utility (e.g., expected proof-length reduction and success lift) using retrieval signals and hard negatives from annotated premise datasets; an LLM then proposes cluster-conditioned candidate lemmas that are verified and scheduled via a contextual bandit to allocate proof/verification budget. The prover retrieves from a continually pruned library prioritized by predicted utility, with periodic compression (merging near-duplicates, removing dominated lemmas) to keep the library small and high-impact. Evaluations on miniF2F and novel-premise splits measure gains in generalization and sample efficiency, with ablations on clustering, bandit scheduling, and pruning showing that explicit utility estimation outperforms prior purely opportunistic lemma growth.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of "over-squashing" in graph neural networks, where information from distant nodes gets compressed and distorted during message passing, limiting GNN performance on tasks needing long-range interactions; this is commonly attributed to graph bottlenecks but lacked a precise formulation. The key insight is that over-squashing corresponds to negatively curved edges in the graph: such edges act as combinatorial bottlenecks that concentrate and distort many incoming messages, and can be detected via a novel edge-based discrete curvature measure. The authors define this new curvature, prove a formal relationship between negative curvature and the deterioration of information flow in message passing, and propose a curvature-driven graph rewiring algorithm that adds or reweights edges to reduce negative curvature; experiments show that this rewiring alleviates over-squashing and improves GNN performance on long-range tasks.

result.text: FetchSGD addresses the dual challenges in federated learning of heavy communication costs and degraded convergence when client participation is sparse. The key insight is to use a linear, mergeable Count Sketch to compress client model updates so that momentum and error accumulation can be maintained centrally inside the sketch rather than on each client, which preserves state across intermittent clients and enables high compression without losing critical optimization history. Concretely, each client sketches its local gradient/update with a Count Sketch, the server merges these sketches to form an aggregate sketch, performs momentum and error correction in sketch space, and reconstructs sparse updates for model updates; the authors prove convergence guarantees for this procedure and validate it empirically on ResNets and a transformer showing strong communication savings and robust convergence.

args.text: We propose Aug-Dispersed Unlearnable Noise (ADUN): tiny, imperceptible perturbations whose directions are randomized and conditioned on the stochastic data-augmentation parameters, so the effective perturbation subspace is dispersed across views and training time. Building on the stability of SEM-style randomized training and SEP’s self-ensembling over checkpoints, we train a per-example perturbation generator that maps augmentation metadata to a perturbation drawn from a low-rank family regularized for high dispersion, forcing models to chase inconsistent shortcuts that a single orthogonal projection cannot recover. We explicitly borrow the notion of dispersibility from untargeted backdoor watermarks to encourage nondeterministic abnormal behaviors across augmentations while preserving human imperceptibility. We hypothesize ADUN better withstands orthogonal-projection recovery and adversarially trained learners than fixed-pattern unlearnable defenses and propose evaluations in both supervised and contrastive pretraining.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of making sorting operations differentiable for learning tasks where only order or ranking supervision is available, noting that existing differentiable sorting methods can be non-monotonic and thus produce misleading gradient signs. The key insight is that by relaxing the conditional swap operation in sorting networks with an appropriately chosen family of sigmoid functions one can guarantee monotonicity, ensuring gradients always have the correct sign for optimization. args.text: We propose Counterfactual Cross-Modal Probing for fake news detection: generate minimally edited, semantically controlled counterfactuals that either align or misalign modalities (e.g., attribute flips, entity substitutions in text; localized diffusion edits on entities/attributes in images/video) and measure prediction sensitivity to quantify inconsistency. Guided by compact, content-relevant KG subgraphs and reading-habit/consistency signals, the probes target entity-level relations most likely to reveal deception while preserving surface form. A probe network learns from these counterfactual trajectories to produce a robustness profile and causal attributions to deceptive patterns (e.g., repurposing, manipulation), extending neuro-symbolic explainability. Evaluated on article+image and short-video settings, the approach improves detection, yields crisper pattern-level explanations, and enables calibrated abstention when robustness profiles are ambiguous.

We propose Bayesian CASTLE: instead of regularizing a predictor with a single learned causal graph, train with a posterior over DAGs and minimize a reconstruction penalty averaged over adjacency samples from a variational graph posterior, so the predictor relies on neighborhoods consistently supported by the data. Concretely, we draw relaxed adjacency matrices from a scalable variational posterior over graphs during end-to-end training and compute stochastic estimates of the expectation-of-reconstruction term, optionally tightening the posterior with interventional or multi-domain invariance constraints when available. This turns structural uncertainty into calibrated regularization, improving out-of-sample generalization and reducing brittleness when any single best-DAG estimate is misspecified.

result.text: We propose Concept-Aligned Idiom Retrieval and Control (CIRC), which unifies an idiom knowledge base with induced conceptual metaphor mappings to translate figurative language by intent, not just phrase lookup. CIRC augments an IdiomKB with source→target concept embeddings learned from unsupervised metaphor-mapping signals, retrieves both idiom paraphrases and conceptual frames for a detected figurative span, and injects novelty/control tokens to steer generation toward an idiomatic equivalent, literal gloss, or explanatory paraphrase depending on user context. The system integrates these controls into prompt designs for LLM-based MT and retrieval-augmented paraphrasing, selecting in-context examples by conceptual-frame proximity. Evaluation targets figurative semantic fidelity using a WMD-backed similarity suite plus human judgments, with ablations isolating retrieval vs. concept-mapping vs. control-token contributions.

result.text: The paper studies the unexplored vulnerability of heterogeneous graph neural networks (HGNNs) to topology adversarial attacks, showing that attackers can easily mislead HGNNs by adding edges from a target node to high-degree “hub” nodes. The key insight is that two HGNN-specific factors exacerbate this weakness: a perturbation enlargement effect due to failing to encode metapath-based transition probabilities, and soft attention mechanisms that assign positive weights to unreliable, adversarial neighbors. To address this, the authors propose RoHe, a defense that adds an attention purifier which uses metapath-based transiting probability as a prior to constrain the influence of potential hubs and learns to mask neighbors with low confidence based on topology and features, thereby reducing malicious attention. Empirical results on several benchmarks and HGNN architectures show that RoHe substantially improves robustness against topology attacks while generalizing across datasets.

result.text: This paper addresses learning mappings (operators) between infinite-dimensional function spaces, specifically for predicting solutions of partial differential equations (PDEs) from input functions, in a way that generalizes across different discretizations and resolutions. The key insight is that a single neural architecture parameterized once can represent such operators by composing nonlinear activations with integral operators whose kernels are implemented via graph-based message-passing, enabling discretization-invariant learning. The method, called a Neural Operator or graph kernel network, approximates the integral kernel by graph convolution/message-passing on a mesh or point cloud, stacks these integral layers with nonlinearities to form an operator network, and trains the shared kernel parameters so the same model generalizes across finite-difference, finite-element, and varying-resolution discretizations. Experiments on PDE tasks demonstrate that this approach achieves the desired resolution and method invariance while matching or improving on state-of-the-art solvers.

result.text: Permutation-aligned masked Fisher merging: first align each task model to an elected base via a symmetry-equivariant aligner to resolve neuron permutations, then attach EMR-style lightweight modulators. For each layer, compute per-parameter importance using a Fisher/curvature proxy relative to the base and perform a small multi-task selection to activate only a sparse set of deltas via binary masks, while suppressing "selfish/catastrophic" conflicts by consensus across tasks. Scale the surviving deltas with uncertainty-aware rescalers to match gradients and reduce interference, yielding a data-free, tuning-free merge that preserves task specializations yet coexists in one backbone. This unifies principled alignment, importance-weighted selection, and mask-based modulation to outperform naive averaging and prior masking-only schemes in multi-task and adapter fusion.

args.text: RhythmAlign proposes a plug-and-play guidance layer for video-conditioned music diffusion that enforces multi-timescale temporal alignment and phrasing without retraining. Building on latent video-to-audio diffusion backbones with strong visual encoders, we add a differentiable alignment objective that combines (i) soft-DTW between video motion-energy curves and predicted audio onset/beat envelopes and (ii) boundary matching between shot/scene-change novelty and music cadence/change points, and apply its gradients during sampling. We realize this as posterior inference with a frozen denoiser: the alignment cost c(x,y) is backpropagated through the diffusion steps to steer samples, while explicit timing embeddings provide controllable durations and tempo ramps. This aims to improve beat-phase lock and scene-level musical structure over long horizons with small runtime overhead and remains compatible with few-step samplers.

result.text: We propose Parse-to-Act, a dual-head VLM that jointly reconstructs simplified HTML/DOM from screenshots and predicts goal-conditioned pixel-level action affordance maps for generic mouse/keyboard control. Training combines Pix2Struct-style screenshot-to-HTML pretraining and Web2Code’s image+instruction-to-HTML supervision with distillation of affordance heatmaps from a strong pixel-only GUI agent, while a cross-consistency loss ties HTML token spans to their spatial regions. At inference, the parsed HTML seeds a lightweight planner (for step decomposition) and the affordance head executes each step via continuous pointing and typing; we then fine-tune with human-prior RL for robustness. We evaluate on OSWorld to test multi-application workflows, hypothesizing the HTML–affordance coupling will close the GUI grounding gap seen in current agents.

args.text: We propose PPG2Lead-ODE, a cross-modal generator that transforms wearable PPG and optional demographics into a low-dimensional cardiac source state evolved by a neural ODE, then renders all 12 ECG leads via a lightly personalized biophysical lead-field to enforce cross-lead coherence. Disease semantics are injected by conditioning the ODE vector field, while an ROI-disentangled diffusion guidance emphasizes P–QRS–T intervals to preserve fine morphology in both time and frequency domains. A brief calibration with a few seconds of paired PPG–ECG adapts the lead-field per patient, enabling accurate multi-lead synthesis from PPG alone for diagnosis, missing-lead imputation, and privacy-preserving augmentation. Compared to prior PPG→ECG translation and disease-aware multi-lead GANs, our physics-consistent cross-modal design better captures condition-specific changes across views.

result.text: To counter latency-raising adversarial inputs in camera-based AD perception, I propose Budgeted Randomized Early-Exit with Latency Regularization (BREELR). During training, optimize a joint objective that penalizes task error and a differentiable runtime proxy while performing adversarial augmentation that explicitly maximizes runtime, so the model learns latency-insensitive features and robust exit gating. At inference, enforce a hard deadline via patience-based early exits and randomized, functionally-equivalent operator/route choices (e.g., kernel variants, feature downsampling paths) to decorrelate attacker gradients from realized compute and to fall back to an anytime, conservative action as the deadline approaches. Evaluate within SlowTrack-style pipelines and SafeBench to show bounded tail-latency and reduced crash rates under white- and black-box slowdown attacks compared to vanilla early-exit and standard adversarial training.

result.text: We propose Performatively Stable Bayesian Optimization (PS-BO), an acquisition strategy that jointly seeks improvement while steering the optimizer’s induced query distribution toward the oracle’s effective training distribution to avoid out-of-distribution hallucinations. Concretely, we alternate autofocused oracle reweighting with acquisition updates that penalize regions of high calibration mismatch, estimated via posterior-sample disagreement and hyperparameter uncertainty, and optimize a Lagrangian trade-off between gain and stability. We frame multi-step query-distribution evolution as an MDP and train a policy to reach performatively stable fixed points where the deployed acquisition and the retrained oracle are calibrated to each other. We hypothesize PS-BO reduces failure cases in protein/small-molecule design versus standard BO or pure autofocusing by explicitly optimizing for calibration-stability alongside utility.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of removing backdoor triggers implanted in deep neural networks—poisoned training-time manipulations that leave clean accuracy intact but force targeted misclassification when a trigger appears. Its key insight is that backdoored models exhibit altered intermediate-layer attention patterns that can be corrected by aligning the compromised model’s attention with that of a cleanly fine-tuned teacher, thereby erasing the trigger’s effect without degrading normal performance. The proposed method, Neural Attention Distillation (NAD), obtains a teacher by independently fine-tuning on a small clean subset and then distills its intermediate attention maps into the backdoored student during further fine-tuning on that same clean data, using attention-alignment losses to guide the student toward the teacher’s behavior. Empirically NAD removes backdoors from models infected by multiple state-of-the-art attacks using only 5% clean data while preserving accuracy on clean examples.

result.text: The paper addresses open-vocabulary object detection, where detectors struggle to leverage vision-language models’ (VLMs) rich zero-shot knowledge because they typically align regions only with coarse category names. The key insight is that VLMs also align visual regions with fine-grained textual descriptors (object parts and attributes), and incorporating those descriptors via conditional context prompts and hierarchical text improves region-text alignment and generalization. The proposed method, DVDet, transforms regional embeddings into image-like representations using conditional context prompts so they can be trained in standard detection pipelines, and it uses large language models to iteratively mine and refine visually oriented textual descriptors for precise supervision. Experiments on multiple large-scale benchmarks show DVDet consistently outperforms prior state-of-the-art by substantial margins.

result.text: We propose Dual-Domain Adversarial Masking (DDAM): a learned masker outputs both spatial patch masks and Fourier-band masks that maximally disrupt an encoder’s invariance, while the encoder minimizes the representation gap between original and doubly-masked views. To prevent degenerate solutions, we add a uniformity regularizer on the encoder’s feature distribution and impose attention-driven saliency priors on the masker, along with a target difficulty curriculum that matches a desired distribution of representation gaps over training. We stabilize the game with auxiliary pixel- and frequency-reconstruction heads that cross-regularize masked predictions, yielding architecture-agnostic pretraining that couples global semantics with fine spatial detail. This unifies adversarial masking with frequency-aware MIM and uniformity theory and is expected to improve both linear probing and dense downstream tasks.

result.text: We propose an intrinsic-rate thermostat for normalized networks: a per-layer control loop that maintains a target intrinsic learning rate by jointly adjusting weight decay and occasional norm projection, using observed rotation speed of weights as the control signal. The target is chosen to sit at the edge-of-stability yet follow a sharpness-reduction flow; a simple PID rule updates decay to keep per-layer rotation near setpoint, suppressing the batchnorm–weight-decay destabilization cycles while preserving their generalization benefits. This removes most learning-rate tuning by tying effective step size to geometry (akin to parameter-free schedules) and can optionally correct finite-step distortions by modestly adapting the nominal step when stationary variance inflates. CurvMix is a curvature-conditioned, channel-wise polynomial propagation scheme for heterophilous graphs. It learns a mixture over smoothing and sharpening operators drawn from a heterophily-aware spectral basis, but assigns mixture weights per edge and channel via a small router that consumes local discrete curvature and structural cues; this densifies information flow across negatively curved bottlenecks without explicit rewiring and suppresses over-smoothing in positively curved regions. The design generalizes trainable per-channel weights to be edge- and curvature-aware and inherits frequency adaptivity, replacing curvature-driven rewiring with a learned curvature-to-filter map. We further propose curvature-dependent stability bounds to guide gain clipping during training.

args.text: We propose selective transparency for performatively fair strategic learning: optimize partial-disclosure policies (e.g., score buckets, feature-importance hints, or example-based cues) that shape how heterogeneous groups infer and respond to a principal’s rule, targeting universal improvement while retaining performative stability. args.text: We propose Privately Equalized Gradient Alignment (PEGA), a DP-SGD variant that targets fairness by equalizing the cosine alignment between each group’s true gradient and the privatized update. PEGA combines geometry-aware, non-isotropic clipping/noise and non-monotonic per-sample weighting with a DP-safe estimation of per-group gradient geometry learned from locally privatized group tags and lightweight gradient sketches, yielding group-specific preconditioners and clipping scales that equalize expected clipping and signal-to-noise across groups. This design reduces gradient misalignment and clipping bias that disproportionately harms minority groups, while requiring no access to raw sensitive attributes and composing cleanly with standard DP accounting. We provide a bound showing that disparities in group-wise update alignment shrink with the error of the privatized geometry estimator, translating into improvements in fairness metrics without degrading overall utility.

args.text: I propose Topo-CAW: augment Causal Anonymous Walks with streaming zigzag persistence images computed on temporal ego-nets along the sampled walks, providing stable topological channels that capture the birth/death of closures, bursts, and churn missing from anonymized count statistics. We fuse these low-dimensional zigzag descriptors with CAW-N embeddings and a lightweight temporal attention/readout for dynamic link prediction and anomaly detection, aiming to improve inductive generalization across systems. Evaluation will use live NFT transaction graphs and large financial fraud graphs under TGB-style protocols and EdgeBank’s hard negative splits to stress robustness rather than memorization. We hypothesize consistent gains on reoccurrence- and motif-heavy regimes where topology evolves rapidly yet node identities are uninformative.

result.text: IA-RED2 tackles the high computational and memory cost of vision transformers by identifying and removing redundant, uncorrelated input patches while preserving accuracy. The key insight is that many tokens contribute little to final predictions and can be dynamically and interpretablely pruned using a learned module that signals which patches are redundant, yielding both efficiency gains and human-understandable explanations. Methodologically, the paper integrates this interpretable pruning module into a hierarchical token-reduction framework that progressively drops uncorrelated tokens across stages, and evaluates the approach on image and video transformers (e.g., DeiT, TimeSformer), achieving up to ~1.4× speed-up with <0.7% accuracy loss and producing visualizations that outperform raw attention and standard interpretation methods.

args.text: I propose curvature-compensated dynamic N:M sparse training that maintains hardware-friendly block sparsity throughout optimization while periodically performing online, block-local quadratic updates to jointly drop and reassign nonzeros. At scheduled steps, each M-sized block solves a tiny CHITA-like subproblem using a diagonal (or K-FAC block) Hessian approximation and a compensated-movement score (accumulated signed gradients modulated by curvature) to pick which connections to prune and which to regrow, with new weights initialized via zero-cost neuroregeneration. The training loop stays always-sparse as in Top-KAST and targets a user-specified speedup by allocating per-layer update frequency and sparsity using an SPDY-style runtime model, yielding practical acceleration. Compared to SR-STE baselines, this online curvature-aware regrowth should reduce topology divergence, stabilize convergence, and improve accuracy at high 2:4 and 1:4 sparsities.

We propose Joint Fisher-Aware Active Learning with Sparse Adaptation (J-FALSA): co-design the query batch and a fixed sparse parameter mask to maximize generalization under compute/communication budgets. We extend BAIT’s Fisher-bound objective to the masked model and regularize it with estimator-variance terms, preferring queries and masks that yield stable Fisher estimates. At each round, we sketch the Fisher to choose a top-k parameter mask as in fixed-Fisher sparse updates, then select a large, diversity-controlled batch whose masked Fisher contribution maximizes bound reduction, using scalable diversification to avoid redundancy. This jointly optimizes which parameters to train and which labels to acquire, enabling resource-constrained streaming or distributed training that preserves BAIT-level label efficiency while reducing memory and communication costs.

result.text: We propose Dual-Space Curvature Smoothing (DSCS), a fast adversarial training regime that prevents catastrophic overfitting by jointly flattening the loss in input- and weight-space at near single-step cost. Concretely, we couple diversified, non-maximal FGSM perturbations with a small-radius SAM step enhanced by a GSAM-style surrogate-gap reduction and random weight smoothing, and add a light GradAlign penalty to explicitly reduce input-loss curvature; a FOSC-based schedule gradually increases these regularizers and adversary fidelity over training. This dual smoothing blunts boundary concentration and stabilizes the inner maximization, yielding robust accuracy competitive with multi-step PGD while maintaining clean accuracy via flatter minima. We evaluate with a parameter-free attack ensemble to ensure no gradient obfuscation and analyze improvements via reduced dominant Hessian eigenvalues and lower variance of adversarial directions.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of giving rigorous, distribution-free guarantees for generative language model outputs by adapting conformal prediction to the combinatorial, sampled-output setting of LMs. The key insight is to treat LM sampling as a sequential set-construction problem and jointly calibrate a stopping rule (when the candidate set is sufficiently likely to contain an acceptable answer) and a rejection rule (to remove low-quality samples), thereby producing small output sets that nevertheless contain at least one correct response with high probability. args.text: We propose an adaptive guard-prefix controller that, for each incoming prompt, synthesizes a minimal defensive suffix conditioned on prompt features and cheap side-signals, and is trained in a min–max game against a population of jailbreak generators spanning search-based black-box attacks, token-level trigger attacks, and output-filter–evasive cipher encoders. Unlike fixed, one-size-fits-all prompt-level defenses, the controller dynamically composes defense primitives—refusal scaffolds, paraphrastic inoculation, or learned information bottlenecks—under a utility-aware objective that penalizes overblocking and latency to preserve benign performance. Trained with curriculum and population-based adversaries and evaluated under attack-aware methodology and defended-LLM benchmarks, the approach targets robustness to adaptive black-box and token-level jailbreaks as well as moderation-bypassing ciphers at comparable utility. Additionally, a lightweight paraphrase-smoothing check around the chosen suffix provides an empirical per-input refusal certificate via concentration bounds, offering probabilistic guarantees against residual jailbreaks.

We propose training a single MIMO-style multihead network that efficiently approximates ensemble diversity. Complementarity is enforced by penalizing conditional mutual information between head features given labels and by maximizing head disagreement on adversarially found OOD-like perturbations, with disagreement-seeking inputs produced either via a teacher ensemble during distillation or via self-play among heads. To prevent on-train collusion, these objectives are computed on a held-out unlabeled pool, and per-head structured sparsity masks induce lightweight architectural heterogeneity. The result is a one-pass model with near-ensemble accuracy, calibration, and OOD detection, with the option to distill the heads into a single deployable predictor.

result.text: This paper addresses how to extend generative diffusion models to data that naturally lives in discrete-state spaces by developing an exact theoretical formulation for arbitrary discrete-state forward Markov processes and their reverse-time counterparts. The key insight is that one can analyze discrete forward diffusions without resorting to variational approximations, deriving exact reverse-time mappings and a score-like object in continuous time that parallels Gaussian diffusion theory but operates on discrete states. Methodologically, the authors derive the mathematics linking discrete forward transitions to exact reverse dynamics, relate this to existing continuous and discrete approaches, and instantiate the framework with "Blackout Diffusion," a model that trains a reverse process to generate images starting from an empty (blackout) state rather than Gaussian noise, demonstrating feasibility on CIFAR-10, binarized MNIST, and CelebA.

result.text: The paper tackles unsupervised/self-supervised image representation learning, specifically removing reliance on contrastive methods that require negative examples while still learning high-quality features. The key insight is that an online network can learn useful representations by predicting the representation of a different augmentation of the same image produced by a slowly evolving target network (an exponential moving average of the online network), without requiring explicit negative pairs or contrastive losses. The method trains two networks—an online predictor and a target encoder—by minimizing a prediction loss between the online output for one view and the target representation for another view, while updating the target network via a momentum update of the online weights; this simple bootstrap mechanism yields state-of-the-art ImageNet linear evaluation and strong transfer and semi-supervised performance.

args.text: We propose an in-context open-vocabulary detector that adapts at inference time from a handful of multimodal exemplars—cropped support images paired with natural-language descriptions—and optional counter-exemplars, without any finetuning. A frozen region proposal and vision–language encoder produce query-region embeddings; a lightweight set-to-set transformer constructs per-class classifiers and a contrastive calibrator on the fly from positive/negative supports, while a CLIP-driven image-level multi-label prior reweights region scores for scene-consistent categories. Trained episodically on base classes to learn the inference procedure, the model aligns to user-specified target semantics far better than name-only or fixed-text detectors and excels on fine-grained or domain-specific concepts. The design is plug-and-play atop existing OVOD/FSOD backbones and unifies text prompts with visual exemplars for robust few-shot alignment at test time.

result.text: The paper addresses the tension in reinforcement learning between on-policy methods’ stability and off-policy methods’ sample efficiency, aiming to retain reliable policy improvement while reusing past experience. The key insight is that policy improvement guarantees can be generalized to the off-policy setting and that these bounds naturally relate to PPO’s clipping mechanism, suggesting a principled way to adapt clipping for off-policy data. result.text: The paper addresses the problem that neural-operator models for solving PDEs typically learn boundary conditions (BCs) only implicitly from data and therefore may violate essential physics-based BCs (Dirichlet, Neumann, periodic) at evaluation, undermining solution existence, uniqueness, and physical fidelity. The key insight is that BC satisfaction can be enforced structurally by modifying the operator kernel rather than relying solely on data or loss penalties, so the network’s mapping inherently respects boundary constraints. The authors propose Boundary enforcing Operator Network (BOON), a refinement procedure that alters the operator kernel to impose BCs exactly, and they demonstrate across multiple PDEs that BOON guarantees BC satisfaction and substantially reduces domain-wide errors. Empirically, BOON yields dramatic improvements (2×–20×) in relative L2 error compared with baseline operators, achieving very low errors (e.g., 8.4e-5 for Burgers’ equation).

result.text: This paper addresses learning mappings (operators) between infinite-dimensional function spaces, specifically for predicting solutions of partial differential equations (PDEs) from input functions, in a way that generalizes across different discretizations and resolutions. The key insight is that a single neural architecture parameterized once can represent such operators by composing nonlinear activations with integral operators whose kernels are implemented via graph-based message-passing, enabling discretization-invariant learning. The method, called a Neural Operator or graph kernel network, approximates the integral kernel by graph convolution/message-passing on a mesh or point cloud, stacks these integral layers with nonlinearities to form an operator network, and trains the shared kernel parameters so the same model generalizes across finite-difference, finite-element, and varying-resolution discretizations. Experiments on PDE tasks demonstrate that this approach achieves the desired resolution and method invariance while matching or improving on state-of-the-art solvers.

args.text: We propose Adaptive Transform Stress-Testing (ATS) for post-training, black-box backdoor detection. ATS combines reverse-engineered candidate triggers scored by expected transferability with a suite of semantically preserving distribution shifts (e.g., blur/color jitter/geometry) and diffusion-based purification to amplify backdoor-specific inconsistencies in model responses, without needing clean data. A K-arm bandit adaptively allocates queries across target labels and transformation types, while topological priors regularize reverse-engineering to favor plausible triggers; for large label spaces we aggregate pairwise statistics via X2X-style transferability clustering. This yields query-efficient, attack-agnostic detection that scales to multi-attack settings and reduces false positives by requiring ET consistency to persist across orthogonal shifts and purifications.

result.text: The paper tackles generative modeling of infinite-resolution data by formulating diffusion directly in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space so models can synthesize arbitrarily high-resolution signals without latent compression. The key insight is to train on randomly subsampled coordinate sets and denoise only those locations using non-local integral operators (rather than pointwise neural fields), which lets the model aggregate spatial context and learn a continuous function that can be evaluated at any resolution. Methodologically, they introduce a multi-scale, function-space architecture that operates on sparse raw coordinates together with a mollified diffusion process that smooths irregularities from subsampling, enabling efficient training and inference that preserves quality even at high subsampling rates and scales beyond training resolution.

result.text: We propose Sampled-Exact-Optimized Tree Search (SEOTS): integrate the exact regularized policy optimizer for MCTS with Sampled Muzero’s action-subset planning. At each node, solve the KL-regularized policy improvement over the sampled actions plus a “tail” pseudo-action that upper-bounds unsampled mass via Good–Turing or count-based uncertainty, yielding optimism-aware selection while preserving scalability. Subset bias is controlled by importance-weighted trust-region constraints derived from the proposal distribution, which is adaptively learned to minimize the per-node duality gap; backups use the optimized stochastic policy to generate targets. SEOTS should improve sample efficiency and control in continuous action domains and Go by reducing over-exploration of sampled decoys while guarding against missed high-value actions.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of efficient learning of directed acyclic graph (DAG) structures from data, where existing continuous optimization approaches enforce acyclicity via costly iterative constraints. The key insight is that weighted adjacency matrices of DAGs exactly correspond to gradients of graph potential functions, so one can search for DAGs by projecting arbitrary weighted graphs onto the space of gradient fields (i.e., curl-free graphs) instead of imposing acyclicity directly. The proposed method, DAG-NoCurl, therefore computes an initial (possibly cyclic) solution to the unconstrained optimization and then applies a Hodge decomposition to extract and retain only the gradient component, yielding an acyclic weighted adjacency matrix; this two-step projection-based algorithm achieves similar accuracy but substantially faster runtimes than prior constrained methods on linear and generalized structural equation benchmarks.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of training and especially serving very large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, whose sparse architectures promise large training cost savings over dense models but create practical bottlenecks in inference, model size, and deployment. The key insight is that coordinated innovations across architecture, compression, and system-level inference optimizations can unlock MoE’s efficiency without sacrificing model quality, enabling MoE models to be both much smaller and much faster/cheaper at runtime than comparable dense models. The authors introduce DeepSpeed-MoE, an end-to-end library extension that combines new MoE architectural designs, model compression techniques that shrink models up to 3.7×, and a highly optimized inference engine that yields up to 7.3× better latency/cost versus prior MoE solutions and up to 4.5× faster or 9× cheaper inference versus quality-equivalent dense models. By integrating these methods into a production-ready system, DeepSpeed-MoE demonstrates a practical path to scale and deploy next-generation sparse models more efficiently.

result.text: We propose a paraphrase-first MT pipeline for figurative language: detect idiom/metaphor spans, then build a controllable source-language paraphrase lattice before translation. Retrieved idiom senses guide an NC-RAPT module to generate multiple paraphrases at calibrated novelty (higher novelty for more non-compositional phrases), which are then translated with prompt-optimized LLM MT; final candidates are re-ranked by alignment to IdiomKB glosses and a human-aligned semantic similarity signal. This decouples semantic interpretation from cross-lingual mapping, reducing literal renderings in low-resource or small-model settings and yielding an explicit explanation via the chosen paraphrase and sense. We also leverage prompt/example selection heuristics to improve both the paraphrasing and translation stages.

result.text: The paper studies the unexplored vulnerability of heterogeneous graph neural networks (HGNNs) to topology adversarial attacks, showing that attackers can easily mislead HGNNs by adding edges from a target node to high-degree “hub” nodes. The key insight is that two HGNN-specific factors exacerbate this weakness: a perturbation enlargement effect due to failing to encode metapath-based transition probabilities, and soft attention mechanisms that assign positive weights to unreliable, adversarial neighbors. To address this, the authors propose RoHe, a defense that adds an attention purifier which uses metapath-based transiting probability as a prior to constrain the influence of potential hubs and learns to mask neighbors with low confidence based on topology and features, thereby reducing malicious attention. Empirical results on several benchmarks and HGNN architectures show that RoHe substantially improves robustness against topology attacks while generalizing across datasets.

result.text: TokenFlow addresses the problem of text-driven video editing with high visual quality and temporal consistency by adapting powerful text-to-image diffusion models to videos without retraining. The key insight is that temporal consistency in edited videos can be achieved by enforcing consistency in the diffusion model’s internal feature space and propagating those features across frames using inter-frame correspondences already available in the model. The method extracts diffusion features during generation, computes correspondences between frames to warp and propagate these features, and applies any off-the-shelf text-to-image editing technique while maintaining spatial layout and motion from the source video. This training-free, model-agnostic framework yields state-of-the-art, temporally coherent edits on real-world videos by combining feature-level propagation with existing text-to-image diffusion editing.

args.text: I propose a two-phase curriculum-balanced GAN training regime that first concentrates on high-density regions to stabilize the generator, then gradually shifts capacity to low-density/underrepresented regions. In phase one, we downweight or temporarily exclude low-density/outlier instances detected in a perceptual-space density model so the generator learns the core manifold. In phase two, we progressively reintroduce and upweight instances flagged by per-instance discrepancy, pairing them with targeted differentiable augmentations and an auxiliary specialist discriminator to avoid overfitting and collapse. This dynamics-aware schedule, motivated by when curricula help, aims to improve both FID and minority coverage without sacrificing stability.

result.text: The paper addresses how to leverage large language models for graph-structured data, overcoming the challenge that graphs do not naturally map to the token sequences LLMs expect. The key insight is that preserving graph structural information while projecting nodes into the LLM token embedding space enables an LLM to reason about graphs without abandoning its general-purpose language capabilities. LLaGA implements this by reorganizing graph nodes into structure-aware sequences and feeding them through a learned projector into the LLM’s token embeddings, allowing a single model to be trained and applied across multiple graph tasks and datasets; experiments show this approach yields strong supervised and zero-shot performance and affords improved transferability and interpretability.

result.text: The paper tackles Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval (ZS-CIR), where models must retrieve images based on a reference image plus a manipulation description across diverse tasks (domain, object, attribute) without task-specific labels. The key insight is that converting the reference image into a context-dependent pseudo-word token tailored to the manipulation intent lets a text-image matching model attend only to description-relevant visual information, yielding more accurate retrieval. To do this, Context-I2W uses an Intent View Selector that learns a dynamic rotation-like mapping to produce a task-specific view of the same image and a Visual Target Extractor that, guided by multiple learnable queries, captures local target regions; these modules jointly produce the pseudo-word token fused with the text prompt for zero-shot retrieval without extra supervision. Empirically, this approach generalizes across four ZS-CIR tasks and improves state-of-the-art performance by 1.88–3.60% over prior best methods.

result.text: Riemannian Masked Graph Pretraining (RMGP) for EEG seizure localization unifies manifold-aware EEG features, instance-adaptive connectivity, and foundation-style tokenization. For each short segment, we map channels or band-limited signals to SPD covariance embeddings, build an instance-adaptive inter-channel graph, and discretize SPD features with a geodesic VQ tokenizer; a graph transformer is then pretrained with joint masked node/edge modeling plus short-horizon next-step prediction in token space, augmented by an imbalance-aware SSL regularizer to capture rare dynamics. Fine-tuning attaches a subgraph anomaly head for zero/semi-shot seizure and channel detection and a supervised classifier for seizure-type recognition, with quantitative localization metrics. We hypothesize RMGP improves cross-dataset transfer, rare-type recall, and focal localization by combining GNN pretraining for seizures, large-scale masked-token learning, SPD-robust EEG encoding, dynamic graph structure, and imbalance-robust SSL.

args.text: Alias-Aware Multiscale Spectral Neural Operators: We propose a neural-operator architecture that explicitly minimizes cross-discretization drift by training with an operator-aliasing penalty and by embedding learnable anti-aliasing filters into the inter-scale transfers. Concretely, we combine (i) direct spectral transforms on irregular points with learned quadrature and sampling patterns to keep only resolvable modes, and (ii) a multigrid-style kernel parameterization whose restriction/prolongation are parameterized by stable, rational activation gates acting as IIR-like filters between scales. Coupled with unsupervised, physics-grounded reconstruction pretraining, the model targets alias-free, resolution-invariant behavior and yields accurate inference on unseen meshes with linear-time evaluation.

result.text: The paper tackles retrosynthesis prediction—finding precursor molecules for a target compound—by aligning model design with chemists’ intuition that reaction cores leave the molecular graph largely intact. Its key insight is to decompose retrosynthesis into two graph-centric stages: predict graph edits that convert the product into incomplete synthons, then expand those synthons into full reactants by attaching leaving groups. The method implements this as a graph-based neural model that outputs edit operations to produce synthons and a subsequent module to grow synthons into complete molecules, yielding interpretable, correctable predictions. This approach achieves state-of-the-art performance (53.7% top-1 accuracy), outperforming prior template-free and semi-template-based methods.

The paper studies the problem of whether neural architectures for point clouds that are equivariant or invariant to translations, rotations, and permutations can universally approximate any target equivariant function. Its key insight is a novel characterization of the space of equivariant polynomials and two sufficient conditions on network architecture that guarantee universality by enabling approximation of those polynomials. Methodologically, the authors derive the polynomial characterization, prove the two sufficient conditions for universal approximation, and then apply these conditions to show that two recent architectures are universal and to construct two new universal equivariant architectures.

args.text: I propose TaTPO-CT: a tool-aware, token-level preference optimization that learns from full inference trees by assigning counterfactual step credit to both successful and failed branches. For each tool-augmented trajectory, we estimate per-step causal contribution via a lightweight process-value MCTS over alternative branches and use these values as weights in a token-level DPO objective with per-batch dynamic beta, enforcing forward-KL control at each token. We further perform active acquisition of prompts/trajectories where the model’s token-level preferences most disagree with the counterfactual step values to maximize label efficiency. This should match tree-of-thought quality at chain-of-thought latency and improve generalization to unseen APIs versus SFT+DPO trained on success-only traces.

We propose Pattern-Aware Re-Masking (PARM) for tabular imputation: replace uniform random re-masking with a learned missingness generator qϕ(m|x) that approximates the observed (potentially MNAR) mechanism and adaptively oversamples rare or high-risk patterns during training. The masked autoencoder is trained under this policy with an additional domain-adversarial penalty to enforce representation invariance across missingness patterns, improving robustness to MNAR shifts. At inference, PARM ensembles imputations by integrating over masks sampled from qϕ and then applies pattern-conditional conformal calibration to produce intervals with valid coverage for each missingness stratum. We hypothesize improved accuracy and calibrated uncertainty under skewed and MNAR masking compared to uniform re-masking approaches.

We propose SyncFlow, a streaming video-to-audio generator that couples rectified-flow spectrogram synthesis with an online synchronization critic to maintain tight, long-horizon alignment under low latency. A rectified flow network maps noise to spectrogram latents conditioned on temporally aligned visual embeddings and a compact rhythmic state (beat phase/tempo) extracted from long visual context, while a lightweight joint guidance critic trained to detect audio–visual misalignment modulates the transport vector field during ODE integration to correct drift in real time. At inference, we use few-step (or distilled one-step) sampling with adaptive guidance strength driven by the critic’s local sync error, enabling rapid updates without sacrificing global rhythmic coherence. This hybrid of straight-path transport and synchronization-aware guidance targets state-of-the-art alignment and quality for live V2A across diverse scenes.

result.text: The paper addresses the gap between current visual instruction-tuned vision-language models (VLMs) and the need for effective multi-step, goal-directed decision-making in interactive environments. Its key insight is that prompting VLMs to produce chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning as intermediate, text-based reasoning steps both enables more efficient exploration and yields better parsing into executable actions for environment interaction. The proposed method fine-tunes VLMs end-to-end with reinforcement learning by (1) providing task descriptions and eliciting CoT outputs, (2) parsing the open-ended text into executable actions that interact with the environment to receive task rewards, and (3) using those rewards to update the whole VLM via RL; experiments show this approach substantially improves decision-making and that CoT is critical to the gains, enabling smaller (7B) models to outperform larger commercial baselines.

result.text: We propose GW-TopoGCD, a topology-preserving prototype alignment framework for generalized category discovery under domain shift that aligns source and target prototype graphs via Gromov–Wasserstein transport, preserving semantic relations while permitting unmatched and many-to-one mappings to naturally accommodate novel target classes. We initialize and refine target prototypes with semantic-weighted soft assignments and decoupled optimization for known vs. novel groups, replacing brittle one-to-one bipartite matching with structure-aware transport that is robust to class splits/merges and unknown-class emergence. To prevent style cues from confounding alignment, we disentangle high-level semantics from low-level domain factors and minimize their mutual information, coupled with style-mixing augmentations to expand domain coverage. The joint objective minimizes GW distance between prototype graphs, enforces semantic–domain independence, and regularizes pseudo-labels, with an optional hierarchical split criterion (e.g., code-length/stability) to recover multi-granularity categories when warranted by target data.

result.text: We propose PPG2Lead-ODE, a cross-modal generator that transforms wearable PPG and optional demographics into a low-dimensional cardiac source state evolved by a neural ODE, then renders all 12 ECG leads via a lightly personalized biophysical lead-field to enforce cross-lead coherence. Disease semantics are injected by conditioning the ODE vector field, while an ROI-disentangled diffusion guidance emphasizes P–QRS–T intervals to preserve fine morphology in both time and frequency domains. A brief calibration with a few seconds of paired PPG–ECG adapts the lead-field per patient, enabling accurate multi-lead synthesis from PPG alone for diagnosis, missing-lead imputation, and privacy-preserving augmentation. Compared to prior PPG→ECG translation and disease-aware multi-lead GANs, our physics-consistent cross-modal design better captures condition-specific changes across views.

Its key insight is that a dynamic meta-buffer of distilled "thought-templates"—compact, task-relevant reasoning sketches extracted across problems—can be retrieved and instantiated to guide per-instance reasoning more effectively than multi-query search-based methods. result.text: The paper addresses the security and practicality limits of watermarking large language model outputs, demonstrating that common watermark design choices create vulnerabilities that attackers can exploit. Its key insight is a "no free lunch" trade-off: increasing robustness against detection-evasion attacks typically degrades utility (text quality) or usability (ease of deployment and verification), so no watermarking scheme can simultaneously optimize all desirable properties. The authors analyze simple but potent attack strategies against prevalent watermark algorithms, quantify how attack success correlates with design parameters, and use those results to derive actionable guidelines and defensive modifications that balance robustness, utility, and usability for real-world LLM watermarking deployments.

result.text: We propose an Interaction-Bounded Fusion Curriculum (IBFC) for in-the-wild affective mental health detection that estimates per-clip audio–visual interaction strength from unlabeled co-occurring data via information-theoretic bounds and uses these estimates to guide training and inference. Training starts on high-interaction segments to teach a cross-attention fusion module stable synergistic patterns, while jointly learning unimodal experts and a routing gate that defers to unimodal predictions when interaction is low or modalities disagree. We evaluate on D-Vlog for depression and StressID for stress, and assess cross-dataset and longitudinal robustness using GLOBEM-style splits, expecting improved generalization, calibration, and reduced overfitting to spurious correlations. By turning interaction estimation into a practical signal for when and how to fuse, IBFC yields adaptive, reliable multimodal decisions in the wild.

args.text: To further reduce spuriousness in NLI training with natural language explanations, we propose Semantically- and Causally-Filtered Explanation Augmentation. For each example, a rationale-aware generator proposes a rationale and a paraphrase set of NLEs; we score each set by (i) semantic entropy over the paraphrase cluster’s aggregated probabilities conditioned on the predicted label to measure meaning-level stability, and (ii) a minimum-conditional-dependence criterion that penalizes residual dependence between unselected input tokens and the label, encouraging causal coverage. We propose diagnostic-aware autoformalization: train an LLM to translate informal math into formal statements/proofs by iteratively proposing formalizations and using fine-grained elaborator/prover diagnostics (e.g., unification failures, type-class resolution misses, missing implicit args, coercion conflicts) as structured guidance for repair. args.text: OperatorBoost-GPDE: a transductive boosting framework that treats short-time graph diffusion steps—implicit Laplacian, fractional Laplacian, and learned GPR-polynomial filters—as weak learners and learns per-node mixtures across scales. Each boosting round performs a small implicit time step (e.g., backward Euler) with the operator chosen to maximally reduce residuals under a penalty tied to the transductive Rademacher complexity of the induced hypothesis increment, yielding convergence and depth-robust test bounds. Fractional operators expand effective receptive fields while implicit stepping constrains smoothing, so the boosted composite remains a contraction yet captures long-range dependencies on both homophilous and heterophilous graphs. By reallocating weight to the most stable operator under topology perturbations, the method should outperform single-operator PDE-GNNs in robustness.

We propose Identifiability-Driven Domain Randomization (IDDR): view the simulator as a latent-MDP mixture and shape the dynamics sampling distribution via constrained entropy maximization augmented with an information/separation constraint that guarantees trajectories under the current curriculum can discriminate between plausible latent models (e.g., maintain a lower bound on pairwise separability or PSR-style test power). Concurrently, train with twice-regularized (R^2) objectives so that value-regularization implements distributional robustness over the current mixture, avoiding over-conservatism while certifying worst-case performance on its support. Using a Lipschitz MDP metric, expand the support until it forms an epsilon-net around the hypothesized real MDP; the sim-to-real gap then admits a computable bound from the coverage radius plus the robust-regularization term, enabling zero-shot transfer guarantees without real-world samples. The framework unifies domain-randomization theory with active curriculum design and robust RL, and predicts that history-dependent policies that aid discrimination can sharply tighten the gap bound in partially observed settings.

result.text: The paper tackles source-free domain adaptation (SFDA), asking whether existing SFDA methods generalize beyond typical computer-vision shifts to challenging, naturally-occurring distribution changes in bioacoustics where only an off-the-shelf model and unlabeled target data are available. The key insight is that current SFDA techniques, benchmarked mainly on vision datasets, can behave very differently or even degrade performance on markedly different modalities, so robustness across diverse domains is not guaranteed. Methodologically, the authors evaluate a suite of existing SFDA algorithms on new bioacoustic shifts, diagnose their failures, and introduce a simple new adaptation approach that empirically outperforms prior methods on the bioacoustic benchmarks while remaining competitive on standard vision datasets, arguing for broader modality consideration when designing SFDA methods.

Methodologically, the authors introduce HVGNN: a Temporal GNN (TGNN) that incorporates a theoretically motivated time encoding to process dynamics, a hyperbolic variational graph autoencoder that models node latents as hyperbolic normal distributions, and a reparameterizable sampler for those hyperbolic normals to permit end-to-end gradient learning; experiments show this approach outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on real datasets.
