args.text: We propose Cal-TEILP, a calibrated temporal interval forecaster for temporal knowledge graphs that augments TEKG-based, rule-guided differentiable random walks with explicit distributional calibration over time. Concretely, we optimize a differentiable D-calibration objective that aligns predicted versus observed event-count histograms across sliding temporal bins (and per relation) jointly with TEILP’s likelihood/ranking loss, learning per-relation temperature and bin-mixing parameters to correct miscalibration under imbalance and drift. This yields sharper yet well-calibrated time densities and ranking scores while preserving TEILP’s interpretable rule attributions. The result enables reliable thresholding and decision-making (e.g., SLA-style constraints) and more trustworthy temporal explanations on large-scale TKG benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses the computational bottleneck of performing tensor products of irreducible representations (irreps) in E(3)-equivariant neural networks, whose cost grows prohibitively with higher-order tensors. The key insight is that Clebsch–Gordan coefficients used for these tensor products are mathematically equivalent to Gaunt coefficients—integrals of three spherical harmonics—so that tensor products can be reframed as pointwise multiplications of spherical functions and thus re-expressed in a 2D Fourier basis. Methodologically, the authors define the Gaunt Tensor Product which converts spherical-harmonic representations to a 2D Fourier basis and uses the convolution theorem with Fast Fourier Transforms to compute products efficiently, reducing complexity from O(L^6) to O(L^3). Empirically, this approach yields substantial speedups and performance gains on molecular benchmarks such as the Open Catalyst Project and 3BPA.

args.text: We propose Speed-Constrained Dynamic N:M Sparse Training (SC-DNM), a training-time method that guarantees target GPU speedups while preserving accuracy. The core idea is to couple a speed-aware layerwise allocator with local-quadratic, multi-weight sensitivity and compensation under enforceable N:M constraints using SR-STE, all within an always-sparse training loop augmented with neuroregeneration for plasticity. Concretely, at periodic intervals we estimate per-layer multi-weight importance via low-rank Hessian sketches and/or L2-distortion scores, solve a speed-bounded knapsack to reassign N:M nonzeros across layers, apply OBS-style compensation to survivors, and regenerate a matched number of connections within each N:M block before resuming SR-STE-constrained updates. This unifies the accuracy of dynamic sparse training with practical acceleration, delivering guaranteed 2:4 speedups with smaller accuracy gaps than static N:M training or post-hoc pruning.

I propose a streaming active learning algorithm that scores incoming samples by their expected MLE error reduction under a Fisher-information objective, while calibrating selection with analytical variance bounds of Fisher estimators to avoid querying on noisy, unstable scores. The method maintains an online block-diagonal/low-rank Fisher sketch for fast scoring, gates candidates with a self-supervised Mahalanobis OOD detector, and learns a purity–informativeness trade-off over rounds; for each micro-batch it adds a submodular diversity term to prevent redundancy and scales to very large batches when needed. An adaptive query-rate controller matches budget without hand-tuning, and we hypothesize theory showing that variance-calibrated Fisher gains translate into improved generalization under streaming MLE assumptions when OOD is filtered. Empirically, this variance-aware, OOD-aware Fisher sampler should outperform uncertainty/diversity baselines and prior Fisher-based methods on imbalanced, OOD-contaminated streams, with efficient implementations via K-FAC-style blocks and fast diversification.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of training convolutional neural networks that are provably 1-Lipschitz under the l2 norm while preserving gradient norms (GNP) per layer—an essential property for avoiding vanishing gradients but one where prior GNP convolutions are slow, accuracy-degrading, and lack approximation guarantees. The key insight is that the exponential of a skew-symmetric matrix is orthogonal, so if a convolutional layer’s Jacobian can be made skew-symmetric, its matrix exponential yields an orthogonal (hence norm-preserving) layer. The method constructs convolutional filters whose Jacobians are skew-symmetric and implements the orthogonal operator via a truncated Taylor series of the matrix exponential, with provable bounds on the truncation error; empirically this Skew Orthogonal Convolution (SOC) yields faster training and improved standard and certified robustness on CIFAR-10/100 compared to prior GNP convolution approaches.

args.text: We propose Dictionary-Factored 3D Gaussian Splatting (DF-GS), which reduces memory and communication bottlenecks in large-scale, multi-GPU training by factorizing per-Gaussian attributes into small spatially local dictionaries with sparse codes. Concretely, we tile the scene and learn per-tile dictionaries for spherical-harmonic appearance and Cholesky-parameterized covariances; each Gaussian stores only a few nonzero coefficients and a tiny residual, pixel-shard workers request just the codes they need for rendering/training, and dictionaries are synchronized across devices via periodic ADMM-style consensus. A rank-aware constraint on covariance atoms discourages degenerate needle shapes while encouraging multi-atom combinations to capture local shape variability. The sparse-code parameterization is also highly compressible with anchor-level context modeling, enabling a unified training-and-streaming pipeline that substantially lowers memory footprint and inter-GPU bandwidth while maintaining or improving large-scene quality.

We propose SeSAM: a memory-augmented selective SSM that adds a tiny set of content-addressable global slots as a low-rank semiseparable augmentation to the state, enabling O(L) updates and reads while preserving accelerator-friendly kernels. Writes to the slots are gated outer-product fast-weight updates keyed by token states to support robust pairwise comparison and long-range recall as in specialized recall SSMs, while the read path mixes slot contents back into the stream via the state-space–attention duality to emulate selective attention when needed. Training follows a staged distillation curriculum that first aligns sequence-mixing behavior and hidden states, then matches teacher attention maps or hierarchical abstraction summaries, plus an auxiliary contrastive recall loss to directly supervise retrieval behavior. We hypothesize SeSAM closes the remaining gap in multi-token comparison and retrieval for pure SSMs, preserving length extrapolation and linear-time scaling with only a handful of global slots.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of reducing communication overhead in distributed optimization when both server-to-worker and worker-to-server links are compressed, aiming for provably efficient algorithms for convex and nonconvex objectives. The key insight is a new way to decouple compression errors from the two directions so that their interaction becomes additive rather than multiplicative, which yields substantially improved communication complexity. Building on the EF21 compressor framework, the authors propose bidirectional compressed algorithms (EF21-P and variants) that tolerate biased gradient estimators and use novel analysis techniques to bound the resulting error, producing the first convex-regime bounds that match gradient descent communication complexity and stronger nonconvex guarantees. Experiments verify the theoretical gains, demonstrating practical improvements in communication efficiency.

args.text: Noise-calibrated scaling with an EOS threshold: I hypothesize that across optimizers and architectures, test loss follows a two-regime law in compute/model/data where the break is set by an effective SGD temperature Θ ≈ η·Tr(Σ_noise)/B projected onto the top-eigenspace; when Θ surpasses a curvature-dependent threshold, training self-stabilizes at the edge of stability and the scaling exponent shifts, producing the observed broken power-law behavior. This yields prescriptive, compute-optimal schedules that trade learning rate, batch size, and steps to keep Θ near the threshold, recovering asymmetric time-versus-parameters tradeoffs in analytically tractable models and predicting how batch-size scaling alters exponents. For MoE, granularity smooths top-eigen curvature and dilutes noise anisotropy, thus raising the threshold and delaying the break; a simple routing/regularization objective that penalizes top-eigenvector–aligned cubic curvature should further improve MoE scaling under fixed compute. The proposal predicts that early-training measurements of Tr(Σ_noise), λ_max, and cubic coefficients suffice to forecast the break location and choose batch/step schedules that avoid it, unifying BNSL fits with EOS dynamics.

result.text: High-Order Coupled Flow Matching: train probability-flow ODEs with a multisample-coupled, high-order objective that jointly matches the velocity and its first/second-order derivatives along stochastic-interpolant paths to close the likelihood gap. Concretely, start from simulation-free flow/stochastic-interpolant training and replace i.i.d. noise–data pairs by cheap minibatch couplings to reduce gradient variance and straighten trajectories; add auxiliary losses that regress divergence and directional Jacobian/Hessian via Hutchinson-style probes and shared finite-difference perturbations across the coupled batch, and use a stable velocity parameterization. Extending recent ODE-likelihood bounds, controlling these high-order errors tightens PF-ODE NLL; combined with couplings that lower transport cost, this yields fewer NFEs for a target fidelity and better likelihoods on CIFAR-10/ImageNet-32. At evaluation, use truncated-normal dequantization to avoid retraining while preserving the likelihood gains.

result.text: The paper addresses the omission of uncertainty assessment in current open LLM evaluation platforms by arguing that uncertainty is a crucial complement to accuracy when benchmarking models. The key insight is that conventional accuracy-focused comparisons can be misleading because models with higher accuracy can be less certain, larger models can be more uncertain than smaller ones, and instruction fine-tuning can increase model uncertainty. To demonstrate this, the authors design a benchmarking framework that integrates uncertainty quantification, evaluate nine LLM series across five representative NLP tasks, and analyze relationships between accuracy, model scale, instruction tuning, and uncertainty to show why uncertainty metrics should be included in LLM leaderboards.

args.text: We propose Disentangled-Disagreement Distillation (D3): train a single MIMO student with K heads distilled from a teacher ensemble while enforcing a conditional mutual information penalty across heads to eliminate conditionally redundant features and encourage complementary mechanisms. To expose the student to functional diversity, we actively synthesize near-manifold inputs that maximize ensemble disagreement (guided by a D-BAT-style objective) and reweight them by data-density estimates so training focuses on realistic disagreement rather than far-OOD artifacts. After learning, we collapse the K-head student into a single head by fitting a lightweight N-to-one feature transform that preserves the ensemble-of-heads predictive behavior on both in-distribution and synthesized-disagreement samples, yielding a single model that better captures ensemble diversity, calibration, and OOD behavior without extra inference cost. This bridges diversity-preserving distillation with principled redundancy control and practical single-pass deployment.

result.text: The paper addresses how to build principled diffusion-style generative models for discrete data by moving from discrete-time noising schedules to a continuous-time formulation. The key insight is that both the forward corruption and reverse generative processes can be modeled as Continuous Time Markov Chains (CTMCs), which admits a continuous-time ELBO for training and enables use of mature CTMC simulation techniques from chemical physics. The method trains the model by optimizing this continuous-time ELBO and simulates/highlights new sampler schemes that exploit CTMC tooling to more efficiently traverse high-dimensional discrete state spaces, yielding samplers that empirically outperform discrete-time counterparts. Additionally, the continuous-time framework permits a novel theoretical bound on the sampling error between the learned and true data distributions.

result.text: I propose a sharpness-mediated account of broken neural scaling: the kinks, delayed gains, and double-descent behaviors captured by smoothly broken power laws emerge when training transitions into a self-stabilized edge-of-stability regime and the time-averaged fraction of unstable (η·λmax>2) steps crosses a scale-dependent threshold. Mechanistically, as model/data/compute scale, λmax grows and constant–step-size GD/SGD undergoes a ballistic-to-diffusive transition at a critical step size; EOS self-stabilization via cubic curvature reduces λmax along the top mode, changing the effective capacity and noise temperature in a non-monotonic way that reshapes performance vs. scale. This yields concrete predictions: the break location is determined by early-training estimates of η·λmax and the cubic coefficient along the top eigendirection; at fixed η it should shift with batch-size–controlled noise and with architectural choices that alter curvature, and large constant step sizes can mimic stochasticity to smooth or delay the break. Empirically, logging sharpness, EOS occupancy, and cubic-term proxies across scales should enable fitting a two-regime scaling model whose boundary is predicted from these dynamics, providing prescriptive levers (LR, batch size, architecture) to induce, move, or avoid scaling breaks.

args.text: We propose Frequency-Equalized Gradient Regularization (FEGR) for GANs: measure the discriminator’s input gradients in a Fourier (or fixed bandpass) basis and penalize discrepancies in gradient energy across frequency bands between real and fake, while enforcing a small floor on high-frequency sensitivity to capture low-magnitude details. Concretely, we compute per-band gradient norms via a differentiable filter bank and match the bandwise distributions for real vs. generated samples, plus a high-frequency floor term; we pair this with light differentiable spectral augmentations to avoid overfitting and artifacts. FEGR directly targets the discriminator’s known insensitivity to low-magnitude high-frequency signals from downsampling, complements spectral-feedback discriminators by shaping gradient signals rather than only scores, and generalizes gradient-gap regularization to the frequency domain. args.text: I propose Banditized Expected Transferability for X2X (BET-X2X), a post-training backdoor detector that scales to many classes and multiple simultaneous attacks by unifying bandit-guided target exploration, prior-regularized reverse-engineering, and ET-based pairwise assessment. result.text: The paper addresses the inability of Conditional Neural Processes (CNPs) to model dependencies across target predictions despite their desirable properties like calibrated outputs and straightforward maximum likelihood training. result.text: The paper addresses realistic black-box attacks on graph neural networks where the attacker can only access and perturb a small subset of nodes, making node selection crucial. result.text: We propose Evidential Set-Preserving Composed Retrieval (ESP-CR), which treats composed image retrieval with iterative text feedback as sequential belief refinement over the target rather than one-shot point matching. At each step, the text is decomposed into degradation and upgradation shifts applied to the reference to produce evidence over a learned bank of visual prototypes; we fuse step-wise evidence via Dempster–Shafer to obtain Dirichlet beliefs whose uncertainty is explicitly regularized to transition from coarse to fine, preserving plausible candidates early. We pretrain the shift operators on large-scale, web-mined instruction triplets and adopt early cross-attention fusion to condition on both image and text, ranking gallery images by expected similarity under the posterior belief. This calibrated, set-preserving objective improves early-stage Recall@K and converged R@1 while enabling risk-aware pruning and better uncertainty calibration.

result.text: The paper addresses how to recover an interpretable, relational action model of a black-box planning agent using only a simple query interface rather than full introspection. The key insight is that targeted, hierarchical query-answering—posing carefully chosen yes/no or outcome queries in a user-interpretable vocabulary—can efficiently narrow the intractable space of possible models to recover the agent’s underlying action dynamics. The method constructs an interrogation policy that generates and sequences queries at multiple levels of abstraction, uses responses to prune and refine candidate relational models, and can incorporate learned predicate classifiers to map perceptual inputs (e.g., images) into the symbolic predicates needed for model learning. result.text: The paper addresses the problem of "narrow vision" in mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, where the gating mechanism routes inputs so strictly that individual experts see limited data and underfit their sub-tasks, constraining overall generalization. The key insight is that moderate mutual distillation among experts can broaden each expert's effective training signal by sharing useful features and predictions learned by other experts, improving individual expert competence on their assigned inputs without collapsing specialization. result.text: The paper addresses the problem of backdoor attacks in federated learning (FL) — stealthy, malicious modifications during decentralized training that cause models to fail on specific sub-tasks — and whether FL can be made robust to such attacks. Its key insight is that strong defenses against backdoors are fundamentally hard: achieving backdoor robustness would imply solving adversarial-example robustness (a major open problem), and detecting backdoors is computationally unlikely under reasonable oracle/time assumptions. The authors introduce "edge-case backdoors," which target rare, tail-region inputs that are unlikely to appear in training or evaluation yet cause targeted misclassification, and they demonstrate how an adversary can reliably insert these across tasks by carefully crafting and tuning poisoned client updates. They validate the concept empirically on diverse tasks (image classification, OCR, text prediction, sentiment analysis) and argue these backdoors pose real risks to fairness and safety in FL.

args.text: We propose a black-box transfer attack tailored to open-vocabulary detectors that jointly exploits their reliance on CLIP-based global scene priors and region–text alignment. The attack optimizes a single image perturbation to (i) steer a CLIP multi-label surrogate toward a decoy set of co-occurring categories at the image level, and (ii) locally misalign proposal-level region embeddings by reducing similarity to true labels while increasing similarity to decoys at proposal locations, using proposal attention to spatially weight gradients. By coupling a learned co-occurrence graph with proposal-driven feature-space objectives, the perturbation transfers across OVOD pipelines that use image-level CLIP reweighting or ViLD-style region–text distillation without accessing their internals. We expect substantial gains in black-box success on OV-COCO/LVIS and provide ablations on decoy-graph choice, proposal weighting, and CLIP surrogate variants.

result.text: We propose EoS-guided Intrinsic Rotation Control: a closed-loop scheduler that maintains per-layer scale-invariant rotation rates near a target chosen from the Edge-of-Stability regime while keeping the intrinsic learning rate (step size × weight decay) stable. Concretely, at each step we estimate per-layer rotation (angle between successive normalized weights) and a scale-invariant sharpness proxy, then use a simple PI controller to adjust decoupled weight decay and/or layerwise step sizes so that rotation equilibrates across layers and sharpness tracks an EoS-setpoint—thereby preventing BN+weight-decay–induced effective-LR spikes and cyclic destabilizations. This unifies intrinsic-rate theory with rotational equilibrium and replaces ad‑hoc warmup or hand-tuned decay schedules with automatic feedback control; it predicts flattened BN cycles, more uniform rotation, and improved convergence/generalization relative to constant or gradient-norm–driven decay. We will benchmark against tuned SGD/AdamW, SWD, and DoG, and ablate rotation-only vs sharpness-coupled control to isolate the contribution of EoS targeting.

result.text: CurvMix is a curvature-conditioned, channel-wise polynomial propagation scheme for heterophilous graphs. The design generalizes trainable per-channel weights to be edge- and curvature-aware and inherits frequency adaptivity, replacing curvature-driven rewiring with a learned curvature-to-filter map. We further propose curvature-dependent stability bounds to guide gain clipping during training.

args.text: We propose unifying domain randomization with distributionally robust RL by treating the simulator-parameter distribution as an uncertainty set over a parameterized MDP family and optimizing a MaxEnt-regularized robust value. Leveraging the equivalence between robustness and regularization (R^2 MDPs), we design a primal–dual training scheme that shapes the randomization distribution via an entropy constraint while enforcing a lower bound on robust value over TV/Wasserstein ambiguity sets selected for favorable sample complexity. The method is identifiability-aware: it monitors separation of latent dynamics and switches to history-dependent policies when discrimination is hard, ensuring the policy either robustly hedges or actively identifies the true dynamics. This yields sim-to-real gap bounds that decompose into a robustness-radius term and an identifiability term, enabling zero-shot transfer when the entropy-expanded set remains within the chosen ball and separation holds.

We propose Local-EFX with cycle-bounded charity: when envy is only considered along a given social network, there exist allocations that are EFX on every network edge while discarding at most β(G) items, where β(G) is the cycle rank of the network. For trees (β(G)=0), Local-EFX always exists and can be computed by dynamic programming over the tree decomposition, while for general bounded-treewidth networks the minimum required charity and a witnessing allocation are fixed-parameter tractable in treewidth. The algorithm adapts cancel/exchange arguments used to achieve almost-EFX to eliminate envy edge-by-edge, charging at most one discarded item to each independent cycle. args.text: Budgeted Value-per-Byte Routing (BVBR) for MoE jointly optimizes token-to-expert assignment and the per-token activation count k under explicit, time-varying bandwidth and compute budgets. A small learned predictor estimates the marginal loss reduction of routing a (token, expert) pair and divides it by predicted communication cost to produce a value-per-byte score; each step uses a fast knapsack-style selection to choose assignments and k adaptively, with topology-aware penalties and an expert-choice capacity prior. We integrate BVBR with a coarse-to-fine granularity schedule that grows or merges experts when persistent bandwidth pressure is detected, and fall back to balanced hashing when the estimator is uncertain to preserve robustness. This co-design targets higher throughput and equal-or-better loss than fixed-k or pure topology-aware dispatch, especially in heterogeneous clusters.

result.text: We propose MM-SEP, a principled framework to measure and train multimodal LLMs to separate user instructions from visual data, directly targeting typographic and cipher-based jailbreaks. We operationalize separation with counterfactual image–prompt triplets that add/remove or translate overlaid text (including ciphers and multilingual instructions) and include adversarially optimized visual perturbations, estimating a separation score from model responses; we then train a dual-path gate that routes detected instructional visual tokens (via OCR plus a learned instruction-detector) through a safety policy while treating scene content as inert, alongside a cross-modal contrastive loss that aligns safety representations across text and image channels. Evaluated against typographic-image attacks, cross-modal embedding attacks, and universal visual jailbreaks, MM-SEP aims to refuse image-borne instructions while preserving helpful visual QA, and can be combined with compact safe instruction datasets for post-hoc alignment. This yields a metric and defense that reduce compliance to visual or ciphered instructions without degrading utility.

result.text: The paper addresses the practical bottleneck in learning-to-defer systems that require many human expert predictions—on top of ground-truth labels—to teach an AI when to defer decisions, which is costly or infeasible when experts change or are scarce. result.text: The paper addresses the vulnerability of Graph Neural Networks to small, discrete perturbations of graph structure at training time that can dramatically degrade performance. result.text: The paper tackles learning implicit neural representations (INRs) for signals defined on unknown non-Euclidean domains where no ambient coordinates or regular lattice exist, so standard INR approaches cannot be applied. The key insight is that a graph sampled from the underlying topological space can be embedded into a continuous coordinate-like representation via spectral embedding, providing an approximate coordinate system that is intrinsic and coordinate-system–independent. The method maps graph nodes to spectral embeddings (e.g., Laplacian eigenmaps) and trains neural networks to represent the continuous signal as a function of those embeddings, allowing reconstruction and interpolation on non-Euclidean domains without knowing the true manifold; experiments demonstrate this approach on various real-world graph signals.

The paper addresses the challenge of learning common spatial patterns for non-stationary EEG signals modeled as symmetric positive definite (SPD) matrices on Riemannian manifolds, where prior SPD-network approaches learn a single embedding and distance metric that is computationally expensive and insufficiently expressive. The key insight is that dividing the global embedding problem into K independent subproblems and learning separate Riemannian distance metrics for non-overlapping data subsets—“separate to learn”—yields richer, more efficient representations than a single unified metric. The method, called Riemannian Embedding Banks (REB), partitions the data and manifold embedding space into K subsets, trains one SPD neural network model per subset to learn K local metrics, and then groups these learned subsets as neurons in the SPD network’s embedding layer so their outputs can be combined for classification; experiments on public EEG datasets show faster convergence and improved generalization for common spatial pattern learning.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of merging multiple finetuned model weights into a single multi-task model without suffering large performance drops or requiring additional data or training. The key insight is that no single model’s weights can simultaneously represent all task-specific solutions, so instead the authors elect a unified base model from the available weights and add extremely lightweight, task-specific modulators that adjust weight direction (via binary masks) and magnitude (via rescalers) to align each task model to the unified base. Their method, EMR-Merging, therefore consists of (a) selecting an elected model as the common backbone and (b) generating and applying per-task masks and rescalers to merge other models into that backbone; this tuning-free approach requires no extra data or training and achieves strong performance across many vision, NLP, PEFT, and multi-modal merging scenarios.

result.text: We propose SyncFlow, a streaming video-to-audio generator that couples rectified-flow spectrogram synthesis with an online synchronization critic to maintain tight, long-horizon alignment under low latency. A rectified flow network maps noise to spectrogram latents conditioned on temporally aligned visual embeddings and a compact rhythmic state (beat phase/tempo) extracted from long visual context, while a lightweight joint guidance critic trained to detect audio–visual misalignment modulates the transport vector field during ODE integration to correct drift in real time. At inference, we use few-step (or distilled one-step) sampling with adaptive guidance strength driven by the critic’s local sync error, enabling rapid updates without sacrificing global rhythmic coherence. This hybrid of straight-path transport and synchronization-aware guidance targets state-of-the-art alignment and quality for live V2A across diverse scenes.

args.text: We propose AnchorGossip-GS, a decentralized, communication-efficient training scheme for 3D Gaussian Splatting across heterogeneous, unreliable networks. This yields prescriptive, compute-optimal schedules that trade learning rate, batch size, and steps to keep Θ near the threshold, recovering asymmetric time-versus-parameters tradeoffs in analytically tractable models and predicting how batch-size scaling alters exponents. result.text: The paper addresses the problem of reliably estimating confidence for large language model (LLM) predictions, noting that many LLMs are poorly calibrated and resist standard post-hoc calibration techniques. args.text: We propose DiffGuard, a diffusion-based prompt purification layer for LLMs that projects inputs onto the manifold of benign instructions before they reach the target model. Inspired by diffusion purification in vision, DiffGuard adds small noise in a text-embedding space and runs a learned reverse text-diffusion process guided by a lightweight safety head to denoise away adversarial suffixes, cipher-like encodings, and other off-manifold artifacts while preserving user intent. Compared to prompt-level defenses based on compression or fixed guard prefixes, DiffGuard aims to neutralize diverse jailbreak families (token-level triggers, cipher outputs, and template-based attacks) with minimal utility loss by manifold projection rather than rule-based filtering.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of efficiently solving PDE-constrained optimal control problems, where repeatedly solving expensive PDEs during control optimization limits practicality. Its key insight is to replace repeated PDE solves with a learned surrogate for the PDE solution operator, trained with special regularizers so it generalizes well and respects physical structure, thereby decoupling expensive simulation from control search. The method proceeds in two phases: Phase 1 trains an operator-learning surrogate (from data or physics-based simulations) to map controls to PDE states, and Phase 2 uses this surrogate to rapidly search for optimal controls—enabling fast inference of optimal inputs for a variety of PDEs (e.g., Poisson, Burgers) and control types without intensive online computation.

args.text: We propose discrepancy-guided adaptive augmentation and projection for limited-data GANs: compute per-instance discrepancy signals between the current model and data (e.g., as in per-instance emphasis) and use them to modulate, per sample, both the probability and type of differentiable augmentations applied to the discriminator. High-discrepancy (underrepresented) samples receive stronger invariance-inducing transforms and a richer set of augment types, while low-discrepancy samples get lighter augmentation, preventing overfitting without uniformly distorting the training signal. In parallel, we feed images through a frozen, pretrained feature pyramid as in Projected GAN but adaptively emphasize resolutions/channels according to each sample’s discrepancy profile so the discriminator focuses capacity where minority modes differ. An annealed curriculum on discrepancy thresholds stabilizes training, aiming to improve minority-mode coverage and overall FID under scarce data.

result.text: The paper addresses how to fine-tune pre-trained graph neural networks (GNNs) efficiently and with better generalization than full fine-tuning, noting that parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods developed for transformers do not transfer well to GNNs. The key insight is that preserving the large pre-trained GNN's parameters while inserting highly expressive, GNN-tailored adapter modules can adapt to downstream tasks with few tunable parameters and reduce generalization gaps, even outperforming full fine-tuning. The authors propose AdapterGNN, a PEFT architecture that integrates adapters optimized for graph structures and show through extensive experiments across chemistry and biology benchmarks that AdapterGNN consistently beats other PEFT methods and outperforms full fine-tuning (with only ~4–5% of parameters tuned), while also providing theoretical generalization bounds explaining why PEFT improves GNN generalization.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of building a single, flexible biosignal encoder that can be pre-trained across heterogeneous clinical datasets and fine-tuned for diverse downstream tasks despite mismatched channels, variable recording lengths, and frequent missing values. args.text: Token-level Tree Preference Optimization (TTPO) distills tree-of-thought search into single-pass chain-of-thought by learning per-token preferences inferred from process rewards. We run a shallow ReST-MCTS* search to compute step-level values for partial traces, convert them into per-token win/loss indicators, and train with a TDPO-style token-level Bradley–Terry objective under per-token forward-KL to a reference, while setting a dynamic beta per batch based on value-variance to balance stability and plasticity. Compared to CPO’s step selection from trees, TTPO uses token-level signals and uncertainty-aware regularization, and we optionally apply active selection of prompts with highest token-level disagreement to cut label cost. We hypothesize TTPO matches ToT accuracy with standard decoding, improves data efficiency over DPO-style baselines, and is robust across domains.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of training large foundation models outside costly homogeneous data-center clusters by enabling model-parallel training across decentralized, heterogeneous, and bandwidth-constrained GPU resources. Its key insight is that training can be made efficient in such environments by formulating the assignment of fine-grained computational "tasklets" to diverse devices as a scheduling and cost-optimization problem that explicitly models compute, memory, and network heterogeneity. The authors introduce a formal cost model and an efficient evolutionary algorithm to search for near-optimal tasklet allocations across geo-distributed devices, and implement this scheduler to drive model-parallel training over realistic, measured networks. Empirical results across multi-city, multi-continent scenarios show substantial speedups—up to 4.8× versus a state-of-the-art homogeneous-data-center system—demonstrating the practicality of decentralized model-parallel foundation-model training.

result.text: We propose Pattern-Aware Re-Masking (PARM) for tabular imputation: replace uniform random re-masking with a learned missingness generator qϕ(m|x) that approximates the observed (potentially MNAR) mechanism and adaptively oversamples rare or high-risk patterns during training. The masked autoencoder is trained under this policy with an additional domain-adversarial penalty to enforce representation invariance across missingness patterns, improving robustness to MNAR shifts. At inference, PARM ensembles imputations by integrating over masks sampled from qϕ and then applies pattern-conditional conformal calibration to produce intervals with valid coverage for each missingness stratum. We hypothesize improved accuracy and calibrated uncertainty under skewed and MNAR masking compared to uniform re-masking approaches.

result.text: The paper tackles the growing memory burden of key-value (KV) caches during decoding in autoregressive transformer LLMs, which becomes prohibitive at long sequence lengths and large batch sizes. Its key insight is that, beyond sharing key/value heads across query heads as in Multi-Query Attention (MQA) and Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), adjacent transformer layers can also share key and value heads without materially harming accuracy. The authors propose Cross-Layer Attention (CLA), an attention block design that reuses KV heads across neighboring layers to halve the KV cache size relative to MQA, and they validate this by training 1B- and 3B-parameter models showing CLA achieves a Pareto improvement in the memory-versus-accuracy tradeoff. This enables inference with longer contexts and larger batches while maintaining near-MQA performance.

result.text: The paper addresses precise quantitative relationships of Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between multivariate Gaussian distributions, aiming to characterize how asymmetric or triangle-like KL behaves for Gaussians and to provide dimension-free bounds useful in applications. The key insight is that for Gaussians small KL in one direction tightly controls the KL in the opposite direction and through intermediate distributions: specifically, when KL( N2 || N1 ) ≤ ε the worst-case KL( N1 || N2 ) equals ε + 2ε^{3/2} + O(ε^2), and for three Gaussians with KL gaps ε1, ε2 the composite divergence is bounded by 3ε1+3ε2+2√(ε1ε2)+lower-order terms, revealing an approximate symmetry and a relaxed triangle inequality that do not depend on dimension. Methodologically, the authors derive exact supremum and infimum constructions and prove dimension-free analytic bounds by exploiting closed-form expressions for Gaussian KL, spectral properties of covariance matrices, and asymptotic expansions for small divergences, and they illustrate utility via applications to flow-based models, anomaly detection, and multi-step robustness in reinforcement learning.

result.text: The paper addresses whether and how one can unsupervisedly factorize (disentangle) the latent symmetry factors of a data manifold—i.e., recover a Lie-group-induced decomposition—solely from observations of its orbit. The key insight is that if the manifold’s true metric is known and each factor has nontrivial holonomy, then invariant subspaces under diffusion reveal the manifold’s de Rham decomposition, so disentangling reduces to metric learning. args.text: We propose a Pareto-Manifold GFlowNet (PM-GFN) that couples a continuous Pareto-set model with reward-proportional sampling to efficiently cover expensive multi-objective fronts. A parametric decoder learns the manifold mapping from preferences to candidate solutions, while a GFlowNet explores a joint latent–preference space and is trained with a hypervolume-based reward to sample diverse, high-coverage solution batches. An active loop alternates between evaluating decoded candidates, refining the manifold model, and adapting the GFlowNet’s scalarizations toward under-covered trade-off regions, delivering batch-friendly exploration with improved sample efficiency. By unifying continuous Pareto-set modeling with GFlowNet-driven diversity and hypervolume training, PM-GFN yields smoother proposals, better coverage, and flexible decision-maker querying compared to pure BO or standalone Pareto front learning.

We propose 3D-MAP, a pretraining-and-control framework that unifies 3D-aware visual representations with masked trajectory modeling and action-conditioned contrast. First, we train a geometry-grounded encoder via multi-view masked autoencoding over a latent 3D field (NeRF-style) or latent 3D keypoints to enforce cross-view, temporally consistent structure. Then we pretrain a decision model by masking tokens in sequences of (3D-latent, action) and reconstructing them while jointly maximizing mutual information between current 3D-latents plus action sequences and future 3D-latents; at finetuning, we run RL from single-view inputs using the frozen or partially tuned 3D encoder. This should yield sample-efficient, viewpoint-robust policies that plan in compact 3D latents and transfer under camera changes and occlusions.

Current alignment pipelines optimize expected reward from aggregated human preferences, which can harm minority groups and invite reward hacking. I propose CVaR-Preference Optimization: learn a calibrated mixture-of-preference reward model that outputs per-component preference probabilities (via an LSC-style log-sigmoid transform), and train a single policy with a direct preference objective that maximizes the CVaR_τ of these per-component rewards across the inferred mixture. Concretely, we alternate EM-style fitting of the mixture and a DPO-like policy update where each preference pair is reweighted by tail risk under the mixture, yielding pessimistic gradients that protect low-utility components without requiring RL or confidence sets. This combines heterogeneous preference modeling with risk-sensitive optimization and probabilistic reward calibration, enabling a tunable fairness–utility trade-off by varying τ.

result.text: SegVol addresses the lack of a 3D foundation segmentation model that can universally and interactively segment a wide range of anatomical structures in volumetric medical images. The key insight is that large-scale pretraining on massive unlabeled CT data combined with a substantial labeled set, plus a design that supports both semantic and spatial prompts, yields a generalizable model capable of segmenting hundreds of anatomical categories. The method scales training to 90K unlabeled and 6K labeled CT volumes to learn rich 3D representations, implements a zoom-out–zoom-in inference mechanism for efficient and precise processing of volumetric scans, and incorporates interactive prompting to guide segmentation; experiments across 22 tasks show SegVol outperforms competitors on 19 tasks, with gains up to 37.24%, and ablations validate the contribution of its key design choices.

result.text: The paper addresses how decentralized stochastic gradient descent (D-SGD) generalizes in non-convex, non-smooth settings and how network topology affects its stability and test performance. The key insight is that the consensus model learned by vanilla D-SGD enjoys topology-aware algorithmic stability that scales as O(N^{-1}+m^{-1}+\lambda^2) in expectation (with N samples, m workers, and 1+λ the spectral gap), leading to an in-average generalization bound O(N^{-(1+α)/2}+m^{-(1+α)/2}+λ^{1+α}+φ_S) that remains non-vacuous even when connectivity is poor (λ close to 1), so better spectral gaps (stronger connectivity) improve generalization and early consensus control helps. Methodologically, the authors derive stability bounds for D-SGD under non-convex non-smooth assumptions by analyzing the effect of topology via the spectral gap, translate these stability results into generalization bounds, and validate the theory empirically with VGG-11 and ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny-ImageNet.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of reliably quantizing large language models (LLMs) to ultra-low precision without accuracy loss, specifically enabling end-to-end 4-bit inference including weights, activations, and KV cache. The key insight is that carefully chosen orthogonal rotations can remove activation outliers (extreme components in hidden states and other internals) while leaving the network’s functional outputs unchanged, making all subsequent tensors amenable to tight low-bit quantization. QuaRot implements this by applying computationally invariant rotations to residual hidden states, feed-forward activations, attention components, and the KV cache, then performing round-to-nearest quantization so all matrix multiplications run in 4 bits (with no channels forced to higher precision); this yields a 4-bit LLaMa2-70B with minimal perplexity degradation and ~99% zero-shot performance retention, and supports lossless 6/8-bit quantization without calibration.

result.text: The paper addresses how to perform differentially private gradient-based learning when examples or users are accessed repeatedly across many epochs, a setting where prior DP methods (like DP-SGD) suffer poor privacy-utility-computation tradeoffs. The key insight is that multi-epoch participation can be modeled as adaptive streaming linear queries and that online matrix-factorization mechanisms—appropriately extended to account for repeated contributions—can dramatically reduce sensitivity and thus privacy noise while remaining computationally tractable. Methodologically, the authors develop the theory to compute sensitivities and derive optimal factorization matrices for the multi-pass setting, provide algorithms to compute those matrices efficiently, and introduce a fast approximate mechanism based on the Fourier transform to scale to very large numbers of SGD steps; empirical results on image and language benchmarks (example- and user-level DP) show substantial improvements over prior baselines including DP-SGD.

Its key insight is that frames should be selected jointly rather than independently so the chosen set covers complementary, “storytelling” moments and avoids redundant or hard-to-classify frames. The proposed SMART method formulates frame selection as a joint optimization (implemented as a lightweight selection module that works with different backbones) to pick a distributed, informative subset of frames per video. result.text: The paper addresses efficient training of N:M structured sparsity—where at most N out of every M consecutive weights are nonzero—without costly pretraining or dense-gradient overhead. Its key insight is to view N:M sparsity as a finite combinatorial selection problem over C(M,N) possible N-sized combinations per M-block and to learn which combinations are best via differentiable scores rather than exhaustively searching. The method divides each M-block into all combination subsets, assigns each subset a learnable score that is jointly optimized with its associated weights, and progressively prunes low-scored subsets during standard training, yielding an efficient divide-and-conquer procedure that models relative importance among combinations and outperforms prior N:M pruning approaches.

result.text: The paper addresses active learning for deep neural networks in realistic streaming scenarios where data arrive sequentially and labels must be requested on the fly rather than from an offline pool. Its key insight is that effective streaming active learning can be achieved by balancing per-sample uncertainty with diversity among a small group of recently seen points, thereby matching a target query rate without hand-tuned hyperparameters. The proposed method, VeSSAL, examines incoming data in small batches, scores candidates by a combined uncertainty-diversity objective, selects a subset to query immediately to satisfy the query budget, and updates the model incrementally; this streaming sampling scheme enables practical batch active learning for DNNs on large, fragmented, or human-in-the-loop datasets.

result.text: The paper tackles the scalability bottleneck of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training, which is typically restricted to a single GPU and thus cannot handle high-resolution or large-scale scenes; the key insight is that because each Gaussian only contributes to a small, dynamic subset of pixels, training can be distributed by communicating only the required Gaussians to the corresponding pixel partitions and dynamically balancing load. They implement this idea in Grendel, a distributed system that partitions 3DGS parameters across GPUs, uses sparse all-to-all communication to transfer relevant Gaussians to pixel shards, supports batched multi-view training (rather than one view at a time), and applies a simple sqrt(batch size) hyperparameter scaling rule. By enabling dynamic partitioning and sparse communication, Grendel scales 3DGS to tens of millions of Gaussians across many GPUs and demonstrably improves reconstruction quality on large, high-resolution scenes (e.g., raising PSNR from 26.28 to 27.28 on Rubble by moving from 11.2M Gaussians on one GPU to 40.4M on 16 GPUs).

args.text: We propose TextDiffPure, a diffusion-inspired purification layer for LLM safety that operates on both prompts and model outputs by adding small stochastic corruption (e.g., embedding noise or token masking) and running a learned text denoiser conditioned on task intent and a safety discriminator to reconstruct a canonical, safe paraphrase. In contrast to static guard prefixes and suffixes, and to pure information-bottleneck filtering, TextDiffPure explicitly projects away adversarial syntax and brittle token-level triggers (including obfuscated or cipher-like encodings) while preserving user intent, and can wrap black-box LLMs with modest query overhead. The denoiser can be trained adversarially against adaptive jailbreak generators and cipher-style attacks, and composed with prompt-level defenses as an outer purification stage to improve transfer robustness. Beyond empirical gains against state-of-the-art black-box attacks, the stochastic reconstruction enables randomized-smoothing-style guarantees over discrete perturbation sets, offering the first steps toward certified prompt-level robustness for LLM safety.

result.text: The paper addresses improving predictive accuracy, calibration, and uncertainty quantification of neural-network ensembles while controlling computational and memory cost. Its key insight is that diversity over hyperparameters—combined with diversity over random weight initializations—yields stronger and more robust ensembles than varying weights alone, so searching and aggregating models across hyperparameter settings increases both performance and uncertainty calibration. The authors introduce hyper-deep ensembles, which perform a stratified random search over hyperparameters across multiple random initializations and aggregate the resulting models, and a parameter-efficient variant called hyper-batch ensembles that leverages batch-ensemble layer structure and self-tuning networks to share parameters while still exploring hyperparameter diversity; both methods deliver better accuracy and calibration than deep or batch ensembles on vision tasks with substantially lower cost than naïve ensembles.

args.text: We propose a gloss-free sign pose generation and translation model that discretizes 3D skeletal trajectories via factorized scalar quantization of joint angles and velocities, then trains a continuous-time discrete diffusion (CTMC) whose transition matrices are constrained by skeletal adjacency, joint limits from a parametric hand model, and absorbing “hold” states common in sign articulation. Compared to VQVAE+discrete diffusion G2P, the FSQ-style code stabilizes the discrete space and enables per-joint, kinematically valid transitions, yielding more physically plausible and temporally smooth pose synthesis. We warm-start the denoiser with BERT-style masked modeling on pose tokens and condition on text via lightweight adapters for gloss-free SLT/SLP. Evaluations on YouTube-mined multilingual sign corpora and standard benchmarks should improve realism and translation metrics while reducing off-manifold motion and mode collapse versus unconstrained discrete diffusion baselines.

result.text: We propose segmented control-variate hybrid gradients for nonsmooth differentiable physics. Long-horizon rollouts are partitioned at detected nonsmooth events (contacts, plastic yielding), and exact simulator gradients are used only within smooth segments as a control variate for a global likelihood-ratio estimator, with a learned per-segment alpha blending based on local smoothness/stiffness metrics estimated via small randomized smoothing probes; this preserves unbiasedness while sharply reducing variance and avoids the structural bias of reparameterization gradients at discontinuities. Event detection and segmentation leverage localized mesh-based contact solvers, and the alpha-scheduler is meta-learned across tasks. We evaluate on PlasticineLab and long-horizon tool-use sequences composed from short-horizon skills, demonstrating improved sample efficiency and stability over prior hybrid estimators.

result.text: Budgeted Value-per-Byte Routing (BVBR) for MoE jointly optimizes token-to-expert assignment and the per-token activation count k under explicit, time-varying bandwidth and compute budgets. A small learned predictor estimates the marginal loss reduction of routing a (token, expert) pair and divides it by predicted communication cost to produce a value-per-byte score; each step uses a fast knapsack-style selection to choose assignments and k adaptively, with topology-aware penalties and an expert-choice capacity prior. We integrate BVBR with a coarse-to-fine granularity schedule that grows or merges experts when persistent bandwidth pressure is detected, and fall back to balanced hashing when the estimator is uncertain to preserve robustness. This co-design targets higher throughput and equal-or-better loss than fixed-k or pure topology-aware dispatch, especially in heterogeneous clusters.

result.text: The paper tackles how to enable frozen large language models (LLMs) to both understand and generate non-linguistic modalities (e.g., images, videos) without changing the LLM weights. The key insight is to map pixels to and from the LLM’s own lexical space via a hierarchical "semantic pyramid" of tokens that jointly encode high-level semantics and fine-grained visual detail, so the LLM can reason about and produce visual content using its native vocabulary. Methodologically, SPAE trains an encoder–decoder that converts images into sequences of interpretable lexical tokens aligned with the LLM’s vocabulary and reconstructs images from those tokens using multiscale latent representations, then uses in-context prompting with frozen PaLM 2 and GPT-3.5 to perform and evaluate multimodal understanding and generation tasks. This approach yields the first demonstration of frozen LLM image generation and substantially improves image understanding performance (over 25% relative) under the same frozen-LM setting.

args.text: Reasoning-focused preference optimization still treats all steps equally and relies on coarse pairwise signals, leading to poor causal credit assignment and sensitivity to hyperparameters. I propose Utility-Weighted Listwise Token-level Preference Optimization (UL-TDPO): estimate each reasoning step’s marginal utility by a cheap lookahead using cached beam/ToT traces or a small MCTS-style rollout (process rewards), then use these utilities to weight a listwise preference loss over multiple CoT candidates while training with token-level forward-KL control and a utility-calibrated dynamic beta. result.text: The paper addresses the inefficiency of repeatedly encoding long prompts into language models’ limited context windows, which wastes compute and storage while prompting remains the primary way to steer multitask LMs without retraining. The key insight is that a model can be trained to compress a full prompt into a small set of learned “gist” tokens that capture the prompt’s semantic content and can be cached and reused, avoiding the need to re-encode the full prompt each time. The key insight is that for Gaussians small KL in one direction tightly controls the KL in the opposite direction and through intermediate distributions: specifically, when KL( N2 || N1 ) ≤ ε the worst-case KL( N1 || N2 ) equals ε + 2ε^{3/2} + O(ε^2), and for three Gaussians with KL gaps ε1, ε2 the composite divergence is bounded by 3ε1+3ε2+2√(ε1ε2)+lower-order terms, revealing an approximate symmetry and a relaxed triangle inequality that do not depend on dimension. Methodologically, the authors derive exact supremum and infimum constructions and prove dimension-free analytic bounds by exploiting closed-form expressions for Gaussian KL, spectral properties of covariance matrices, and asymptotic expansions for small divergences, and they illustrate utility via applications to flow-based models, anomaly detection, and multi-step robustness in reinforcement learning.

An optional lightweight joint discriminator provides cross-modal guidance, while a text prompt steers musical style so that video controls timing/structure; the base prior (e.g., a timing-aware latent audio diffusion) preserves fidelity and length control. result.text: The paper tackles the lack of disease-aware generative models that can synthesize multi-view (multi-lead) ECG signals reflecting specific heart conditions, which limits data augmentation, privacy-preserving data sharing, and downstream diagnostic training. The method, ME-GAN, implements a disease-conditioned GAN that uses a novel "mixup normalization" to inject condition information into appropriate temporal locations, projects the learned representation to multiple standard ECG views, and trains with a view discriminator that reorders shuffled leads to supervise accurate view characteristics; they also introduce rFID as a metric to evaluate synthesized ECG quality and show that ME-GAN generates multi-view signals with faithful morbid manifestations.

result.text: The paper tackles improving the reliability of chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting for complex reasoning in large language models, where standard greedy decoding often yields brittle or incorrect single reasoning paths. Its key insight is that many problems admit multiple valid internal reasoning routes that converge on the same correct answer, so sampling a diverse set of reasoning chains and then choosing the most consistent final answer across them reduces error. The proposed method, called self-consistency, samples many stochastic reasoning trajectories under CoT prompting, collects their final answers, and selects the answer with highest marginal agreement (majority vote) rather than relying on one greedy chain; experiments show large accuracy gains across arithmetic and commonsense benchmarks (e.g., GSM8K, SVAMP, AQuA, StrategyQA, ARC-challenge).

result.text: The paper addresses the practical failure modes of Expected Improvement (EI) and its variants in Bayesian optimization, where acquisition values often underflow to zero in many regions as observations, dimensionality, constraints, or parallel evaluations increase, leading to poor and inconsistent optimization performance. The key insight is that these failures are largely numerical rather than conceptual: taking a numerically stable transformation (logarithm) of the EI-style acquisition functions preserves their optima (exactly or approximately) while avoiding vanishing values and other pathologies that hinder optimization algorithms. The authors introduce the LogEI family—log-domain reformulations of EI, Expected Hypervolume Improvement (EHVI), and their constrained, noisy, and parallel extensions—derive analytic and approximate expressions that maintain equivalent maximizers, and implement them within standard optimization routines. Empirically, LogEI variants substantially improve optimization reliability and performance over canonical EI formulations and surprisingly match or surpass several recent state-of-the-art acquisition functions, underscoring the critical role of numerical stability in acquisition optimization.

args.text: We propose keyed invertible activation scrambling (KIAS): insert a few lightweight, key-conditioned linear maps (e.g., orthogonal/permutation-plus-sign flips) at bottleneck layers so that, without the secret inverse applied inside a TEE, intermediate features are systematically scrambled and the public model outputs near-random predictions, while a compact seed regenerates the inverses on the fly for authorized use. Unlike storing a sparse set of critical weights, generating the transforms via a cryptographic PRF enables frequent key rotation and eliminates a static secret payload, making fine-tuning or model surgery far less effective at recovering functionality. To support ownership verification, we integrate a passport-aware normalization branch whose responses are conditioned on the same key, and pair it with DeepAuth-style key samples that elicit distinctive logit patterns under the correct inverse, enabling both white- and black-box authentication. KIAS thus unifies active protection (key-gated functionality) with robust ownership proofs while keeping inference overhead minimal for authorized users.

result.text: This paper tackles the problem of crafting transferable adversarial perturbations for complex natural scenes containing multiple semantically related objects, where prior attacks have largely focused on single-object images and single-object classifiers. result.text: The paper addresses the limitation that graph neural networks using polynomial spectral filters rely on a fixed, hand-chosen polynomial basis whose suitability strongly affects performance, and asks whether one can learn or compute an optimal basis from data and graph structure. The key insight is that (1) by parametrizing the space of orthonormal polynomial bases via recurrence relations from Favard’s theorem, one can learn a flexible, data-adaptive orthonormal basis (FavardGNN), and (2) the previously deemed “unsolvable” optimal-basis problem can be formulated and solved directly for a given graph and node features to yield an optimal polynomial basis (OptBasisGNN). Methodologically, FavardGNN learns basis recurrence coefficients together with filter coefficients to span all orthonormal polynomial bases for spectral filtering, while OptBasisGNN computes the optimal basis tailored to the graph Laplacian and signal to minimize approximation error of the target filter; both models are validated empirically to outperform fixed-basis polynomial GNNs.

result.text: The paper tackles fast, high-quality 3D object generation from multi-view or single-image inputs without requiring 3D supervision, focusing on probabilistic modeling of unseen object parts and sharp texture synthesis. The key insight is to integrate a transformer-based 3D large reconstruction model that represents scenes as a triplane NeRF and performs denoising in the 3D reconstruction-rendering loop, so multi-view diffusion noise can be removed in a geometry-aware manner. The method trains this model on large-scale multi-view image datasets using only image reconstruction losses, and uses the trained model to denoise noisy multi-view images (or single-image-conditioned noises) via NeRF reconstruction and differentiable rendering, enabling single-stage 3D generation in ~30s on a single A100 GPU. result.text: The paper addresses how to separate aleatoric (data) and epistemic (model) uncertainty in large language models to improve reliability and interpretability when inputs are ambiguous or under-specified. The key insight is that generating and conditioning on multiple plausible input clarifications turns input-driven ambiguity into measurable aleatoric variability while residual disagreement across clarifications reflects epistemic uncertainty, enabling a decomposition analogous to Bayesian neural networks. The method, called input clarification ensembling, automatically produces a set of clarifying reformulations of a prompt, queries a pre-trained LLM on each clarified input, and ensembles the resulting predictions to compute separate aleatoric and epistemic components; experiments on several language tasks show this yields accurate and reliable uncertainty estimates.

The paper tackles the challenge of sample-efficient reinforcement learning across both online interaction and offline (fixed-dataset) settings, where prior methods excelled at one but not both. The key insight is that model-based policy and value improvement can be applied offline to existing transitions by reanalyzing and generating improved training targets without new environment interactions, unifying learning across data regimes. They implement this with Reanalyse—an operator that uses a learned model to perform planning and produce stronger targets on stored data—and integrate it into MuZero to create MuZero Unplugged, which learns from demonstrations or arbitrary replay buffers without special offline adaptations. Empirically, this single algorithm achieves state-of-the-art performance on RL Unplugged offline benchmarks and standard online Atari, demonstrating effectiveness across data budgets.

result.text: We propose Bio-Token SFDA, a domain-adaptive masked token prediction framework tailored to bioacoustics with long, sparse events. We pretrain on BirdSet using dual teachers—one CQT-based to supply pitch/tonal tokens and one event-segmentation teacher for syllable/onset tokens—and iteratively distill them into a stronger discrete tokenizer and masked token predictor, following the tokenizer–encoder co-evolution paradigm. At deployment on unlabeled target soundscapes, we perform source-free adaptation by enforcing consistency between the model’s token posteriors and the fixed teachers on target audio, while jointly optimizing a multi-scale MAE-style masked reconstruction head with local window attention to stabilize updates under covariate shift. This hybrid token-consistency + reconstruction objective is designed to mitigate the negative transfer observed in prior SFDA baselines and improve species ID and event detection under strong domain shift.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of scaling dataset distillation—specifically trajectory-matching-based methods (MTT)—to large-scale datasets like ImageNet-1K, where prior approaches fail due to excessive memory use and poor convergence with many classes. The key insight is that the unrolled gradient used by MTT can be computed exactly with constant memory complexity, enabling a ~6x reduction in memory footprint, and that class-rich datasets benefit from a novel soft label assignment to improve convergence. Methodologically, the authors derive a constant-memory procedure to compute the unrolled SGD gradient, integrate a soft-label scheme for per-class synthetic images, and apply this at scale to distill ImageNet-1K up to 50 images per class on a single GPU. The resulting algorithm achieves new state-of-the-art distilled-data performance on ImageNet-1K—using only 4.2% of the original data with a 5.9% accuracy gap to full-data training and an 18.2% absolute gain over prior SOTA.

result.text: The paper tackles the computational intractability of the Projection Robust Wasserstein (PRW) distance—a robust variant of the Wasserstein distance designed to compare high-dimensional probability measures but hindered by a non-convex, non-smooth optimization formulation. result.text: We propose an adaptive guard-prefix controller that, for each incoming prompt, synthesizes a minimal defensive suffix conditioned on prompt features and cheap side-signals, and is trained in a min–max game against a population of jailbreak generators spanning search-based black-box attacks, token-level trigger attacks, and output-filter–evasive cipher encoders. Unlike fixed, one-size-fits-all prompt-level defenses, the controller dynamically composes defense primitives—refusal scaffolds, paraphrastic inoculation, or learned information bottlenecks—under a utility-aware objective that penalizes overblocking and latency to preserve benign performance. Trained with curriculum and population-based adversaries and evaluated under attack-aware methodology and defended-LLM benchmarks, the approach targets robustness to adaptive black-box and token-level jailbreaks as well as moderation-bypassing ciphers at comparable utility. Additionally, a lightweight paraphrase-smoothing check around the chosen suffix provides an empirical per-input refusal certificate via concentration bounds, offering probabilistic guarantees against residual jailbreaks.

result.text: Communication-Aware Broken Scaling for MoE: we propose a two-resource scaling law for sparse transformers that jointly models compute and interconnect as coupled, smoothly broken power laws, yielding actionable predictions of when training or serving becomes bandwidth-limited. args.text: We propose LongVID-CF, a counterfactual long-form video benchmark that tests whether multimodal LLMs can perform do-style causal reasoning over hour-scale narratives rather than just retrieval or ordering. The core idea is to programmatically create counterfactual pairs of long videos by minimally intervening on causal segments (e.g., swap outcomes, mute/shift disambiguating audio cues, or reorder cause–effect snippets) while holding surrounding context fixed, then pose paired predictive/explanatory/counterfactual questions that require reasoning across distant segments. Concretely, we extend synthetic manipulation to targeted causal interventions, adapt automated across-time QA generation to paired worlds, and measure minimal sufficient temporal windows via temporal certificates; evaluation on curated long YouTube videos reports answer accuracy, intervention localization, and counterfactual consistency across original/edited pairs. This setup complements prior diagnostic skills by scaling counterfactual testing to long horizons and revealing whether models can maintain/update world state over time, closing a gap left by existing long-video and perception benchmarks.

args.text: We propose decision-aware active learning for neural PDE operators that explicitly targets downstream control performance rather than surrogate accuracy. At each round, we train a compact, quality-aware decision surrogate of the PDE-constrained control problem and use it to estimate the expected reduction in control regret from acquiring candidate simulations, selecting batches that maximally improve the induced control policy. The operator learner (e.g., FNO) is updated on the acquired data, and the surrogate is co-refined, enabling fast, stable bilevel acquisition that prioritizes decision-relevant regions of the parameter and boundary-condition space. result.text: The paper addresses the vulnerability of deep neural networks to backdoor attacks, noting that existing methods use uniform, reusable triggers that are detectable by defenses. Its key insight is to make triggers input-aware and diverse so that each poisoned input carries a distinct, nonreusable trigger, which defeats trigger-aggregation and verification defenses. The method trains an input-conditioned trigger generator optimized with a diversity loss and a cross-trigger test to enforce nonreusability, then embeds these varied triggers during poisoning so the model learns the backdoor while conventional defenses and inspection tools fail to find a common pattern. Experiments across datasets and attack scenarios show high attack effectiveness and robustness against state-of-the-art defenses, demonstrating the stealthiness of the approach.

result.text: The paper addresses why value baselines help on-policy stochastic policy gradient methods and closes theoretical gaps explaining their empirical benefits, particularly for natural policy gradient (NPG). The key insight is that baselines do not primarily work by reducing variance of gradient estimates—in fact variance can remain unbounded—but instead by tempering the aggressiveness of policy updates, which prevents optimal actions' probabilities from vanishing and ensures sufficient exploration. Methodologically, the authors prove that with a state-value baseline the expected NPG progress satisfies a stochastic non-uniform Łojasiewicz inequality and that the baseline guarantees almost-sure prevention of action-probability collapse, yielding global O(1/t) convergence to the optimal policy; empirical experiments corroborate that controlling update aggressiveness, not variance, explains the baseline’s utility.

result.text: The paper addresses multimodal fake news detection, aiming to overcome shallow fusion of modalities and insufficient modeling of cross-modal inconsistencies. Its key insight is to mimic diverse human "reading habits" to guide deeper, cognition-aware fusion of multimodal features and to explicitly reason about semantic coherence and deviation between modalities (including user comments) to expose inconsistencies indicative of falsehood. The proposed Multi-Reading Habits Fusion Reasoning (MRHFR) network implements a cognition-aware fusion layer that learns dependencies among visual, textual, and other modal representations according to three distilled reading habits, and a coherence-constraint reasoning layer that measures semantic consistency between comments and each modality and constrains unimodal-induced deviations from the multimodal content. Experiments on two public datasets show MRHFR improves detection performance and offers a new paradigm for capturing multimodal inconsistencies.

result.text: The paper addresses learning directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) from observational data by providing a continuous, differentiable acyclicity characterization that improves detection and optimization compared to prior methods. The key insight is to exploit the nilpotency of DAG adjacency matrices via a log-determinant (log-det) based acyclicity function defined over a domain of M-matrices (to handle asymmetry), yielding an exact, differentiable certificate that has stronger sensitivity to large cycles, better-behaved gradients, and much faster evaluation in practice. The method, called DAGMA, replaces augmented Lagrangian approaches with a central-path-like scheme where each iterate solves an unconstrained objective regularized by the log-det acyclicity term and the limit of this central path yields a guaranteed DAG; empirical results on linear and nonlinear SEMs show substantial speed-ups and lower structural Hamming distances versus state-of-the-art methods.

The key insight is that computing routing scores on a low-dimensional hypersphere mitigates this collapse by decoupling routing similarity from high-dimensional magnitude and promoting more uniform, stable token-expert assignments. Its key insight is that explicitly modeling dialogue discourse relations and injecting symbolic knowledge from knowledge graphs together provide complementary structure and background context that improve emotion understanding. The proposed SKIER method parses dialogues into structured discourse graphs (improved via transfer learning) and integrates diverse symbolic knowledge-graph relations to produce knowledge-enhanced utterance features, which are then used for emotion prediction. result.text: The paper tackles how to bring the rich semantic understanding of Large Language Models (LLMs) to Text-Attributed Graphs (TAGs) while retaining the computational efficiency of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Its key insight is that carefully tuned LLMs can provide both fine-grained local semantics and global structural cues for graphs, and that a layer-adaptive, multi-scale contrastive distillation can effectively transfer these complementary signals into a compact GNN. The proposed LinguGKD framework first performs TAG-oriented instruction tuning to align LLM outputs with graph-specific tasks, then applies multi-granularity contrastive objectives that match node-, subgraph- and graph-level representations between LLM and GNN layers, enabling a distilled GNN to inherit semantic richness without heavy compute. Empirically, distilled GNNs produced by LinguGKD outperform prior distillation methods and often match or beat larger teachers and more complex GNNs while remaining much more efficient.

result.text: The paper tackles automated EEG-based seizure detection and classification, focusing on three gaps in prior work: modeling EEG's non-Euclidean spatiotemporal structure, improving performance on rare seizure types, and providing quantitative interpretability for seizure localization. The key insight is that graph neural networks (GNNs) can better capture electrode geometry or dynamic brain connectivity in EEGs and that self-supervised pre-training—predicting the next time period’s preprocessed signals—boosts downstream detection/classification performance and helps rare-class learning. The method builds EEG graphs (geometry- or connectivity-based), trains GNNs with a self-supervised next-step signal prediction objective before supervised fine-tuning, and introduces a quantitative interpretability metric to evaluate localization ability. Evaluated on a large public dataset, the approach outperforms prior methods on detection (AUROC 0.875) and classification (weighted F1 0.749), notably improving rare seizure classification and precise localization of focal seizures.

result.text: The paper addresses the lack of realistic datasets for predicting hardware performance of complete tensor programs—i.e., full computational graphs of ML workloads—on accelerators, which limits the ability of compilers and autotuners to optimize end-to-end models. The authors introduce TpuGraphs, a dataset of computational graphs paired with compilation configurations and measured execution times on TPUs, providing orders-of-magnitude more and much larger graphs than previous benchmarks to enable graph-level performance prediction research. result.text: RhythmAlign proposes a plug-and-play guidance layer for video-conditioned music diffusion that enforces multi-timescale temporal alignment and phrasing without retraining. We realize this as posterior inference with a frozen denoiser: the alignment cost c(x,y) is backpropagated through the diffusion steps to steer samples, while explicit timing embeddings provide controllable durations and tempo ramps. This aims to improve beat-phase lock and scene-level musical structure over long horizons with small runtime overhead and remains compatible with few-step samplers.
